en: The *Śrīrāmajaya* is the *Paribhāṣenduśekhara*.
Having bowed to the Mother, Śiva, and Brahman, the wise Nāgeśa composes the *Paribhāṣenduśekhara* for the easy understanding of beginners, after having examined the fourfold *anubandhas*.

In this Pāṇinian system, those paribhāṣās which were merely verbal injunctions (*vācanika*) in the ancient grammatical systems, but are established here by means of *jñāpaka* (indicatory evidence) and logical reasoning (*nyāya*), and are recorded in the Bhāṣya and Vārttika, shall now be explained.
[This begins] the section concerning the purpose of establishing the status of the science [of grammar].
Now, since two *ṇ* sounds are employed in the two sūtras *laṇ* and *aiuṇ*, there arises uncertainty and a lack of determination regarding rules that mention *aṇ* or *iṇ*; therefore, he says:
The specific application [of a rule] is understood from its explanation; for a rule is not considered non-definitive simply because it gives rise to doubt. (Paribhāṣā 1)

The meaning is this: because the understanding—that is, the certainty—of a specific [meaning] consisting of one of the alternative senses arises from an interpretation (*vyākhyāna*) performed by the learned (*śiṣṭa*), a treatise (*śāstra*) that is indeterminate due to doubt is a non-characteristic (*alakṣaṇa*), since it does not lead to practice; for a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) must appropriately produce a definitive determination (*nirṇaya*). To the extent that the goal is the successful accomplishment of practice free from doubt, it is understood here in this treatise that there is no dependence on any cause other than interpretation, since doubt is removed by the teacher’s usage (*vyavahāra*) in the form of ambiguous utterances.

Therefore, in order to avoid this [objection], it is clearly stated in the Bhāṣya on the *laṇ* sūtra that the term *aṇ* is used in the preceding [sūtra] and the term *iṇ* is used in the following [sūtra]. 1.

Regarding that, he states two positions concerning technical terms (*saṃjñā*) and interpretive rules (*paribhāṣā*): "Technical terms and interpretive rules are according to their enunciation" (*yathoddeśaṃ saṃjñā paribhāṣam*); [or] "Technical terms and interpretive rules are at the time of the operation" (*kāryakālaṃ saṃjñā paribhāṣam*). (Paribhāṣā 2)
"Not overstepping the instruction" means according to the instruction; "instruction" (uddeśa) refers to teaching (upadeśa) or place (deśa),
and this [term] is derived from the locative case as its instrument.

In whatever context (*deśa*) a rule is taught, linguistic usage throughout the entire treatise proceeds by means of the understanding of the sentence-meaning in that very context, through the apprehension of word-potency (*śakti*), and through the apprehension of the meaning of technical definitions (*paribhāṣā*). Here, "context" (*deśa*) refers specifically to the time of utterance. This position—found in the *īdūdeddvivacanaṃ pragṛhyam* sūtra—is intended for a student who grasps the literal text and is satisfied merely by the knowledge that "once the meaning of each respective sentence has been understood, some purpose will be served by this [rule]."

However, some maintain that in the domain of technical definitions (*paribhāṣā*), regarding the comprehension of the meaning of sentences such as "in that [context]" (*tasmin*), when one considers whether the locative case indication applies or not, and all those respective rules (*vidhi*) are brought to mind, a restriction (*niyama*) is established through syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) by postulating a distinction in grammatical function (*guṇabheda*) for the sake of all those respective operations (*saṃskāra*).
In the view that the time of operation is the same as the time of application (*kāryakālapakṣa*), however, the distinction is that even the three subsequent chapters (*tripādī*) are brought to mind.

Intending exactly this, it is stated in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra "ṣaṣṭhīsthāne" that "authority (adhikāra) is of three kinds: one kind, residing in a single location, illuminates the entire treatise, just as 'a well-kindled lamp illuminates the entire house.'"
By the word *adhikāra*, a *paribhāṣā* (technical rule) is also expressed because it exists for the sake of another;
Kaiyaṭa states that some [rules] are of the nature of *paribhāṣās*.
Just as a lamp illuminates an entire house by means of its light, so too does this [rule] benefit the entire treatise by means of generating its own cognition; such is the intended meaning.
And this commentary is common to both positions,
since in both cases it is understood from its syntactic unity with the specific passage.

In this regard, there is this much distinction: when a *paribhāṣā* (metarule) is enunciated, one should conceptually attribute a distinct nature (*ātmabheda*) to it within the cognition of all the operational rules (*vidhisūtra*), and thus [understand] the *paribhāṣās* as forming a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) with them.
As it has been stated by Kaiyaṭa on the sūtra *kiṅiti ca*:
"When primary elements are brought together for their own refinement (*saṃskāra*) at the point of enunciation, they bring about a differentiation of their subordinate qualities (*guṇabheda*)."
However, at the time of operation, there is syntactic unity with the specific injunctions through the cognition of the *paribhāṣā*.
Here, by the phrase "situated in one place" (*ekadeśastha*), he precludes its being situated in those various places even when it is present in the cognition regarding each instance;
just as, for example, although speakers travel to many different places for the sake of their business, they do not acquire the designation of belonging to those respective places.
However, this is merely a conventional designation (vyavahāra) based on its origin in that region;

likewise, because prohibitive statements also require a specific object of prohibition, they are construed as forming a single syntactical unit (ekavākyatā) with an injunction, and thus they are treated as *paribhāṣās* due to their similarity to [actual] *paribhāṣās*. In the rule "kiṅiti ca," there is a single syntactical unit with the exclusion (*paryudāsa*); even in the case of a simple negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*), the convention of being a single syntactical unit is used simply because there is a comprehension of the sentence-meaning together with that [injunction].
In the *kāryakāla* (time-of-operation) view of the science of grammar (*saṃjñāśāstra*), however, there is no separate comprehension of the sentence-meaning;
rather, it occurs only together with the rule of the specific location (*pradeśavākya*).

For this very reason, with respect to the rule "after *a-soma*" (*aso-māt*), the substitution of *m* (*mutva*) and so forth is not considered non-established (*asiddha*) because [the former] has entered into a single syntactic unit (*ekavākyatāpanna*) with the rule "for *aṇ* which is not a *pragṛhya*" (*aṇo 'pragṛhyasya*).
Since the status of being *asiddha* (not established) serves a functional purpose (*kāryārthatayā*), its application occurs only after the knowledge of that function;

and since the knowledge of the function exists only at the specific location [of the rule], the *asiddha* status residing in that location is not grasped by the prior mention [of the subsequent rule].

Thus, it is only after the cognition of that [prior rule] that the realization of conflict (*virodha*) arises; this is the seed for the application of the *vipratiṣedha* sūtra based on the priority of that [subsequent rule].

For this very reason, it is stated in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *adaso māt* under the view that grammatical operations take place at the time of application (*kāryakālapakṣa*): "The designation *pragṛhya* applies only after [vowels] beginning with *a*."

However, regarding the technical designations (*saṃjñā*) such as *bha* which fall under the jurisdiction of the rule *ā kaḍārād ekā saṃjñā*, only the *yathoddeśa* (nominally existent) view applies; thus, the relationship between the sublated and the sublater is determined solely by their relative position within that specific section.

Since the acquisition of the expressive power (*śaktigraha*) for these designations such as *pada* occurs there, their linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) extends even to the *tripādī* (the final three chapters).

Therefore, in the rule *pūrvatrāsiddham*, having raised the objection that the *paribhāṣās* do not apply within the *tripādī*, it is said that the matter was resolved by resorting to the *kāryakāla* (the view that rules take effect at the time the operation is to be performed) theory;
whereas the *yathoddeśa* (the view that rules remain where they are stated) theory is [discussed] in the Bhāṣya on the section concerning the *pragṛhya* designation.
Regarding the phrase *kāryakālam*, the meaning is that "it is brought [to the time] by the operation" (*kāryeṇa kālyate*), that is, it is brought into proximity with its own application.

In other words, for the sake of its own refinement (*saṃskāra*), the operations bring about the implication (*ākṣepa*) of those technical rules (*paribhāṣā*) which are marked by their respective indicators (*liṅga*).

For this very reason, in the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the rule *pūrvatrāsiddham*, having raised the objection that because the three quarters (*tripādī*) are not established (*asiddha*), the technical rules located in the first seven chapters and a quarter (*sapādasaptādhyāyī*) would not apply there, [the author] states: "Even though this [rule] is not established there..."

Having stated that this [point] is established here, when the question "How so? is asked—intending that even by that much there is still no establishment—it is said: "The technical names (*saṃjñā*) and rules of interpretation (*paribhāṣā*) are present at the time of the operation (*kāryakālam*); they should be regarded as being present wherever the operation occurs. And in the view that the time of the operation is the time of application, in rules such as *aṅgasya hrasvāt*, [the paribhāṣās] "from that which follows" (*tasmād ity uttarasya*) and "when that which is specified is the antecedent" (*tasminn iti nirdiṣṭe pūrvasya*)...

When both paribhāṣās [“pūrvasya” and “tasminniti nirdiṣṭe pūrvasya”] are simultaneously applicable, the statement from the Bhāṣya on the sūtra "tasmin"— "in the case of a dual mention, the mention in the ablative case is stronger"—
would be inconsistent; for it would be impossible to justify the phrase "due to being subsequent" (paratvāt) since both rules occupy the same location.
And this should be stated clearly as Kaiyaṭa’s view on the rule *iko guṇavṛddhī*;
for there is no fault in resorting to the "priority based on the order of recitation" (*pāṭhakṛtaparatva*) found within the *Aṣṭādhyāyī* in the case of the rule concerning conflict (*vipratiṣedha*),
since that [priority] does not disappear merely because of the *kāryakāla* (time-of-operation) perspective.
Because there is no distinction between the two positions regarding the production of cognition within specific locations;
for even in that position, it is impossible for an insentient scripture to leave its own location and travel to another place,
nor does it abandon its own location by producing cognition in people such as ourselves.

For this very reason, Kaiyaṭa, in his commentary on the *bhāṣya* regarding that sūtra (*tasmin*), states: "The status of being subsequent (*paratva*) is the determinant [of application] with respect to the recitation of the sūtras. However, Kaiyaṭa's commentary on the sūtra *iko guṇavṛddhī* is intended for that specific context alone; otherwise, since all grammatical rules exist for the sake of usage and thus constitute only a single part of the actual usage, there would be no status of being subsequent anywhere at all.

Furthermore, according to Kaiyaṭa’s interpretation of the sūtra *kiṅati ca*, if the injunction-sūtras (*vidhisūtra*) were to exist in their own location (*yathoddeśapakṣa*), their status as "subsequent" (*paratva*) would be obstructed by their proximity to the location of the paribhāṣās.

In that case, in forms such as *vṛkṣebhyaḥ*, the substitution of *et* by the rule *bahuvacane jhalyet* would be preempted by the rule *supi ca* due to its subsequent position, and thus such rules would be rendered null; so, enough of this.

The indicatory letters (anubandhas) bear their respective names; regarding them, because there arises doubt as to whether they are parts [of the word] or not parts, it is said: "The indicatory letters are non-final" (Paribhāṣā 3).
The meaning is that they are manifold and partless.
For whatever is partless is always perceived there;
however, this [object] is not so.
Since that which is to be enjoined (*vidheya*) is never seen to be identical with its own meaning,
in cases such as *śit-kid-ādi*, a compound should be understood through the metaphorical attribution (*āropa*) of being a constituent part (*avayavatva*) to what is proximate.

As for [the rule] *vuṇ-chaṇ-kaṭha-ādi*, the fact that an operation conditioned by the marker *ṇ* applies only to the preceding element and so forth must be determined through [traditional] commentary (*vyākhyāna*).
In the rule "halantyam," the word *antya* (final) denotes that which is in proximity to what follows.
In reality, however, they are absolute. (Paribhāṣā 4)
This alone is logical, because it is observed as such in the treatises and is not observed otherwise;
for a partless entity such as a crow is perceived in connection with houses, trees, and so forth, through a relationship of a single class.
This is certainly not so;
for in this way, even the *bahuvrīhi* compound is established by logical necessity,
and there is no need for figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in the word "beginning" (*ādi*).
Furthermore, if [the suffix] were partless (anavayava), then in forms such as *ṇaśaka*, the substitution of *i* for *ṇa* and so on would not occur,
because it would lack the status of being the initial element of a suffix (*pratyayāditva*); moreover, the letter *c* in *dadhnac* would result in being redundant.
And this is clear in the Bhāṣya on the rule *tasya lopaḥ*;
for there it is stated:
"It is more logical that the *anubandhas* are entirely external"—this is the direction [of the argument].

But if [the substitute] is unitary, then by the very fact that it is not multiliteral (*anekāl*), the status of *auś* and other such substitutes as being replacements for the whole (*sarvādeśa*) is established; thus, the mention of *śit* in the rule "anekāl" would be redundant. To this, he says: "Multiliterality is not caused by an indicatory letter (*anubandha*). (Paribhāṣā 5)
The inclusion of the marker *ś* (in *śit*) is itself the indicator (*jñāpaka*); by this, [the substitution] in rules such as "arvaṇas tṛ" is not a replacement for the whole word (*sarvādeśa*).

However, in the case of [substitutions] beginning with *ḍ*, since there would be no status as an *anubandha* without being a replacement for the whole word, the result is established through the sequence [of operations].

But even so, in the case of "avadātaṃ mukham" (a bright face), after the elision of *p* (*palopa*) and the subsequent substitution of *ā* (*ātva*), the prohibition of the designation *ghu* for the root *dāp* would not apply; for while *daip* contains the letter *p*, the condition of "not ending in a vowel" (*anejanta*) is not met, and since the *p* disappears after the elision, this [root] lacks the quality of being *dāp*. Therefore, he says: "The quality of not ending in a vowel is not caused by an indicatory letter (*anubandha*). (Paribhāṣā 6)

The grammatical indication "udīcām āṅaḥ" is the indicator (jñāpaka) for this [rule]. By the rule "ādeca upadeśe," the substitution of *ā* is prescribed for a root ending in *ai* or *au* as it is taught; however, if the letter *ṅ* were present, there would be an absence of the status of ending in *ai* or *au*, and consequently, since the substitution of *ā* would not apply, that [indication] would be inconsistent.
Furthermore, since it lacks the status of being a verbal root (*dhātu*) in this state, how could there be *ātva* (the substitution of *ā* for *e*);
for in that case, the term "of a verbal root" (*dhātoḥ*) is no longer applicable. This is explained in detail elsewhere.
And this is clear from the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *dādhāghvadāp*.
But even so, one might object that by the rule *vāsarūpa*, there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of the suffix *aṇ* occurring in certain instances; therefore, he says:
"Dissimilarity [of form] is not caused by an indicatory letter (*anubandha*). (Paribhāṣā 7)

The rule "dadāti-dadhātyor vibhāṣā" (Pāṇini 3.1.139), which prescribes an option for the suffix *śa* that would otherwise be superseded by *ṇa*, serves as the indicator (*jñāpaka*) for this [principle].
Consequently, it is clear from the Bhāṣya on the "vāsarūpa" sūtra that *aṇ* does not apply in forms such as "godaḥ."

But surely, if "number" (saṃkhyā) were taken [as the meaning], only *bahu* and the others would be included, because it is established that context determines the denotation, according to the maxim: "Between the technical (kṛtrima) and the non-technical (akṛtrima), the operation applies to the technical term."

And since in the present context there exists a topical section (prakaraṇa) consisting of the knowledge that the designation "number" (saṅkhyā-saṃjñā) applies to *bahu* and so forth, and not to the "one," "two," and so on well-known in common usage, he says:
"In this [context], both ways of understanding apply. (Paribhāṣā 8)
In this treatise,
the prohibition "of a numeral [ending] other than one ending in *ati* or *śat*" (*saṅkhyāyā atiśadantāyāḥ*) is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) of this [rule];
for there exists no artificial (*kṛtrima*) numeral that ends in *tya* or *śat*.

Consequently, in rules such as *kartari karmavyatihāre*, *kaṇvameghebhyaḥ karaṇe*, and *vipratiṣiddhaṃ cānadhikaraṇe*, there is an understanding of worldly actions, substances, and so forth. In that regard, in some cases there is an understanding of both [the primary and secondary meanings], while in others there is an understanding of only the non-artificial (akṛtrima) meaning.
In the matter of "only the technical (kṛtrima) [term]," the only recourse is an interpretation that follows the actual usage of the system (lakṣyānusārin).
For this very reason, by the word *āmreḍita*, only the technical term is understood, and not merely that which is uttered twice or thrice.
This is clear from the Bhāṣya on the rule defining the technical name for number (*saṅkhyā-saṃjñā-sūtra*).

As for the claim that— according to the maxim of the artificial and the non-artificial (*kṛtrimākṛtrima-nyāya*)— the purpose of technical rules (*saṃjñāśāstra*) in my system is to serve as restrictive rules (*niyama*), meaning "by this word only these [terms] are [to be understood]," that is not correct; for since those rules can be taken as injunctions (*vidhi*) by virtue of conveying the power (*śakti*) of words not previously grasped, it is inappropriate to treat them as restrictive rules.
The assertion that "all words denote all meanings" is also made from the perspective of a yogi,
not from our own perspective,
because it is impossible for us specifically to know the meaning of every word.
However, it has been established elsewhere that general cognition (sāmānyajñāna) is useful for the arising of [specific] knowledge.

Now, one might object that in forms such as *adhyetā* and *śayitā*, there would be a prohibition of *guṇa* substitution because the roots √iṅ and √śīṅ are marked with the indicatory letter Ṅ; therefore, he says: "For an element undergoing an operation is not taken as the cause [of that very operation]. (Paribhāṣā 9)
The grammatical indication (jñāpaka) in the rule *sthaṇḍilācchayitari* serves as evidence for this [interpretation],
namely that [the suffix] "undergoes the grammatical operation" (*kāryamanubhavan*) in order to establish forms such as *ūrṇunaviṣati*.
For in this case, by the rule *dvirvacane 'ci*, there is reduplication of the element *nu*.

Otherwise, because the word "asanyaṅoḥ" ends in the genitive case, the suffix *san* would be the object of the operation (*kāryin*), and since *iṭ* would not be the cause for the doubling [of the root], that rule [Pāṇini 6.1.2] would not apply.

In reality, however, since the distinction between the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) and the instrumental cause (*nimittakāraṇa*) is well-established in all worldly systems, and since this [distinction] is not accepted as such [here], this point is not something to be proven by an *jñāpaka*.
For this very reason, the particle *ha* has been employed.
For that [word *tattvena*] indicates that the reason is established when there is no recourse to its actual meaning (*tattva*);
this has been suggested in the Bhāṣya on the rule *dvirvacane 'ci*.
Now, an objection is raised: in forms such as *praṇidāpayati*, the designation *ghu* prescribed for the root *dā* (in the form *dā*) would not apply to the root *dāp*. To this, he says:
"That which is an augment is included by the mention of that [to which it is attached], being subordinate to it. (Paribhāṣā 10)

The meaning is this: that which is intended for which a grammatical operation (*āgama*) is prescribed becomes subordinate (*guṇībhūta*) to it; since it is taught by the treatise as being a constituent part (*avayava*) of that [operation], it is therefore grasped, understood, and denoted by the word that grasps, understands, and expresses that [operation].
In this context, the phrase "becoming subordinate to it" constitutes the statement of the seed (*bīja*).
In common worldly usage as well, when Devadatta has an extra limb, he is perceived through the mention of "Devadatta" only as qualified by that [limb].
Because of the statement "that for which [the suffix] is prescribed," in examples such as *praṇidārayati*, the substitution of *ghu* does not apply to the element *dā*.
This [substitution] is non-obligatory (*anitya*) due to the force of the rule prescribing the augment *muk* in the sūtra *ānemuk*.

Otherwise, in cases such as *apacamānaḥ*, when the *muk* (elision) of the vowel *a* occurs, it would be evident that this paribhāṣā is useless, because the *savarṇadīrgha* (vowel lengthening) would apply to the resulting specific form.
Consequently, in forms like *didīye*, there would be no application of *yaṇ* substitution and so forth; and in forms like *jahāra*, the rule *āta au ṇalaḥ* would not apply.

Nor should it be asked how another phoneme can be a constituent part (*avayava*) of a phoneme such as *a* or *ā*; for its status as a constituent is established by explicit scriptural statement (*vacana*).
Furthermore, it should be understood that this status as a constituent culminates in a similarity [of form].

Nor should it be said that this [rule] does not apply when *varṇa* is understood from the aforementioned indicator (*jñāpaka*); for if that were so, the statement in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *āne muk*— which raises the objection that in the form *apacamānaḥ*, the accent prescribed by *tāsyanudāttet* would not occur if the meaning were "muk is an augment of a portion of the *aṅga* ending in ā," and then replies that it will be grasped as being part of the original instruction (*upadeśa*) by virtue of being included in that term— would become inconsistent.

Furthermore, regarding the meaning of the rule *ṅamo ṅamuṭ*—"after a short vowel, the augment *ṅamuṭ* follows a *ṅam*-ending word-part"—one might raise the objection that in cases such as *akurvan āste*, since the augment *ṅamuṭ* would follow the *ṅam* (the *n* of *kurvan*), the substitution of *ṇ* (*ṇatva*) would result.

Anticipating this, [the author] invokes the maxim *yadāgamāḥ* ("that which is an augment is like the original element"), whereby even the initial *n* of *an* is included by the term "end of a word" (*padānta*).
Consequently, the prohibition "of the end of a word" (*padāntasya*) applies, and thus [the objection is resolved] by this [maxim].

Otherwise, the *bhāṣya* on the *sūtra* "aṅamuṭ" would be inconsistent with its intention that, by way of a metarule (*paribhāṣā*), the specific nature of the augment (*āgama*) is also conveyed [by the term denoting the original element].
Furthermore, if the substitution of *apara* (short *a*) were applied to the *guṇa* and other elements, one would have to accept that the *guṇa* and so forth are qualified by the letter *r*;
otherwise, the restriction that "the *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* substitutes for the vowel *ṛ* are only *ar* and *ār*" would not hold.
And this [rule] would not be consistent if it did not apply when there is the apprehension of a *varṇa* (phoneme).
For this very reason, the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *radābhyām* states: "There is *guṇa*, there is *vṛddhi*."
"The [root] called *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* arises with the letter *repha* (r) at its head.

For this very reason, rules such as "not before *iṭ*" (*neṭi*) and "before that which lacks *iṭ*" (*ṇeraniṭi*) become meaningful. As for the statement "those without an augment have substitutes with an augment," its meaning is as follows: once it is understood that an augment *iṭ* is applied to the *ārdhadhātuka* suffix...

In the case of eternal words (*nitya-śabda*), since the prescribed grammatical operations (*āgama-vidhāna*) would otherwise result in the undesirable consequence of a cognition devoid of the augment *iṭ*, one must assume another sentence based on presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) stating that "the cognition of *iṭ* must be performed.
Thus, just as in the case of substitutes (*ādeśa*), here too there is a transformation of cognition; consequently, there is no loss of eternality.
Furthermore, such a substitution (*ādeśa*) is not what is intended by the term "substitute-like" (*sthānivat*) in the *sūtra*.
Because [the rule] has its utility (*cāritārthya*) when the relationship between the substituendum (*sthānin*) and the substitute (*ādeśa*) is directly taught by Pāṇini 1.1.56;

furthermore, if this were the case, since the operation would proceed solely through the cognition of the substituendum, there would be an inconsistency with the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) that "the augment *aṭ* applies in the state of the vowel *al*.

Regarding the application of the paribhāṣā "of that which is not being specifically pointed out" (*anirdiśyamānasya*) in the context of the status of being a substituendum (*sthānivadbhāva*), one might raise the objection that in the word *tisṛṇām*, after the substitution of *tisṛ* (by Pāṇini 7.2.99), the substitution of *traya-* (by Pāṇini 7.1.53) would apply by virtue of the status of being a substituendum due to the subsequent [rule].
There is no fault [in the objection], because the subsequent Bhāṣya provides a solution according to the principle of "single transition" (*sakṛdgati*).

In rules such as *eruḥ*, since the genitive case denotes the *sthāna* (the element to be replaced), the rule is understood to refer to the entire substitute for the whole complex by virtue of the force of the term *ādeśa* (substitute) itself; thus, when that [term] is included in the *sthānivadbhāva* sūtra, there is no defect.

Even when the relationship between the substituendum (*sthānin*) and the substitute (*ādeśa*) is conceived as inferential, there is no abandonment of the relationship between the substituendum and the substitute as established by direct Vedic revelation (*śrauta*); thus, there is no inconsistency with rules such as *acaḥ parasmin*.
By this, the view that the maxim *yadāgamāḥ* (whatever are augments) is already covered by the rule *sthānivat* is refuted.
All of this is made clear in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *dādhāghvadāp*.
But in this case, in forms such as *udasthāt*, there would result the substitution of the preceding homogeneous vowel by the rule "udaḥ sthā-stambhoḥ pūrvasya" [P. 8.4.61]; therefore, he says:
"Substitutes apply to that which is being pointed out [as the element to be replaced]. (Paribhāṣā 11)
The rule "ṣaṣṭhīsthāne yogā" (P. 1.1.49) is repeated.

Therein, this is the meaning of the second [occurrence]: that which is indicated by a genitive ending—whether it be the actual word being uttered or something of the same class as what is being uttered, or specifically a constituent part of what is being indicated—is connected with its *sthāna* (place/position), that is, with a relationship defined by that *sthāna*.
But the meaning is not that it is being perceived (*pratīyamāna*).
By this, the following is established:
there is no contingency of long vowels (*dīrgha*) becoming substitutes in rules such as *asyacvau*.
It should be stated that there is no fault because they are not being specifically mentioned [as individual instances]; for in the view that the term refers to the genus (*jāti*), there is no defect.

Furthermore, by the prohibition "not after *bhū* or *sudhī*" (*na bhūsudhiyoḥ*), since those words included by the rule of mention (*grahaṇaka-śāstra*) are understood as having the status of being specifically mentioned (*nirdiśyamāna*), there is no fault.

The *ṅit* designation for *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ*, however, is for the purpose of ensuring they are substitutes for the final sound—since the rule "ivarṇāntasya ca śnoḥ" (P. 6.4.77) specifies that they replace the vowels *i* and *u* at the end of verbal roots and the word *bhū*.
The *ṅit* designation for *rīṅ* and *riṅ*, on the other hand, serves merely to clarify the meaning.

By this, the view that the *ṅit*-designation [of the suffixes] serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the non-application of the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) "when a specific letter is mentioned, it denotes itself" is refuted;

for the purpose of the mention of the *ayogavāha* sounds in the sūtra *hayavaraṭ* is stated to be "the application of the rule regarding the final letter [of the preceding element], as in *vṛkṣasttatra*."
This is not the case, as it contradicts the Bhāṣya which states: "There is no need for this [paribhāṣā], for it is already established by the very words 'of that which is being designated'.
By means of this paribhāṣā, there is the communication of the absence of *sthānivadbhāva* for a *tadanta* (ending in that) element as taught by the sūtra *yenavidhiḥ*.
The phrase *yadāgamāḥ* refers to that which has been acquired [by way of an augment]. By this, the formation of forms such as *supadaḥ* and *udasthāt* is established.
Furthermore, by means of this [principle], there is indeed a co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of rules such as *alo 'ntyasya*, which are brought into proximity by their respective individual causes.
There is no relationship of the sublated and the sublator, because there is no contradiction;
nor is there a relationship of subordinate and principal between these two.
Because both [rules] serve the purpose of another, there is no conflict between them;
therefore, in the rule *anekāl śit*, everything indicated by this paribhāṣā is understood to be included.
As for the claim that only the rules *ādeḥ parasya* and *alo 'ntyasya* are its sublaters (*bādhaka*), that is not correct.
"Because this [rule] has been applied (*sañcārita*) in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *pādaḥ pat* with respect to the domain of the rule *udaḥ sthā-*;
nor is this [latter rule] a sublater (*bādhikā*) of these two,
because that would result in those two becoming devoid of scope (*nirviṣayatva-prasaṅga*)," so says Kaiyaṭa on the rule *ti-viṃśateḥ*.
This rule does not apply in the case of an *akaj* suffix,

because by the principle of "becoming like the substitute" (*sthānivadbhāva*) and the principle of "falling in the middle of that" (*tanmadhyapattanyāya*), it produces the grammatical operation precisely for the sake of the understanding of that [original element].
And this [principle] applies even in the case of a genitive in the sense of a constituent part (*avayava-ṣaṣṭhī*).
For this very reason, the substitution of *s* occurs in the rule "tadoḥ saḥ sāu" (Pāṇini 7.2.106), but it does not occur for the *t* of the prefix in the example "atisyaḥ.
Furthermore, the forms *yūyam* and so on apply only to that which ends in the stem *yuṣmad*, etc., as specified by the rule.
However, in cases such as *atiyūya*, it should be understood that [the substitution] applies to the final phoneme (*apṛkta*) which is part of a word containing a prefix (*sopasarga*).
This is clear from the *Bhāṣya* on the sūtras "pādaḥ pat" and "ṣaṣṭhī sthāne".
Now, in cases such as *cetā*, since the short vowel *i* is similar to *a* in terms of its measure (*pramāṇa*), might not *a* also [be substituted] on account of that similarity? To this he says:
"Where there is a multiform similarity, similarity of place (*sthāna*) is more powerful. (Paribhāṣā 12)
This [substitution] is determined by various types of *sthāna* (position), *guṇa* (quality), and *pramāṇa* (measure).

Regarding this, the term *sthāna* is understood through the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of a portion from the rule "ṣaṣṭhī sthāne" (P. 1.1.49); yet, in the subsequent sūtra "sthānentaratamaḥ" (P. 1.1.50), the term *sthāna* is explicitly mentioned again.

This is because that [term], being transformed into the instrumental case (*sthānena*), functions through a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*) to mean: when a substitute arises in place of an original element (*sthānin*), provided such a possibility exists, it must be the most similar [to the original] specifically by way of its position (*sthānataḥ*).
The inclusion of the term *tama* (the superlative suffix) itself indicates proximity (*āntarya*) of many kinds;
"by position" (*sthānataḥ*) means by place of articulation (*sthānena*). Among these, proximity by position is exemplified in the rule *iko yaṇ aci*.

This is well known from such instances as *ityādi*. According to the established principle (*siddhānta*) that "in cases such as *paddanno*, a substitute (*ādeśa*) must be capable of expressing the meaning of the original element (*sthānin*)," that which is capable of expressing a particular meaning is the substitute for that [original]. Therefore, those [substitutes] possess the same meaning and the same phonetic form (*varṇa*) as the original word (*pada*), and so forth.
And [the term] "tṛjvat-kroṣṭuḥ" [is used] by way of quality, as in "avāgghariḥ" and so forth;
and by way of measure, as in "adaso 'seḥ" and so forth.
This is clearly stated in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra "sthāne 'ntaratamaḥ."
Now, one might object that in the word *proḍhavān*, the rule *prādūhoḍheti* would require the substitution of *vṛddhi*; therefore, he says:
"When there is the mention of a meaningful element, an element devoid of meaning is not included. (Paribhāṣā 13)

The basis for abandoning [the principle of] connection when it is possible for a present object to function as a qualifier with respect to a word in the assumption of a specific form is the absence of evidence;

this is clear in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *saṅkhyāyāḥ* (P. 5.4.73), where it is stated that "object" (*artha*) includes even that which is technical (*śāstrīya*), being constructed through imagined positive and negative concomitance (*kalpitānvayavyatireka*).
This is clear from the Bhāṣya on the rule *al-asya* regarding the inclusion of phonemes (*varṇa-grahaṇa*).
For this very reason, the elders (*vṛddhāḥ*) maintain that this [principle] applies specifically to cases where a particular form is mentioned.

It is precisely based on this that it is stated in the Bhāṣya on the rule *yena vidhis* (P. 1.1.72): "A compound ending in a meaningless element (*anarthaka*) is included [in the application of a grammatical operation]."
Furthermore, in the grammatical treatise [Pāṇini’s Aṣṭādhyāyī], in the rule "one's own form" (*svarūpam*), the word *sva* denotes that which belongs to oneself (*ātmīya*),
while the word *rūpa* denotes the actual form (*svarūpa*).
Thus, the meaning of that rule is that both of these constitute the technical name (*saṃjñin*) for the word.
In that context, the meaning (*artha*) is not the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), because it is impossible for it to be assisted by a grammatical operation; rather, it is a qualifier of the word (*śabda*).
And thus, the result is that the word qualified by the meaning is the designatum (*saṃjñin*).
Therefore, it is clear in the Bhāṣya that this technical definition is established.
But even so, in the case of "mahān bhūtaś candramāḥ," the substitution of *ā* by the rule "ānmahataḥ" would result; therefore, he says:
"Between the secondary (gauṇa) and the primary (mukhya), the operation applies to the primary. (Paribhāṣā 14)
That which comes from a quality (*guṇa*) is *gauṇa* (secondary). For example, the referent of the word "cow" (*go*), such as a Vāhīka person, is based on qualities like dullness (*jāḍya*).
Furthermore, even names (*saṃjñā*) and the like that are not [primarily] well-known are understood precisely through the superimposition (*āropa*) of those qualities.

Because it is primary (*pradhāna*), like a face (*mukha*), it is "primary" (*mukhya*), meaning "first. For when a word is employed in a secondary sense (*gauṇa*), it functions by superimposing the primary meaning [onto that secondary one]. Thus, in this context, "secondary-ness" (*gauṇatva*) consists in being unfamiliar and being metaphorical or indicative (*gauṇa-lākṣaṇika*).
Therefore, in examples such as *priyatrayāṇām*, the substitution of *traya-* indeed occurs;
for even though the meaning of the word *tri-* functions as a qualifier of another [word] there, the aforementioned status of being secondary (*gauṇatva*) does not apply.
Furthermore, this principle does not apply to operations concerning nominal stems (*prātipadika*).
However, [the rule] applies only to such a word-operation where the specific form, having been acquired, brings about the specific meaning.

For in cases such as "gaur vāhīkaḥ" (the Vāhīka is an ox), the perception of figurative usage occurs when the fully established form is connected with another word; it does not occur at the time of the formation of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Thus, because it is an internal operation, it is impossible for a previously produced grammatical refinement (*saṃskāra*) to be sublated;
this is the reason for the non-application of the nominal stem operation.
In order to establish forms such as *aśvāśuriḥ*— which means "the offspring of one similar to a father-in-law" (*śvaśura*)— the phrase beginning with "upāttam" (that which is mentioned) is stated.
Nor should it be argued that the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) itself is such [a word],
because while the nominal stem presents its meaning through its status as a nominal stem, it lacks the capacity to present a specific meaning [on its own].

A particle-word (*nipātapada*), however, brings forth the *cādi* group precisely by virtue of being a member of that class; thus, when a grammatical operation is prescribed with reference to that group—as in the rule "before *o*" (*ot*)—this [principle] applies, and there is no fault in cases such as *gobhavatyā*.

In the case of *agnīṣomau māṇavakau*, even though the well-known compound of deities (*devatādvandva*) denoting Agni and Soma refers here to boys who resemble them, the substitution of *ī* (*ītva*) and the substitution of *ṣ* (*ṣatva*) still occur because they are internal (*antaraṅga*). However, in a compound where the words *agni* and *soma* are used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) to mean those who resemble [the deities], or where the meaning is "those named [Agni and Soma]," the substitutions of *ī* and *ṣ* do not occur.
Because in the first case [the word] is figurative or secondary (gauṇa-lākṣaṇika), and in the latter case it is not established [in that sense];

for this very reason, in the example "The boy is Agni-Soma," the rule is intended to prevent the application of the *śatva* substitution according to the principle of the primary and the secondary (*gauṇa-mukhya-nyāya*).

The commentary on the *sūtra* "agneḥ stutstomasomāḥ" is consistent with this view. In expressions such as "gāṃ pāṭhaya" ("teach the cow"), since the primary meaning of the word "cow" cannot be the object of teaching, the speakers perceive its figurative sense at the time of the production of the case-ending (*vibhakti*). Nevertheless, because a non-word (*apada*) is never used, the hearers everywhere [understand] only the word (*pada*).

Since the Bhāṣya employs forms such as "atvaṃ tvaṃ sampadyate," "amahān mahān bhūtaḥ," and "tvadbhavati ṭhaḥ"— thereby applying the substitutes *tvā* and others, as well as lengthening and so forth— it is appropriate to conclude that this maxim pertains specifically to operations concerning words (*padakāryaviṣayatva*).
Otherwise, on the view that *saṃskāra* (grammatical refinement) applies to the sentence as a whole, those [individual word-meanings] would not undergo such refinement.

Furthermore, according to the statement, “When ‘white’ is uttered, the object (*karman*) is indicated, but neither the agent (*kartṛ*) nor the action (*kriyā*) are indicated,” and so forth, in examples such as “Now, Devadatta, bring the black cow here,” everything is indeed indicated: the object is specifically the cow.

By the Bhāṣya on the *arthavat* sūtra, which conveys the meaning "Devadatta alone is the agent" and "the act of driving [cattle] (*abhyāja*) alone is the action," there arises the contingency that when only a *kāraka* (participant in action) or the like is used, all possible actions would be understood by ellipsis.

Therefore, the employment of a word expressive of an action and so forth serves the purpose of restriction (*niyama*). This is intended to mean that, in general, when one intends to express merely the status of being the locus of a result produced by an action...

The meaning obtained is that there is a grammatical justification (*sādhutvānvākhyāna*) for the second and subsequent cases; thus, at the time of connecting them to the act of recitation (*pāṭhana-kriyā*), both the listener and the speaker perceive the word itself as having a secondary meaning (*gauṇārthatva*).
It is on this basis that the verse beginning with "those words whose meanings are manifested" (*abhivyaktapadārthā ye*) also concerns the domain of word-level operations (*padakārya*).
This has been indicated by the author of the Vārttika, while introducing the prohibition for those [words] that function as technical names (*saṃjñā*), in the rule *sarvādīni*.
By the author of the Sūtra, who stated "in the absence of a technical name" (*asaṃjñāyām*) in the rule *pūrvaparā*,
and by the author of the Bhāṣya, who rejected that [rule] on the grounds of its being a descriptive name (*anvarthasaṃjñā*),
this occurs only when there is reliance upon the meaning.

Regarding the statement "in the case of [the bases] *vṛddhi* and *ātva* which are the substrata of words," the meaning of the *Bhāṣya* on the *sūtra* "ot" is that this maxim applies to those substrata of words that possess the capacity for worldly meaning; whereas in the case of substrata of words devoid of that [meaning], the rule does not apply.
This is because, in the *sūtra* "gotaḥ" as heard [in the text], there is the inclusion of a specific form, and thus [the rule] functions according to the aforementioned method.
Since the commentary is that which is to be explained, this is sufficient.
He states an exception to the rule "when there is the mention of a meaningful [element]" (arthavadgrahaṇe):
"Mentions of *an* and *in* cause the application of the rule of 'specification by the final element' (*tadantavidhi*) both with a meaningful [element] and with a meaningless one. (Paribhāṣā 15)

In the Bhāṣya on the rule *yena vidhiḥ*, this [sūtra] is cited in the form of a statement (*vacana*). Consequently, in examples such as *rājñā* and *sāmnā*, there is the elision of the case-ending (*allopa*);
whereas in examples such as *daṇḍī* and *vāgmī*, the restriction (*niyama*) of the rule *inhan* applies.
In examples such as *supayāḥ* and *susrotāḥ*, the lengthening [of the vowel] is established by the rule *atvasantasya*;
and in examples such as *suśarmā* and *suprathimā*, the prohibition of the suffix *ṅīp* by the rule *manaḥ* is also established.

Others, however, argue that because the term *aṅga* (stem) is included in the rule *iṇaḥ ṣīdhvam*—which is formulated to exclude the substitution of *ḍha* in *parivīviṣīdhvam*—the *arthavat-paribhāṣā* (the maxim that a word denotes only its meaningful constituent) is not universally obligatory (*anitya*).
They say that this [rule] is based on that [previous one].

Regarding the rule *vibhāṣeṭaḥ*, since only the meaningless *ṣīdhvam* is possible there, others [add] the word *aṅgāt* ("from a stem") here as well, in order to prevent the misconception that only that [meaningless form] is being referred to.

Now, one might object that in the rule *uśca*, the term *ātmanepadeṣu* alone should be connected [from the preceding rule *liṅsicau*], because it is immediately adjacent; therefore, he says: "For elements enjoined together in a single grammatical operation (*ekayoganirdiṣṭa*), there is either simultaneous application or simultaneous cessation. (Paribhāṣā 16)
The word *vā* has the sense of *eva* (only/indeed).
The meaning is that words whose referents are mutually connected undergo both persistence (*anuvṛtti*) and cessation (*nivṛtti*) together.
The underlying idea is that this is observed in the world in the case of many [agents] appointed to a single task.

As for the argument that the evidence here is the re-mention of *iṭ* in the rule *ārdhadhātukasyeṭ* while *iṭ* is already being carried over from the rule *neḍvaśi*, and that this is for the purpose of preventing its connection with the word *na*: that is not correct; because in the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the rule *dīdhīvevīṭām*, it is stated that when the mention of *iṭ* is being carried over from that [previous] context, the re-mention of *iṭ* is intended to signify a modification of *iṭ* into the form of *guṇa*.

The exclusion (*nivṛtti*) of *nañ* is established by the maxim that "in some cases, even a single part [of a word] continues to apply. However, in reality, the Bhāṣya on the rule *dīdhīvevīṭām* is merely the statement of a partial view (*ekadeśyukti*),
because the inclusion of the term *iṭ* in the rule *ārdhadhātukasya* was rejected in the Bhāṣya on the rule *neḍvaśi*.
Because it is improper to reject this by resorting to an excessively great effort for its accomplishment.

But is it not the case that the *aluk* (non-elision) rule is governed by the heading [of "compound"] prior to the *anaṅ* rule, while the heading concerning the "subsequent member" (*uttarapada*) is governed by the heading prior to the *aṅga* rule; thus, [the claim] is untenable because they are taught in a single grammatical connection (*ekayoganirdiṣṭa*)?

Likewise, in rules such as *adāmahāyanāntācca*, it is untenable to claim that while the phrase *saṅkhyādeḥ* ("beginning with a numeral") is understood from the previous rule *saṅkhyāvyayādeḥ*, the phrase *avyayādeḥ* ("beginning with an indeclinable") ceases to apply; therefore, he says: "Even when [elements] are prescribed in a single grammatical operation (*ekayoganirdiṣṭa*), they may be understood separately. (Paribhāṣā 17)

"Connection" (*yoga*) means a relation within a single meaning; by that, it refers to those two [words] indicated as a collective by a *dvandva* compound—this is the meaning according to Kaiyaṭa on the sūtra "pakṣāttiḥ.
This point is obtained through the force of the formal declaration (*pratijñā*) regarding the *svarita* accent for that much alone.
And this is clear from both the preceding [discussion] and the *bhāṣya* on the sūtras "dāmahāyanāntācca" and "auto 'mśasoḥ."
[Objection: But would not [the rule] "atyadādīnām aḥ" (P. 7.2.102) cause an anusvāra in cases such as "imam"? To this, he says:
"There is no inclusion of homogeneous sounds by means of a sound that is being produced [as a substitute]. (Paribhāṣā 18)

In the rule *aṇuditsavarṇasya cāpratyayaḥ*, [the term *apratyayaḥ*] applies by virtue of its inherent capacity (*sāmarthyāt*) to what is obtained through the rule itself, to what is not obtained under the view that [phonemes] denote classes (*jātipakṣeṇa*), and to what is obtained by treating [substitutes] as non-different from their original qualities (*guṇābhedakatvena*).

The meaning is "no. For this very reason, in the rule *aṇudit* (Pāṇini 1.1.69), after explaining in another manner the absence of the inclusion of homogeneous sounds (*savarṇagrahaṇābhāva*) regarding suffixes (*pratyaya*), substitutes (*ādeśa*), and augments (*āgama*), [the author] teaches the prohibition "provided it is not a suffix" (*apratyaya*) even though [the desired result] was already established.
This indicates that there is this paribhāṣā: "That which is not being taught itself does not include its homogeneous counterparts (*savarṇa*).

Furthermore, since the long vowel would have been established by proximity (*antarya*) in the rule *jyād ā īyasah*, the explicit mention of the long vowel in *jyādāt* is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) of this principle.
This is clear in the Bhāṣya on both the *aṇuditsavarṇasya cāpratyayaḥ* sūtra and the *jyādāt* sūtra.

In rules such as *coḥ kuḥ*, there is the inclusion of homogeneous sounds (*savarṇagrahaṇa*) even by that which is being prescribed (*bhāvyamāna*), due to the force of the explicit utterance of the marker *u* in the element to be enjoined. It is with this very intention that it is said: "Those being prescribed do not [include] their homogeneous sounds..."
The moderns read [the text] as "gṛhṇāti."

But in that case, by the rule "adaso 'seḥ" and others, the prescription of the long vowel in forms such as "amū" would not occur; therefore, he says: "Even when being prescribed, the phoneme u includes its homogeneous counterparts. (Paribhāṣā 19)
The inclusion of the long vowel marker (tapara) in the rules *diva ut* and *ṛta ut* is the indicator (*jñapaka*) for this [principle];
this is clear in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *titsvaritam*.

Now, an objection is raised: in cases such as *go-hitam* ("beneficial for a cow"), the substitution of *av* and so forth would result by virtue of the rule regarding the presence of an affix (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*). To this, he says: "When [an operation] depends on a phoneme (*varṇa*), there is no application of the rule regarding the presence of an affix" (Paribhāṣā 20).
This concerns the primacy of a phoneme (*varṇa*).

Regarding its true nature: although the result is already established by the recurrence of the term *sthānivat* in the rule *pratyayalope*, the explicit mention of *pratyayalakṣaṇa* indicates that "primacy" consists in not being a qualifier of anything other than the affix.
Similarly, the primacy of a phoneme consists in not being a qualifier of anything other than [the affix], and it takes the form of being the qualificand as defined by the affix.
Therefore, in examples such as *agohitam*, [the substitution of] *av* was not applied;
and in examples such as *citrāyāṃ jātā citrā*, the *a*-suffix (*aṇ*) and the subsequent *ṅīp* were not applied after that which ends in it.

It is clear from the Bhāṣya that this [rule] serves as a prohibition of the rule regarding the application of suffixes (*pratyayalakṣaṇa*), even though the status of being "as if the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*) does not apply in the case of a rule prescribing a phoneme (*alvidhi*).

Now, an objection is raised: since the inclusion of *kami* is already established by the rule "ataḥ kṛkami," the inclusion of *kaṃsa* is redundant; to this he replies: "The *uṇādi* suffixes form underived nominal stems (*prātipadika*). (Paribhāṣā 21).
"Kaiaṭa and others maintain that this very [rule] is the indicator for this [case];
however, it does not apply to *kaṃsa*, because *kaṃsa* is not denoted [by the suffix]."
This is clear in the *Bhāṣya* on rules such as *pratyayasya luk*;
it is also established in the *Bhāṣya* on rules such as *ṇvultṛcau* that [words] are derived [in this manner].
This is according to the system of Śākaṭāyana.
It has been established in the *Śabdenduśekhara* that for Pāṇini, however, there is only the position of non-derivational derivation (*avyutpattipakṣa*);
this is clear in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule "āyaneyī" (Pāṇini 7.1.2).

But surely, in cases such as *devadattaccikīrṣati*, there would result the undesired application of the status of a verbal root (*dhātutva*) and so forth to *deva* and the rest, because they are parts of a complex form ending in a suffix (*sannanta*); therefore, he says: "When a suffix is mentioned [in a rule], what is denoted by that term includes that which begins with the element after which that suffix is prescribed and ends with that suffix. (Paribhāṣā 22)
In the sūtra *yasmāt pratyayavidhis tadādi pratyaye*, the rule is divided into two parts: *yasmāt pratyayavidhiḥ* and *tadādi pratyaye*.
The ellipsis is that [the first part] applies to what is being grasped (*gṛhyamāṇa*). By this, the portion consisting of that which begins with it and ends with it (*tadādyanta*) is established.

The portion ending with that [suffix], however, is established by the rule *yenavidhiḥ* (Pāṇini 1.1.72). And that [rule] applies when there is no other qualificand (*viśeṣya*) present, taking the word-form itself as the qualificand. As for the argument that the *tadantavidhi* (the rule concerning what ends in that) occurs because the suffix implies a composite whole of which its own base is a part, and thus [the base] serves as a qualifier for that [whole]—[that is not the case here].

That is not so; for in cases such as *iyān*, there is the possibility of an implication [of the entire form] due to the deviation of that [suffix] from such a collection [of base and suffix]. Where a suffix is accepted as the cause [of a grammatical operation], there is only the presence of the portion ending in *tad* and so on; this is stated in the *Bhāṣya* and *Kaiyaṭa* on the rule *aṅgasya*.

Likewise, wherever a suffix is understood as following a word ending in the fifth case (ablative), there too the portion ending with "tadādi" (beginning with that) is presented; however, in those cases, it is the state of ending in the fifth case that is relevant.
For this very reason, in the sūtra *eṅhrasvāt*, the meaning "ending in *eṅ*" is obtained.
Another purpose of this paribhāṣā is in the rule *yenavidhiḥ*.
It is stated in the Bhāṣya: "paramagārgyāyaṇaḥ.
Even when analyzed as "the descendant of paramagārgyāyaṇa," the suffix is applied from the word *gārgyāyaṇa* itself.
It does not arise from that which is distinguished [from it].
Even though there is no formation of a single integrated meaning (*ekārthībhāva*) by merely extracting [a part] from that, the application of the term certainly occurs.
And on this point, the Bhāṣya itself is the authority; the details are elsewhere.
"This [suffix] applies when there is the apprehension of a suffix alone,
and not when there is the apprehension of both a suffix and a non-suffix," according to the Bhāṣya on the rule "ugitaśca."
This technical designation "aṅga" is clear in both the Sūtra and the Bhāṣya.
In the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *yena vidhis tadantasya*, an exception (*apavāda*) to the portion concerning "that which ends with it" (*tadanta*) is recited:
*pratyayagrahaṇe cāpañcamyāḥ* (Paribhāṣā 23).

The meaning is that where a suffix following a word ending in the fifth case (the ablative) is adopted for the purpose of prescribing another grammatical operation, there the rule of "taking what ends with that" (*tadantavidhi*) does not apply;
as, for example, in the rule *radābhyāṃ niṣṭhātonaḥ*.
Therefore, in examples such as *dṛṣattīrṇa*, there is no substitution of *ṇ* for the *t* of the verbal root.

Even if the portion "ending in that" (*tadanta*) is not present [in the rule], since the portion "preceded by that" (*tadādi*) is present, the meaning is "of the *niṣṭhā* suffix following a word ending in *r* or *d*," and thus there is no fault; for there is no evidence against the presence of that portion.

If, however, there were the presentation of that which ends with [the suffix], then both [the suffix and the element] would have the same object, and thus the fault would certainly remain in examples such as *dṛṣattīrṇaḥ*.

In rules such as *syatāsī ḷluṭoḥ*, since the meaning is "when *ḷ* and *luṭ* follow," and because [the rule] necessarily requires a limit (*avadhi*), the word *dhātoḥ* (of the root), which is presented as requiring a limit, is construed as the limit; therefore, there is no apprehension of [an element] ending with that.

However, there is no fault in cases such as *ṅy-ābhyaḥ*, because there, in the absence of an expectancy for a fixed limit (*avadhi*) expressed by "from what" (*kasmāt*), the word ending in the fifth case cannot function as a qualifier of the suffix.

In the rule defining the technical term *aṅga* (*aṅgasya*), however, when the meaning is "before a suffix following that [which begins with the fifth-case word]," it is clear that the word ending in the fifth case serves as a qualifier.
For this very reason, the grammatical rules such as "uttamaikābhyām" and so forth are consistent.
But in that case, in examples such as *kumārī brāhmaṇī-rūpā*, the rule *gharūpa* would result in a short vowel; therefore, he says:
"In the section concerning the subsequent member (*uttarapada*), when there is a mention of a suffix (*pratyaya*), there is no inclusion of that which ends with it. (Paribhāṣā 24)
This is because of the inclusion of the term *lekha* in the rule *hṛdayasya hṛllekhayalādeśeṣu*;
in that context, *lekha* is not a word ending in the suffix *ghañ*, as it would not otherwise be designated [by the rule].
And this is clearly explained in the Bhāṣya on the very sūtra "hṛdayasya".

[Objection: But in this way, just as in the case of *paramakārīṣagandhīputraḥ*, would the rule "there is vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) of the element ending in *ṣyaṅ* before the words *putra* and *pati*" not apply here as well in *atikārīṣagandhyāputraḥ*? To this, he says:
"Nor [does it apply] when a feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*) is present and is not a subordinate member (*anupasarjana*). (Paribhāṣā 25)
This is a locative of domain (*viṣayasaptamī*).

The meaning is this: where a feminine suffix denotes a female being as the primary element, there is no restriction regarding the initial word of that stem; however, where it denotes a female being as a non-primary element, the restriction regarding the initial word certainly does apply.

By virtue of proximity (*pratyāsatti*), the condition for the application of this paribhāṣā is precisely that a word must not be a subordinate member (*anupasarjana*) with respect to that whose status as ending in a feminine suffix belonging to a compound is to be inferred.

Therefore, in examples such as *atirājakumāriḥ*, although the referent of the word *rājakumārī* is subordinate with respect to the referent of the word *ati*, it is nonetheless not subordinate with respect to its own referent; thus, due to the absence of the restriction [that the short vowel applies only] to that [subordinate member], the shortening is established.
For this very reason, there is no technical (śāstrīya) status of being a subordinate element (*upasarjana*) here in this paribhāṣā, because such a status is impossible.

This is because the present rule is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rule "when a suffix is mentioned" (*pratyayagrahaṇe*), and because it forms a single syntactic unit (*ekavākyatā*) with that rule; thus, the word "mention" (*grahaṇa*) applies here as well.
Through this connection, there is application when there is the apprehension of the general category of feminine suffixes and also when there is the apprehension of their specific instances,
but not when there is the apprehension of feminine suffixes and non-feminine suffixes. And this has been indicated by the rule "arthavat" (Pāṇini 1.2.45).
In the Sūtra and the Bhāṣya;
and this [rule] is indeed based on direct statement (*vācanika*).
It is clear in the Bhāṣya on the Sūtra "ṣyaṅaḥ."

But in that case, by the rule “*tarap-tamap-au ghaḥ*” and others, a technical designation (*saṃjñā*) would apply to forms ending in *tarap* and so on; therefore, he says: “In a rule prescribing a technical designation, when a suffix (*pratyaya*) is mentioned, there is no inclusion of what ends with it. (Paribhāṣā 26)
The inclusion of the word "anta" (end) in the rule *suptiṅantam* is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) for this [paribhāṣā].

Nor should it be argued that even if the paribhāṣā were indicated, there would be no purpose [for it], because even if the technical designation *pada* were applied to two suffixes, the paribhāṣā governing the mention of a suffix (*pratyayagrahaṇaparibhāṣā*) would preclude the inclusion of what ends with it;
for the designation *pada*, in its scope under the rule *svādiṣu*, resides in the base (*prakṛti*), and thus the mention of the word *pada* does not refer to the suffix alone.
This is clear in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra "sup-tiṅ-antam."
Now, one might object that in examples such as *avatapte nakulasthitam*, a compound would not be possible because the word *nakulasthita* lacks a suffix ending in *kta*; therefore, he says:
"When there is the mention of a *kṛt*-suffix, there is also the inclusion of that which is preceded by a *gati* or a *kāraka*. (Paribhāṣā 27)

And regarding this [rule], the inclusion of the term *anantara* (immediate) in the sūtra *agatiranantaraḥ*—which means that when a word ending in the suffix *kta* follows as a subsequent member (*uttarapada*), an immediate *gati* retains its original accent (*prakṛtisvara*)—is an indicator (*jñāpaka*).
For that [term] is intended to prevent over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in cases such as *abhyuddhṛtam*.
This is because, by the *paribhāṣā* "when there is mention of a suffix," *uddhṛta* lacks the status of being a word ending in *kta*.
If [the rule] were not established, that [statement] would be useless as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for those present.

Nor should it be argued that in examples such as *abhyuddhṛtam*, because of its subsequent status, the *anudātta* (low-pitched accent) of *abhi* is indeed governed by the rule "a verb following a verb" (*gatir gatau*),
since it stands at the beginning of a metrical quarter (*pādādistha*).
And because there is an absence of being subsequent to a word (*pada*), that [rule] does not apply.

However, if the term *anantara* (immediate) is included, then by its very force, only the immediate sequence as determined by a verbal root (*dhātu*) implied by the action is understood; thus, there is no fault.

Nor should it be argued that in examples such as *abhyuddhṛtam*, even though *udaḥ* lacks the status of being a prior member (*pūrvapada*) when compounded with *abhi*, that [term *anantara*] is nevertheless for the sake of the accent (*svara*).

In the rule *kārakād datta* (Pāṇini 6.2.148), by dividing the connection as *kārakāt* and carrying forward the mention of *gati* from that context, there is a restrictive rule (*niyama*) stating that a word ending in *kta* preceded by a *gati* and following immediately after a *kāraka* alone has its final syllable acute. Consequently, since the accent of *thā-thādi* (Pāṇini 6.2.144) does not apply, the acute nature of the vowel *u* in *ud-anna* is established by the general accent rule for verbal derivatives (*kṛt-svara*). Therefore, the inclusion of the term "immediately following" (*anantara*) is solely for the purpose of excluding cases where there is an intervention; thus, it serves merely as an indicator (*jñāpaka*).

Where a *kṛd*-derived form is mentioned in grammatical co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhṛta*) with a verbal root (*dhātu*) or a case-role (*kāraka*), in that instance, when there is a mention of a *kṛt* suffix, only that which is qualified by such co-occurrence is understood. By the word "also" (*api*), it is meant that even the simple [form] not so co-occurring is included.

Otherwise, in matters concerning the mention of a *kṛt* suffix, because this rule is subsequent, it would simply override the *paribhāṣā* regarding the mention of an affix (*pratyayagrahaṇa-paribhāṣā*); therefore, the inclusion of the word "also" is made.

For this very reason, when a compound is formed with a *kṛt*-derived word by means of the two *paribhāṣās*—"the [words] *gatika*, *kāraka*, and *upapada*" and "the mention of *kṛt*"—the suffix *aṇ* is established from the specific form [of the compound] alone; it does not follow that the statement in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *puṃyogāt* (Pāṇini 4.1.48) regarding the form *saṅkauṭinam* would otherwise be inconsistent. Otherwise, since even the simple form *kūṭin* ends in the suffix *inuṇ*, the suffix *aṇ* could be applied to it as well, and a potential fault would be unavoidable.
All of this is clear from the Bhāṣya and Kaiyaṭa on the rule *samāse 'nañpūrve* [Pāṇini 6.2.172].

However, regarding the rule *gatiranantaraḥ* [Pāṇini 6.2.49], since an operation is prescribed for the prefix (*gati*) which is the prior member when followed by a word ending in *kta* as the subsequent member, it should be understood that even in the presence of such a compound, the term refers to the suffix *kta* alone.
And this applies both when a specific *kṛt*-suffix is intended and when a *kṛt*-suffix in general is intended.
But it is not [the case that] there is no mention of "formed" (kṛt) and "unformed" (akṛt);
this is clear in the Bhāṣya on the rule *anupasarjanāt*.
In the section concerning the feet and their members, [the rule applies] to that [element] and to what ends with it.
The word *pada* is the term to be qualified (*viśeṣya*) by the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), and there is an application of the rule regarding the final element (*tadantavidhi*).
Consequently, in cases such as *iṣṭakacitam* ("built with bricks") and *pakveṣṭakacitam* ("built with baked bricks"), [the suffix applies].
By the rule "iṣṭakeṣīkāmālānāṃ cita," there is a short vowel; [the forms are] mahān,
paramamahān.
In examples such as *paramātimahān*, the lengthening [of the vowel] is established by the rule *sāntamahataḥ*.
For this very reason, it is clear from the Bhāṣya that the reading "of that which has a subsequent word" (*taduttarapadasya*) is incorrect.
Here, by the word *pada*, the governing heading (*adhikāra*) concerning the "subsequent word" (*uttarapada*) is intended.
And there is the governing rule for the word *pada* alone:
in the rule "pādasya padājyāti," there is no inclusion of that which ends in *pada*, because it must conform to the observed linguistic usage (*lakṣya*). This is the whole point.
This is clear in the Bhāṣya on the rule *yena vidhiḥ*.
But in that case, in examples such as *asyāpatyam iḥ*, the suffix *iñ* would not apply because there is no nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ending in *a*; therefore, he says:
"In the case of a single [entity], it is like that which possesses a designation" (Paribhāṣā 29).
That which possesses a specific designation (*vyapadeśin*) is so called because it has a primary linguistic usage based on the existence of a defining characteristic (*nimitta*).
However, that which lacks a designation due to the absence of a cause for such designation and is without a companion (*asahāya*), behaves in the same manner as that [designated entity].
The meaning is that even when there is only one [element] in relation to the grammatical operation (*kārya*), that operation must still be performed.
Therefore, since the vowel *ā* also ends in *t*, there is no fault.
Because of the statement "in the case of one," the vowel *ā* in *sabhāsannayane* does not have the status of being initial (*ādi*).
There is no end to the irregularity (*avikāra*) regarding the root *daridra* and the root *ghā*.

Otherwise, in the sense of "occurring in the bringing together of those who are not members of the assembly" (*asabhāsannayane bhavaḥ*), the suffix *cha* prescribed by the rule "vṛddhācchaḥ" would apply, and consequently, the suffix *atta*—which is characterized by having a vowel other than *i* or *u* as its penultimate letter—would have to follow [due to the presence of *i* in *daridra*].
For this very reason, in forms such as *hariṣu*, the status of being a *pada* does not apply to the suffix *su*.

In the world as well, when there are many sons, there occurs the conventional usage of "eldest," "youngest," and so forth, such as: "This one is my eldest," "this one is the youngest," and "this one is the middlemost."
However, it applies specifically to a *satva* that has only one son;
by this, there is an extension (*atideśa*) even to what is not prescribed in the technical treatises.
For this very reason, in forms such as *iyāya*, the doubling based on having a single vowel (*ekāctva*) is established.
For this very reason, in forms such as *bhavati*, the status of *bhū* as an *aṅga* (stem) is established;

and in forms such as *iyān*, under the view that the application of grammatical operations occurs at the time of their actual functioning (*kāryakālapakṣa*), its status as a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) based on its being a derivative ending in a *taddhita* suffix is also established.
Otherwise, because it would lack the property of beginning with that [element] from which the suffix was prescribed, these results would not be obtained.
As for the claim that the designation "single vowel" (*ekāj*) applies there based on the inclusion or exclusion of the meaning—
that is, as Kaiyaṭa says in examples such as *iyāya*, this refers to the single vowel-form belonging to a meaningful verbal root (*dhātu*)— that is not correct.
In the case of the expression "an *ṛc* consisting of a single word" (*ekapadā ṛk*), there exists primary usage according to the method stated in the Bhāṣya;
for it is said in the Bhāṣya: "In the expression 'an *ṛc* consisting of a single word,' the designation is justified by its meaning."
The intention [of the author] is that since the term *ṛktva* and so forth applies to both the object and the word, the "single part" refers to the word (*pada*) as a form consisting of sound alone.

Therefore, just as the designation of "eldest" and so forth occurs simultaneously through the superimposition of various attributes upon a single entity, and just as in expressions such as "the body of a stone statue" (*śilāputrakasya śarīram*), there is the usage of "its body" and so forth by superimposing the nature of a composite whole through multiple superimposed states upon a single thing; [so too is the case here].
Likewise, the application of designations such as "having one vowel" (ekāc) and so forth is established here by worldly convention; this is proven by common usage.

Nor should it be argued that because this [designation] applies only when [a word] is without a companion, the form *bhū* would fail to attain the status of an *aṅga*, since it is accompanied by a companion.

Since this [term] is prescribed as being at the beginning of that which is to be effected when a suffix (aṅga) follows, it lacks the status of having a companion; thus, even though there may be daughters of a different class and so forth in the world, for a man with only one son, there is the common usage: "he alone is the eldest," and so on.

Nor should it be argued that this renders the *Bhāṣya* statement—"the four single-vowel (*ekāc*) roots are *ni-j-*"—inconsistent, because the vowel *i* lacks the status of not having a companion, and therefore its being a single-vowel root (*ekāctva*) would be untenable therein.
This [rule] operates because it was formulated without due consideration of the word "in one" (*ekasmin*).
In the rule *arthavatā vyapadeśivadbhāvaḥ*, the term *arthavat* (meaning-bearing) also implies the state of being unaccompanied (*asahāyatva*).
Its meaning is that a word which conveys meaning obtains a grammatical operation similar to that of a *vyapadeśin* (a primary designator).
Generally, [a sound] is indeed without a companion because it possesses meaning;

for instance, in examples such as *kurute*, whether one follows the convention that "the vowel *a* in the word *ta* is the final of the vowels" (*acām antyaḥ*) or the convention that "it is the initial of that which follows," it remains without a companion.
In that case, the designation *ṭi* is established through the principle of "behaving like that which has a designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*). This is explained in detail elsewhere.
But surely, by the rule of extension to what ends in [a specific base], the suffix *yañ* prescribed after bases such as *garga* would also apply to *paramagarga* and the like; therefore, he says:
"There is no extension to what ends in [a base] when that base is used as a technical term (*prātipadika*) for its own grammatical operation" (Paribhāṣā 30).

And this is a restatement of the portion concerning suffixes (*pratyaya*) from the Vārttika: "In the rules for compound formation and suffix application, there is a prohibition, with the exception of those involving *ugit* [stems] and the mention of phonemes. For this very reason, the explanation in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *yena vidhis tadantasya* (P. 1.1.72) regarding the rule *aptṛn* (P. 6.4.11)—which is distinct from a rule for suffix application—and its demonstration that even the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) being mentioned therein undergoes the *tadantavidhi* (the rule applies to what ends with that), as well as the examples *svasā* and *paramasvasā*, becomes consistent.
For this very reason, just as the prohibition regarding "samāsa" and so forth is mentioned in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra concerning *tadanta* rules, this [prohibition] is not mentioned there.

Furthermore, that prohibition applies only to those base-sūtras (*prātipadika-sūtra*) where the nominal stem is specifically grasped in its particular form. And this has been indicated [by the author].

In the *Bhāṣya* on the rule “*asamāse niṣkādibhyaḥ*,” there is the following indicator (*jñāpaka*): the rule “*sapūrvācca*. Otherwise, since [the desired forms] would already be established by the application of the maxim of "extension to that which ends with [the stem]" (*tadantavidhi*) in the rule “*pūrvādiniḥ*,” what would be the purpose of that [latter rule]?

But if this were so, then by the principle of "treating as if possessing a designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*), suffixes such as *ṭhak* [in *sūtrāntāṭṭhak*], *ḍaḥ* [in *daśāntāḍḍaḥ*], and [the suffix after] *eka* [in *ekagopūrvāt*] would apply even to the isolated words *sūtra*, *daśan*, and *eka*; therefore, he says:
**Paribhāṣā 31:** *Vyapadeśivadbhāvo 'prātipadikena* (The treatment as if possessing a designation does not apply when a non-prātipadika is involved).

It should not be argued that the separate formulation of the rule is for the sake of continuity (*anuvṛtti*) with the sūtra "iṣṭādibhyaḥ," such that the forms *aniṣṭī* and others are thereby established; for if that were the case, one could have simply formulated a single rule as "pūrvāt sapūrvād iniḥ. Thus, this separate formulation serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*).

Because, by the authority of the subsequent Bhāṣya which serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*), formations such as *aniṣṭī* and so forth are undesirable; and because even if they were part of a single rule (*ekayoga*), there would be no obstacle to their continuing (*anuvṛtti*) into the subsequent rules.
For this very reason, the rule "nāntādasaṅkhyādeḥ" (Pāṇini 5.2.49) is purposeful;

otherwise, even in cases such as "pañcamaḥ," since the word would be treated as beginning with a numeral by virtue of the principle of "designation-like behavior" (vyapadeśivadbhāva), the rule would clearly be rendered useless.
And this [rule] applies only when a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is being mentioned, not when both a nominal stem and what is not a nominal stem are being mentioned.
Therefore, there is no fault in the rule "ugitaśca" (Pāṇini 4.1.6); this is clear in the Bhāṣya on that very point.

Furthermore, this *paribhāṣā*—"that which possesses a marker of inclusion" (*grahaṇavatā*)—pertains exclusively to the domain of rules prescribing suffixes (*pratyayavidhi*), according to the *Bhāṣya* and *Kaiyaṭa* on the rule "asamāse niṣkādibhyaḥ.
Consequently, the application of [the elision of the *ṭi*] in forms such as *paramāhan* (from *parama-ahan*) and in the word *ahan* alone is established; the details are explained elsewhere.
But how is it that in rules such as *vānto yi*, the meaning is "when a suffix beginning with *y* [follows]"? To this, he says:

*yasminvidhistadādāvalgrahaṇe* (Pariśiṣṭa 32). "When there is a grammatical operation (*vidhi*) with reference to a certain element, that operation applies to what begins with that element, provided that the term is not used in the sense of the mere sound itself (*algrahaṇa*)."
This is an exception to the rule of *tadanta-vidhi* (application of a grammatical operation to that which ends with the specified element).
It is stated explicitly in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *yena vidhis tadantasya*.
In this rule, the locative case (*saptamī*) is a cause (*nimitta*) by virtue of its actual presence (*svarūpasatī*).
For this very reason, in rules such as *neḍvaśi kṛti*, the meaning "of a *kṛt* suffix beginning with *vaś*" and so forth is obtained.

Furthermore, this [principle] operates only when both the qualified (*viśeṣya*) and the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) end in the locative case, by virtue of the inclusion of the term "beginning with *val*" (*valādeḥ*) in the rule *ārdhadhātukasyeḍ*.
Consequently, in rules such as *ḍaḥ si dhuṭ*, the interpretation "of what follows that which begins with *s*" (*sādeḥ parasya*) does not apply.
Just as the meaning of "beginning with *ta*" and so forth is obtained in rules such as *tīṣasaha* and *se 'sicī*,
so too has it been explained in the *Śabdenduśekhara*.
To establish forms such as *ghaṭapaṭam* (pot and cloth) and *ghaṭapaṭau* (pot and cloth), he says:
"Every *dvandva* compound optionally becomes a singular. (Paribhāṣā 33)
The meaning is that every *dvandva* compound falls within the scope of the section beginning with the rule "dvandvaśca prāṇi" (Pāṇini 2.4.2).

This is established by logic (*nyāyasiddha*), because the rule "cārthe dvandvaḥ" (Pāṇini 2.2.29) prescribes the *dvandva* compound without distinction for both collective (*samāhāra*) and copulative (*itaretarayoga*) senses.
The inclusion of the term "bahuvacanasya" (of the plural) in the rule "tiṣyapunarvasvoḥ" (Pāṇini 1.2.63) serves as the indicator (*jñāpaka*) of this principle.

In the case of the expression “tiṣyapunarvasu,” this [sūtra] is for the purpose of excluding that [previous rule]. Nor should it be argued that even so, this sūtra is redundant because the plural number would not occur here due to the obligatory singular form prescribed by the rule “jātiraprāṇinām” (P. 2.4.6); for by this very sūtra, it is indicated that that [rule] is optional.
Nor should it be said that these are not living beings,
for according to the Vedic scripture, "Life-breath consists of water," those whose life-breaths wither in the absence of water are indeed no longer living beings;
and this is clearly stated in the Bhāṣya on the Sūtra regarding Tiṣya and Punarvasu.

For this very reason, there is no contrary restriction—that the *samāhāra* (aggregation) applies only to parts of living beings and so forth—as might be inferred from rules such as "the *dvandva* [compound] ending in a vowel is also [neuter], provided it refers to a living being."
