All rules in the Vedic language (chandas) are subject to optionality.

In the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the rule *vyatyayo bahulam* ("there is extensive transposition"), this [phenomenon] is established by means of splitting the rule *bahulam* and by splitting the rule *ṣaṣṭhīyuktaśchandasi* with the particle *vā*. By this, forms such as *pratīpamanya ūrmiryudhyati* are justified;
otherwise, one would expect *yuddhayate*.
But how is it that *iyaṅ* occurs in forms such as *kṣiya*? To this he says:
"An imitation is like its original" (Paribhāṣā 35).

The mention of *kṣiya* as having the *iy-aṅ* substitution is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of this [fact]. In that case, because the formation of a case ending is based on its being a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), this [substitution] is not permanent; this is clear from the Bhāṣya on the rule "kṣiyo dīrghāt" (Pāṇini 1.1.5).

But [one might object]: in cases such as *rāmau*, once the *vṛddhi* substitution has been applied, how can there be "wordhood" (*padatva*) under the *kāryakālapakṣa* (the view that a rule applies at the time its effect is to be realized)?

For when both ends are relied upon, there is neither "endness" nor "beginningness"; since that which is excluded from one end lacks the status of being either its beginning or its end, he therefore says:
*Ekadeśavikṛtamananyavat* // P. 36 // (That which is modified in one part is not different [from the original]).
The phrase "not like another" (*ananyavat*) means "not as another. In that case, when similarity to another is negated, the absence of being another (*anyatvābhāva*) follows all the more.
Precisely for this reason, there arises an understanding of the meaning from such [a statement].

Otherwise, there would be no understanding from that [sequence] due to the lack of knowledge regarding the sequential order (*ānupūrvī*) which serves as the delimiting factor for its expressive power (*śaktatāvacchedaka*). And thus, since *rāṇ* ending in *m* is prescribed after something [else],
and *au*— by virtue of being like the beginning of what follows— is considered a case-ending (*suptva*), it possesses the status of being both the beginning and the end of that [compound].
The reality [of the term's application] is established by worldly convention, just as the usage of the word "dog" persists even when the tail has been cut off from a dog;
for this very reason, it is stated in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *prāgdīvyataḥ*.
Having stated that this is an imitation of the word *dīvyat*, which is a constituent part of the word *dīvyati*, [the author asks:
for what purpose is this distorted presentation?
By this very [distortion], the Teacher indicates that there exists this metarule (*paribhāṣā*): "That which is modified in one part is not different [from the original]," as it has been said.
By this, the view that "this rule applies only to a grammatical operation (*kārya*) and only to a grammatical modification (*vikāra*)" is refuted.
However, this does not apply to an operation based on a modified constituent part,
because it is difficult to justify the linguistic usage of a "modified constituent" in the same way one uses the expression "the dog has a tail" even when its tail has been cut off.
Thus, even when there is the apprehension of a stated measure (*parimāṇa*), this [rule] does not apply,
according to the reasoning already stated; this has been indicated by both the Bhāṣya and Kaiyaṭa under the rule *yena vidhis tadantasya*.
However, where half or more than half [of the constituent parts] are modified,

since the reality [of the original form] is not perceived due to the absence of the perception of the majority of the parts that manifest the genus (*jāti*), the rule *sthānivat* is formulated for the sake of accomplishing the grammatical operation and for the sake of perceiving the modified nature of the constituent parts.
In some instances, however, one does not rely on this logic in accordance with the requirements of the specific linguistic examples (*lakṣya*).
By this, the derivation of forms such as *ābhīyāt* is established;

furthermore, that in certain instances a grammatical rule does not apply has been clearly demonstrated by Kaiyaṭa in his commentary on the rule *prathamayoḥ pūrvasavarṇaḥ*, as is explained at length elsewhere.
Thus ends the first section, titled "The Attainment of the Status of a Treatise," in the *Paribhāṣenduśekhara* composed by the illustrious Nāgeśabhaṭṭa.
Now begins the second chapter, titled "The Seeds of Sublation."
Among the rules concerning priority, posteriority, permanence, internal application, and exception, each subsequent one is stronger than the preceding.
That which follows is stronger than that which precedes it,
because of the rule of conflict;
that is to say, the subsequent [rule] sublates the preceding one.
But in this case, in the word *bhindhi*, since *tātaṅ* would apply later [in the order of rules], it would sublate *dhi*; therefore, he says:
"It is established by the principle of re-application (*punaḥ-prasaṅga-vijñāna*). (Paribhāṣā 38)
Now, one might object that in the case of *tisṛṇām*, since the substitute *tisṛ* applies first due to its higher status, the substitute *traya* would apply again; therefore, he says:
"When two rules conflict and have applied once, that which has been superseded remains superseded. (Paribhāṣā 39)

In that regard, since it is impossible for both operations to occur simultaneously when one has already fulfilled its purpose, there is no sublater [of the other]. Thus, when both rules apply in alternation—just as in the case of the suffixes *tṛc* and others—the "Conflict" (*vipratiṣedha*) sūtra serves as a restrictive rule (*niyama*). This establishes the principle of "once-occurrence" (*sakṛdgati*). It is just as when a single servant belongs to two masters of equal power.
He performs his duty for the two of them by turns;
however, when they both send him out simultaneously with tasks in different directions, he does not do it for both, because simultaneity is impossible.

Likewise, when there is non-comprehension because two grammatical rules (*śāstra*) whose objects are to be characterized (*lakṣya-artha*) cannot apply simultaneously to a single characterized object (*lakṣya*), this [principle] serves the purpose of a subsequent rule (*para-vidhi*).

In that case, if a prior application (*pūrva-prāpti*) occurs once it has been performed, then that too indeed takes place; thus, the establishment of the "re-occurrence of application" (*punah-prasaṅga-vijñāna*) is clearly stated in the *Bhāṣya* on the *Vipratiṣedha* Sūtra.

As for what Kaiyaṭa and others have said—that since the application of a rule (*lakṣaṇa*) varies with each specific instance (*lakṣya*) when the word-meaning is the individual (*vyakti*), both rules would fail to achieve their purpose regarding their respective instances;

and thus, when both are applicable by turn, this [sūtra] serves as a restrictive rule (*niyama*) stating "only the latter" (*param eva*), thereby establishing the maxim of "single application" (*sakṛdgati*);
in this view, by virtue of this restriction, there is simply no application of the preceding rule to that particular instance.

Regarding the view that [the rule] pertains to the entire class (*jātipakṣa*), they say: when two rules, both of which have already found their application in some instance of the object to be designated (*uddeśyatāvacchedakākrānte lakṣye*), meet in a situation of conflict where the simultaneous occurrence of both is impossible—according to the logic of counter-arguments (*satpratipakṣanyāya*)—and neither is applicable, this [present rule] serves as a subsequent injunction (*paravidhi*); thus, the establishment of the understanding through re-application (*punaḥ-prasaṅga-vijñāna*) is achieved.

That is not so; for there is no evidence that the entire range of objects to be characterized (*lakṣya*) is covered by the treatise (*śāstra*) only under the view of individuals (*vyaktipakṣa*) and not under the view of universals (*jātipakṣa*).

Indeed, in the *Bhāṣya* on rules such as "one shall not kill a Brāhmaṇa," we see that the recourse to the universal-view is precisely for the sake of including all individuals who are the substrata of the universal.

For this very reason, in the *Bhāṣya* on the "Sarūpa" rule, it is stated that when the word-meaning is a universal, an injunction operates non-partially—that is, in its entirety—and thus, in cases such as "a cow is to be sacrificed" (*gaur anubandhyaḥ*), since it is impossible to sacrifice every single cow, [the injunction applies to] the class of actions.

Furthermore, in the theory that words denote substances (*dravyavāda*), since not all substances are understood [by a single word], it has been stated regarding such injunctions as "A cow is to be sacrificed" (*gaur anubandhyaḥ*) that one [cow] is prescribed by the scripture while another is not.

Moreover, there is no evidence for the claim that the example of the suffix *-tṛc* and others cited in the *Bhāṣya* applies to the theory of denoting individuals (*vyaktivāda*) alone and not to the theory of denoting classes (*jātipakṣa*).

Furthermore, even in the theory of denoting individuals, since these two [words] have already fulfilled their purpose by obtaining other individual forms as their objects, they cannot—due to the contradiction with the individual [intended]—have that specific individual as their own object.
It can be said that it conceptualizes;

even in the case of the theory of universals (*jāti-pakṣa*), it has as its object only the individual instance which is the locus of that universal, and not this particular instance— this is what is meant here.
There is no fixed rule [for this].

It should be understood that in this regard, following the nature of the subject matter (*lakṣya*), the path favored by the *Bhāṣya*— which sometimes relies on scriptural examples (*śāstrīya-dṛṣṭānta*) and sometimes relies on worldly examples (*laukika-dṛṣṭānta*)— is indeed the appropriate one.
The contradiction (*vipratiṣedha*) useful for the treatise consists precisely in the impossibility of two operations occurring simultaneously;
this is clear in Kaiyaṭa’s commentary on the sūtra *iko guṇavṛddhī*.

For example, in cases such as *aśiṣṭāt*, when both the substitution of *tātaṅ* and the change to *śī* apply simultaneously, it is impossible for each to have immediate proximity (*nantarya*) to its own respective cause.

Although that [proximity] certainly exists by virtue of the status of the substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) for *tātaṅ* and the rest, nevertheless, that [status] occurs only after the application of the substitute has taken place.
But not at the time of its own operation.
Thus, in cases such as *priyakroṣṭūni*, there is an impossibility of the simultaneous application of the *num* augment and the treatment as *tṛj-vat*;
for the rule *yadāgamāḥ* (that which is an augment is as if it were not) operates only after the *num* augment has already taken effect.

Similarly, in the case of *bhindhi*, one should understand that there is an impossibility of both the substitution of *tāt* and the substitution of *dhi* occurring simultaneously in relation to a single *sthānin*, as well as an impossibility of the proximity (*ānantarya*) of the cause consisting of the form of the stem (*aṅga*).

Furthermore, regarding *num* and *nuṭ*, there is a conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) due to impossibility: *nuṭ* obstructs the proximity of the case-ending beginning with a vowel (*aj-ādi-vibhakti*), while *num* obstructs the stem ending in a short vowel (*hrasvanta-aṅga*). Thus, because of this impossibility, a conflict of rules arises.

In some cases, by following what is desired, on the strength of the declaration of *svarita* status in the earlier treatise (*pūrvaśāstra*), the rule "that which is marked with *svarita* has greater force" (P. 1.4.2) applies first by implication;

thus, all prior *vipratiṣedha*s (rules of conflict) are subsumed under it—so it is stated in the *Bhāṣya* on the sūtra "svaritena. Furthermore, because the word *para* in the *vipratiṣedha* sūtra denotes "what is desired," those [prior rules] are included—so it is stated in the *Bhāṣya* on the *vipratiṣedha* sūtra.

But in this case, in forms such as *edhate*, because the vikaraṇa suffix would apply by virtue of its higher status, rules such as "anudāttaṅitaḥ" would become inapplicable due to the intervention [of the vikaraṇa];
therefore, he says:
A restrictive rule is stronger than the addition of suffixal markers.

In this regard, the rule *vṛdbhyaḥ syasanoḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.92), which prescribes the optional application of the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) endings after roots beginning with *vṛt* when followed by the suffixes *syat* and *san*, serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*).

Otherwise, if the restriction did not apply even when there was an intervention by its own [suffix], both forms would be established by the general rule; thus, the prescription of an option would be redundant.
Once this meaning is indicated, it is clear from the *Bhāṣya* and *Kaiyaṭa* on the rule *anudāttaṅitaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.12) that the term *asya* therein is a locative of scope (*viṣayasaptamī*).
The fact that this rule operates even when there is an intervention by an affix (*vikaraṇa*) is indicated as a *jñāpaka* (indirect evidence) in the Bhāṣya on the rule *śadeḥ śitaḥ*.
In reality, due to this *jñāpaka*, the section beginning with *anudāttaṅitaḥ* is prescriptive insofar as it forms a single syntactical unit with the rules prescribing the *tiṅ* suffixes and others.
In that context, the ablative case in *dhātoḥ* is prescribed [by Pāṇini 3.1.91].

The coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with that [root] is indeed a qualifier prescribed by rules such as *anudāttaṅitaḥ* (P. 1.3.12). And thus, even when there is the intervention of *sy-* in the state of the suffix *la*, the attainment of *taṅ* (the ātmanepada endings) is established. However, in the case of roots beginning with *śap*, the restriction applies even earlier.

Alternatively, since substitutes depend only on the letter *l*, they are internal (*antaranga*), whereas suffixes such as *syat* and others, depending on specific *l*-letters, are external (*bahiranga*). Thus, even with a fifth case ending characterized by connection with direction (*digyoga-lakṣaṇa-pañcamī*), there is no fault.
On this view, the rule *vṛdbhyaḥ syasanoḥ* should be explained as referring to the domain of *sya*.
The essential point is that, in cases such as *ātmanepada* and *śabda*, one must rely on the designation (*saṃjñā*) of "about to be" (*bhaviṣyat*).

However, if a restriction is applied to those things prescribed by a general rule through the formation of separate sentences, then the exclusion of the genus (*jāti*) must be accepted via that restriction, just as it is by means of elision (*luk*) and so forth.
It would be like saying to someone who has already eaten, "Do not eat!"

The maxim, "What would be achieved by that? is not appropriate to rely upon here in this treatise, because it would result in the futility of rules and other prescriptions in the scriptures. This has been indicated in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra "sthāne 'ntaratamaḥ" (Pāṇini 1.1.50).
The pointlessness of the treatise (*śāstrānarthakya*) has been refuted in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule concerning the technical term *vṛddhi*.

However, according to the method of Kaiyaṭa as found in the commentary on the *Sarūpa-sūtra*, the production [of a form] by means of a general rule would require the postulation of a base (*prakṛti*) through the assumption of a distinction in the subordinate element (*guṇa*) in accordance with the principal element (*pradhāna*).
Furthermore, upon the cessation of the suffix (*pratyaya*), the cessation of even that postulated base must be assumed; thus, there is prolixity (*gaurava*), as explained in detail elsewhere.
A subsequent [rule] is always more powerful. Paribhāṣā 41.
Because it would entail the consequence of both what has been established and what has not;
in that regard, rather than postulating the non-existence of one whose non-existence is unestablished, it is more appropriate to postulate that for one whose non-existence is already established.
This is the reason why the eternal [scripture] possesses greater force.
Thus it is said:
"That which applies to both what has been done and what has not been done is eternal;
that which is the opposite of that is non-eternal. (Paribhāṣā 42)
For this very reason, in forms such as *tudati*, the suffix *śap* and others occur by virtue of their being obligatory (*nitya*), even overruleing the subsequent *guṇa*.

With the apprehension that if an operation applies once in connection with a particular individual, it might apply again in connection with that same individual, leading to the fallacy of *kṛtākṛtaprasaṅgitva* (the contingency of having already been performed or not yet performed), he says:
"A rule that applies to another word becomes non-eternal (*anitya*). (Paribhāṣā 43)

This is clear from the Bhāṣya on the sūtra "śadeḥ śitaḥ. For there, regarding the form *nyaviśata*, it is stated that the augment *aṭ* is applied after the entire verbal base once the suffix (*vikaraṇa*) has been added, whereas if the suffix has not been added, *aṭ* is applied only after the root alone; thus, *aṭ* is considered non-obligatory (*anitya*).
By this same principle, he says:
"There is non-eternality for that which is obtained from one word [to another], and for that which is obtained from one word to yet another word. (Paribhāṣā 44)
He states this very point based on that root principle:
"A rule that applies by means of another occasion is non-permanent" (Paribhāṣā 45).
Regarding the subject of extended application (*atideśa*), this was stated by Kaiyaṭa in the commentary on the sūtra "asiddhavat."

But when the consideration of eternality and so forth pertains solely to the operation enjoined by that rule—apart from the specific wording of the treatise—and even when there is no recourse to a particular individual [as its substratum], then it is said:
"In some cases, eternality [is established] merely by the contingency of the operation having been performed or not performed" (Paribhāṣā 46).

The point is this: once a second [instance] has been established, it is merely the recurrence of that which is intended to be eternal that serves as the basis for the conventional designation "eternal"; it is not the case that even a recurrence characterized by a result uncontradicted by sublation (bādhaka) functions in that way.
Regarding this, it is said:
"And that whose cause is obstructed by another rule is not considered *anitya* (non-eternal). (Paribhāṣā 47)
In some cases, however, only a *prasaṅga* (an undesired consequence) that is not sublated by a sublater (*bādhaka*) and is accompanied by a result is understood; as he says:
"And that for which the cause is obstructed by another rule is also [considered] non-eternal" (*Paribhāṣā* 48).
Kaiyaṭa, in his commentary on the seventh book (*Mahābhāṣya*), has cited two instances of worldly usage to support this.
Even though Vālin was killed by the Blessed One while Vālin and Sugrīva were fighting, people do not speak of Sugrīva’s superiority over Vālin;
yet, although victory was obtained by the Pāṇḍavas with the assistance of the Blessed One, they do speak of the Pāṇḍavas’ superiority.
All of this is established in accordance with the requirements of the poetic context (lakṣya).

In the Bhāṣya on the sūtra "luṭaḥ prathamasya," it is stated: "A rule that applies to that which has undergone a change of its own vowel (svarabhinnasya) is considered non-eternal (anitya). (Paribhāṣā 49)
Thus it is recited. However, where a single effect possesses both posteriority (*paratva*) and eternality (*nityatva*),
then— according to one's intention— either one of those two, or both together, must be specified as the determining factor for its relative strength.

For this very reason, it is stated in the Bhāṣya regarding that [topic] as "because of its posteriority and its permanence. In reality, however, the statement "because of its posteriority" in that context belongs to a partisan (ekadeśin).
And this is clear from Kaiyaṭa’s commentary on the *vipratiṣedha* rule.

Regarding the rule *ṇau caṅi*, the Bhāṣya states that doubling occurs first because it is both obligatory (*nitya*) and internal (*antaraṅga*) with respect to the short vowel; thus, it is precisely "because of its obligatoriness" that is mentioned there. Likewise, it should be understood that the relative strength of two rules—both of which are obligatory and internal—is also determined only when their simultaneous application is impossible.
That which is internal (*antaraṅga*) is stronger even than that which is eternal (*nitya*);
for the external (*bahiraṅga*) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) when the internal is to take effect. Thus it is said: "The external is non-existent with respect to the internal" (Paribhāṣā 50).
*Antaraṅga* means that whose constituent parts or causes are internal— that is, situated within the interior of the collection of external, technical grammatical conditions.
Thus, that which has its constituent parts (*aṅga*) situated outside the collection of its own causes is *bahiraṅga*.
This is clear from the commentary (*bhāṣya*) and Kaiyaṭa’s gloss (*kaiyaṭa*) on the sūtra “*kharavasānayoḥ*” and on the sūtra concerning “*asiddhavat*.”
In this context, by the word *aṅga*, only the cause (*nimitta*) consisting of the phonetic form (*śabdarūpa*) is understood,
because that alone is primary in the science of grammar (*śabdaśāstra*).
Therefore, that which is caused by the meaning (*arthanimittaka*) does not possess the status of being "external" (*bahiraṅga*).

For this very reason, the prohibition "na tisṛcatasṛ" is purposeful. Otherwise, since the substitution of *traya* would be more internal (*antaraṅga*) than *tisṛ*—which is conditioned by the meaning of femininity—the said prohibition would clearly be inconsistent.

For this same reason, the Bhāṣya, Vārttika, and other works located in the sūtra "sthānivat" are consistent with the statement: "there is a prohibition of that which ends in *sr* when the substitution of *traya* occurs."

By this, the objection that in forms such as *gaudheraḥ* and *paceran*, the elision of *val* (consonant) would not occur because the substitution of *ey* and so on is dependent upon the designation (*saṃjñā*) of the base (*aṅga*) and is therefore "external" (*bahiraṅga*) and thus considered non-existent (*asiddha*), is refuted;
for the substitution of *ey* and the like is "internal" (*antaraṅga*) because it does not depend on any subsequent cause.

Now, an objection: according to the rule *yenavidhistadantasya* (Pāṇini 1.1.72), as explained in the Bhāṣya, even in rules such as *iko yaṇ aci*, if the designation of the final element (*tadantavidhi*) were applied, then in the word *asyonaḥ*, the substitution of *yaṇ* would—on account of its being an *antaraṅga* operation—be intended to override the *guṇa* substitution;
however, that [result] would not be established.

It has been stated that, because the substitution of *yaṇ* depends upon the word *ūna*, whereas the *guṇa* substitution depends upon the word *śabda*, the *guṇa* alone would occur due to its being *antaranga*.
Regarding this, Kaiyaṭa says:

In the case of the word *sivi* (the agentive suffix), due to the diversity of rules (*bāhulaka*) and the application of the *na* suffix under the *auṇādika* rules, when there is the contingency of both *guṇa* and *val-lopa*, the substitution of *ūṭ* subordinates the *val-lopa* because it is an exception (*apavāda*) to it;

however, it subordinates the *guṇa* because the latter is an internal operation (*antaraṅga*). For *guṇa* depends upon a light penultimate vowel (*upadhā*) characterized by the *ig-lakṣaṇa* rule pertaining to the stem (*aṅga*), as well as an *ārdhadhātuka* suffix.

If it is argued that [the substitution of] *ūṭ* is *antaraṅga* because it depends on fewer factors—namely, that the stem ends in *v* and the suffix begins with a nasal—and that once this has been applied, the *yaṇ* and *guṇa* substitutions would consequently follow; and thus, it is clearly stated that even that which depends on a technical designation (*saṃjñā*) is *bahiraṅga*. [Response: This is not so. For the application of *ūṭ* depends upon the presence of the suffix *kta*, whereas the application of *yaṇ* and *guṇa* depends upon the presence of the suffixes *liṭ* and *laṅ*. Since the former depends on more factors than the latter, it is indeed *bahiraṅga*. Furthermore, the fact that a rule depends on a technical designation does not by itself constitute its *bahiraṅga* status. For example, the substitution of *śn* for the root *śvi* is *antaraṅga* despite depending on the designation "root" (*dhātu*), while the substitution of *guṇa* for the root *iṇ* is *bahiraṅga* despite depending on the designation "affix" (*pratyaya*). No; for even under the rule regarding the inclusion of the final element (*tadantavidhi*), the designation *bahiraṅga*—in the sense of depending on many constituent elements—is present in the case of a *guṇa*, which would render the Bhāṣya’s statement regarding the fault therein inconsistent.

Furthermore, the concepts of "depending on many" (*bahvapekṣatva*) and "depending on few" (*alpāpekṣatva*) are not obtained through the inherent meaning of the words *bahiraṅga* and *antaraṅga* themselves.
If that were the case, [the author] would have simply said, "That which depends on many is unestablished (*asiddha*) with respect to that which depends on few."

For this very reason, in the commentary on the *vipratiṣedha* sūtra, the example given for the statement "the substitution of *aṇ* [for *i*] takes place because it is *antaraṅga* to the *guṇa*" is *syonaḥ*;
however, it was not stated that "the substitution of *ūṭh* [takes place] because it is *antaraṅga* to the *guṇa*. According to your view, that too ought to have been stated.
Or rather, it would have been more appropriate to state that very point because of its priority;
however, I did not mention it because it is impossible to prevent [the application of] that [rule] by means of the *antaraṅga* paribhāṣā.
Furthermore, according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), since [the rule for] *ūṭh* is eternal (*nitya*), it applies prior to the *guṇa* substitution.
However, the *guṇa* substitution is non-eternal (*anitya*) because it is superseded by the *yaṇ* substitution.
The statement in the Bhāṣya beginning with "relying on the word *ūna*" and so forth should be considered in light of its apparent inconsistency.
Furthermore, it is not correct to say that the *antaraṅga-paribhāṣā* does not apply when there is elision of a *val* sound.

In that very sūtra, the Bhāṣya itself raises the objection regarding the over-extension of elision (*lopa*) in the case of roots such as *vraśc* and others, stating: "It does not [apply] because of the force of the original instruction (*upadeśa-sāmarthyāt*).

Nor is there any utility [for the rule] in forms such as *vṛścati*, because the substitution of semivowels (*samprasāraṇa*) is external (*bahiraṅga*) and thus considered non-existent (*asiddha*), so that the elision would apply even earlier. This is what the Bhāṣya says.

As for the claim that because the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) is considered "as if not having taken effect" (*asiddha*) for the purpose of the technical designation "six" (*ṣaṭ-saṃjñā*), the prohibition "not [for] six" (*na ṣaṭ*) applies in the case of the word "pañca," that is to be reconsidered;
for the elision of *n* must be said to be "external" (*bahiraṅga*) due to its dependence upon the designation of a word (*pada-saṃjñā*).
And that is not so; for the extrinsic nature (*bahiraṅgatva*) caused by a technical name (*saṃjñā*) is not resorted to in the case of "pañca."

However, it should be understood that the prohibition regarding the feminine gender applies by the force of the interpretation "that which would otherwise apply, [it] does not," taking into account the state of having been six in the past (*bhūtapūrva-ṣaṭtva*).
For this very reason, the mention of *kṛti* and *tu* in the rule is purposeful.
In examples such as *vṛtrahabhyām*, although the elision of *n* (*nalopa`) is conditioned by the status of being a word (*padatva*), it does not lack the quality of being "external" (*bahiraṅga*).
Even though the suffix *bhyām* is the cause for the designation of a word, the elision of *n* is not caused by that [designation].
Resorting to the status of being "external" by taking a mediated causality (*paramparā*) as the basis, however, lacks authoritative support.
This has been implied in the *Bhāṣya* on the sūtra "nalopaḥ sup" (Pāṇini 6.1.68), and it has been explained in that very same place in the *Bhāṣyapradīpodyota*.

The meaning is: when an internal operation (*antaraṅga*) is to be performed, an external operation (*bahiraṅga*)—whether already arisen or due to arise at that same time—is considered as if non-existent (*asiddha*).
In the view that word-formation (*pada-saṃskāra*) applies to roots such as *vraśca*, it should be understood that both [the internal and external operations] indeed occur simultaneously.
By this, the notion that "that which is internal is stronger than that which is external" is a separate *paribhāṣā* is refuted;
for that [separate rule] was rejected in the *Bhāṣya* on the *vipratiṣedha* sūtra by relying on this very principle.
Its internal characteristic is its status as a grammatical rule (*śāstra*). And this [rule] does not apply within the Tripādī,
because the Tripādī is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) [with respect to it].
And in this regard, the inclusion of *ūṭh* in the sūtra "vāha ūṭh" serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*). This [indicator] resides in the first quarter of the seventh chapter (*sapādasaptādhyāyī*).

Otherwise, by merely prescribing *samprasāraṇa*, the *guṇa* substitution for a light penultimate vowel would apply, and then by the rule "vṛddhi reci," the *vṛddhi* substitution would result; thus, the form "viśvauhaḥ" and others would be established, making the inclusion of *ūṭh* clearly redundant.

For if this [rule "vāha ūṭh"] were present, the *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel would not take place because the external *samprasāraṇa* is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) [with respect to internal operations].
Furthermore, in the rule *puganta* (Pāṇini 7.3.86), the cause (*nimitta*) is not a qualifier of the *ik*;

for this very reason, there is no *guṇa* substitution in forms such as *bhinatti*. Likewise, one should not ask how the application of the *paribhāṣā* [of the same name] occurs here, given the prohibition in the rule *nājānantarye* (Pāṇini 1.1.5).
Because the portion of the suffix (*pratyaya*) has its expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) aroused and thus undergoes syntactic connection (*anvaya*) with that [suffix],

and because in rules such as *puganta* (Pāṇini 7.3.86), the interpretation as a *karmadhāraya* compound— meaning "the light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhā*) which is a part (*avayava*) of the member (*aṅga*) subsequent to the suffix"— is accepted, resulting in the sense "there is *guṇa* substitution for the light penultimate vowel which is a part of the member subsequent to the suffix," this is consistent with the intent of the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *iko guṇavṛddhī* (Pāṇini 1.1.3); furthermore, there is no fault in cases such as *abhinatti*.

When a prefix ending in *a* and a word ending in *na* (other than *an*) are present as upapadas, the suffixes *ṇvi* and *vic* are optionally applied to the roots *vah* or *vāh*; however, because of non-usage (*anabhidhāna*), they do not occur after the root *nas* alone. As for forms such as *vāryūhi*, they should be understood as derived from the root *ūh* with the *kvip* suffix;
there is no lack of semantic consistency, as verbal roots possess multiple meanings.
The form *prauhaḥ* and others are indeed incorrect, because the rule for vṛddhi does not apply here;
since this *uha* is purposeless, the rule *prādūhoṭha* (Pāṇini 6.1.89) does not apply either.
Nor should it be argued that, under the view that rules apply at the time the effect is to be produced (*kāryakālapakṣa*), the application of this [rule] within the Tripādī is unavoidable;

for since a subsequent rule is considered *asiddha* (non-existent) with respect to a preceding one, there is an absence of an *antaranga* (internal) operation, and consequently, the preceding rule cannot possess the status of being *bahiranga* (external) relative to it.
Thus, it is impossible for that [subsequent rule] to establish the *asiddha* status of the former.

Nor should it be argued that because the former [rule] is unestablished due to its non-existence, it is impossible to state by means of the phrase "in the former" (*pūrvatras*) that the latter is unestablished with respect to it; for if this were so, both rules would fail to apply due to a lack of a deciding factor (*vinigamanāviraha*).
Furthermore, since the rule "in the former" (*pūrvatras*) is perceptible (*pratyakṣa*), it is more appropriate that it should sublate this inferential (*ānumānika*) rule.

Therefore, having introduced the *kāryakālapakṣa* (the view that rules apply at the time the operation is to be performed) and stated the aforementioned arguments, the proponent of the final position (*siddhāntin*) states in the Bhāṣya on the *visarjanīya* rule: “Hence, this solution is improper, or rather, it is not [proper] because [the cause] is external (*bahiraṅga*). The meaning of this is that when an internal (*antaraṅga*) rule belonging to the *tripādī* is to be applied, the proposed solution is not tenable;
rather, his intention is that a specific formal statement (*vacana*) must be formulated.
For this very reason, in examples such as *nigālyate*, the statement "that is its fault" was specifically formulated for the sake of establishing the substitution of *l* (latva).
Otherwise, because the elision of *ṇi* (*ṇilopa*) is internal (*antaraṅga*), if the optional *l* were to apply prior to that elision, the [rule] would clearly be rendered useless.

Even those who, for the sake of conforming to specific grammatical illustrations (*lakṣya*), claim that the rule *pūrvatra*—which is established by direct perception—is set aside by the inferential internal-rule maxim (*antaraṅga-paribhāṣā*), should not be heeded by those whose only eye is the grammatical rules (*lakṣaṇa*). This is the direction [of the argument]. For this very reason, the inclusion of the term *āṅ* in the rule *omāṅośca* serves a meaningful purpose.

For indeed, in the case of *khaṭvā ā ūḍhaḥ*, even though the rule for *savarṇa*-dīrgha (P. 6.1.101) follows later, it is set aside by the *guṇa* substitution because the latter is *antaraṅga*; subsequently, when the condition for *vṛddhi* arises, this [substitution of] the subsequent form (*pararūpa*) is intended. Since the verbal root (*dhātu*) is joined with the prefix (*upasarga*) prior to the production of the suffix that expresses the *sādhana* (the agent), whereas the word *khaṭvā* is joined with the entire complex [of root and prefix] afterwards, the *guṇa* is *antaraṅga*. This is stated in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *samprasāraṇācca* (P. 6.1.108).
This is clear.
However, when the imitation-form ‘ehi’ is connected with words such as *śiva*, this [rule] does not apply;
for this is established by the authority of the Bhāṣya on the rule “*samprasāraṇācca*” (Pāṇini 6.1.108), which serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) [of its non-application].

This is because, having acquired the status of being an auxiliary (*aṅga*) by means of the extended application (*atideśa*) "an imitation [is treated] like its original" (*prakṛtivadanukaraṇam*), this [rule] does not apply.
As for the statement: "First the verbal root is joined with the prefix (*upasarga*), and afterwards with the suffix;
[the prefix] is that which bears the technical name *upasarga*."
"By means of the instrument (*kāraka*) and the effect produced by it;

for this very reason, in expressions such as 'it is experienced' (*anubhūyate*), the *lakāra* (verbal suffix) is established in the sense of the object because of its transitivity"— this is not correct, because action is that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*).

Because of the cognition [of the root], and because that which is to be accomplished (the *sādhya*) requires a means (*sādhana*), it is only after the connection with that [means] that there is a cognition of the action as determined; and only after the engagement in the operation of the means does the designation of *upasarga* (preverb) apply to that which is the cause for the connection with the action.

For this very reason, in the rule "suṭ kātpūrvaḥ" (Pāṇini 6.1.135), having stated "first the verbal root [is joined] with the preverb," it is said: "This is not the essence; first the verbal root [is joined] with the means."

It is appropriate; for after stating [the objection], its very propriety has been asserted through the aforementioned reasoning in the Bhāṣya, beginning with: "For the means of accomplishment (sādhana) brings about the action.

Since the meaning [of the prefix] manifested by the preposition is included within the verbal root itself when expressing the meaning, the formation of the *lakāra* suffixes and so forth in the sense of the object (*karman*) is established among those cases mentioned.
The connection with the prefix (*upasarga*), which serves as an indicator, occurs subsequently for the sake of the listener's understanding.

Thus, the *suṭ* augment, caused by the prefix whose meaning is more internal (*antaraṅgatara*), operates prior to reduplication and other operations in the state [of the verbal root] ending in *-kṛti-*,
after which reduplication and so forth take place.
For this very reason, the substitution of *ṇ* in forms such as *praṇidāpayati* has been established in the Bhāṣya by the maxim *yadāgamāḥ* ("that which is an augment [is like the original element]").
For this very reason, the derivation of *pratyayaḥ* as "that which goes toward" (*pratyeti*) and so forth is established.
An operation caused by a prefix that depends on the meaning of the prefix is *antaraṅga* (internal), because its cause is a specific prefix.
However, where that is not the case, the internal factor (*antaraṅga*) is precisely that which is caused by a preceding means of proof (*sādhana*).
For this very reason, it is stated in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *na dhātu-* regarding the form *preddhaḥ*: "The *guṇa* [substitution] is external (*bahiraṅga*)."

Furthermore, it is clearly stated in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *upapadam atiṅ* that "if a prefix were joined first, there would be the undesirable consequence of a single accent (*aikasvarya*) for the root and the prefix in a compound.
The suffix denoting the abstract action (*bhāvārtha-pratyaya*) also arises only at the very beginning.
For this very reason, the grammatical formulation *ṇeradhyayane* is consistent.
And this is an indicator based on general application,
because even a verbal noun ending in a *tiṅ* suffix arises prior [to the formation of the compound]; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of a compound occurring in that case.

There is no fault in that case because of the prohibition "not before a *tiṅ*," provided that there is a connection with a prefix (*upasarga*) even before a *bhāva*-derived *tiṅ*. As for the statement:

"That which depends on a general property is more internal (*antaraṅga*) than that which depends on a specific property," this is because in the case of dependence on a specific property, an additional specific attribute serves as the cause.

Just as in the rule "rudādibhyaḥ sārvadhātuke," there is both the status of being a root beginning with *rud* and the status of being a *sārvadhātuka* suffix; in that context, for the cognition of a *sārvadhātuka*, it is necessary to have the cognition of the base as a root and the cognition of the affix as an affix— thus, *yāsuṭ* is an *antaranga* [operation].
By this, that which was stated by Kaiyaṭa regarding the rule *anudāttaṅitaḥ*— namely,

"the substitutes beginning with *ti* are *antaraṅga* because they depend only on the *la*-affixes, whereas the substitutes beginning with *si* are *bahiraṅga* because they depend on specific *la*-affixes"— is refuted.
[Objection: Even if that [suffix] depends on a specific property (*viśeṣa*), since it lacks the status of being caused by a general property (*sāmānyadharma*), its reality is difficult to establish;
furthermore, because they depend on another factor, [the suffixes] *syādi* are extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*).

[Response: That is not so; for although the pervader (*vyāpaka*) is presented through inference because the specific property is the pervaded (*vyāpya*), there is no evidence that it serves as the cause [of the suffix], and thus it cannot be established that the suffix is caused by an additional property.
Furthermore, there is no mention whatsoever in the Bhāṣya of such a relationship between the internal (antaraṅga) and external (bahiraṅga) as that;
and as for what is stated in the Bhāṣya on the *matup* sūtra— "he who has five cows..."— [it does not establish this].
Regarding the term "pañcaguḥ," having raised the objection that the suffix *matup* would apply there, [the author] states: "Because of the lack of semantic capacity in each individual member,
because the aggregate is not a nominal stem (*aprātipadika*), and because it is a compound (*samāsa*)."

When the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntin) states, "Because it has been stated in brief," the opponent (pūrvapakṣin) replies in the Bhāṣya: "This is not sound; for even when the meaning of the suffix has already been expressed, a secondary derivative (taddhita) arises after a *dvigu* compound, as in the example ‘pāñcanāpitiḥ’.
This is because a secondary derivative occurs after a *dvigu* whose meaning is that of a secondary derivative, since the elision (luk) is prescribed by the rule ‘dvigor lug anapatye’."
And Kaiyaṭa’s intention regarding the term *pañcagu* is that it is a *dvigu*.

Then, with the thought that in cases such as *dvaimāturaḥ*, *pāñcanāpitiḥ*, and "prepared in five potsherds" (*pañcasu kapāleṣu saṃskṛtaḥ*), the *bahuvrīhi* would override the *dvigu*—which otherwise finds its scope there—because the former is subsequent [in the order of rules], the proponent of the established view (*siddhāntin*) says: "This is not a *dvigu*;
it is a *bahuvrīhi*. Not understanding this scope, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) objects: "Because it is an exception (*apavāda*), the *dvigu* should apply."

Kaiyaṭa maintains that since the *bahuvrīhi*—which is prescribed for any word ending in a case-suffix when it denotes another referent—is superseded by the *dvigu* (prescribed when a numeral denotes a secondary derivative meaning) due to the latter being specifically ordained, the *dvigu* ought to prevail.
To this, a certain partisan of the final view (*siddhāntaikadeśin*) replies:
"The *bahuvrīhi* prevails because it is more internal (*antaraṅga*)."
What is an internal member (*antaraṅga*)?
A *bahuvrīhi* compound [is formed] when the external referent (*anyapadārtha*) is intended;
a *dvigu* compound [is formed] when that external referent is qualified.
And regarding that [term], the inclusion of the word "asti" (is) is made in the *taddhita* rule;
Kaiyaṭa says that the *dvigu* compound, which is caused by the sense of possession (*matvartha*), is extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*) because it depends on the sense of "exists.
This, however, is not the statement of the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).
Even by this much, the status of [the rule] as an exception (apavāda) is not lost;

for we observe that the long vowel (*dīrgha*), which depends on a specific homogeneous vowel (*viśiṣṭasavarṇa*), sublates the *yaṇ* substitute which depends on the general category of vowels (*acsāmānya*).
Furthermore, according to the aforementioned method, sublation is established by virtue of [the rule] being *para* (subsequent).

Moreover, in this context, the status of being *bahiraṅga* (external) is due solely to the requirement of additional factors, and not merely to the requirement of specific factors; thus, the notion that something requiring specific factors is *bahiraṅga* is not supported by the Bhāṣya.

For this very reason, it is not stated in the Bhāṣya that the *bahuvrīhi* depends on the general category of nominal stems (*subanta-sāmānya*), while the *dvigu* depends on its specific instances (*tad-viśeṣa*).
Nor is this [objection] untenable on the grounds that the extrinsic nature (*bahiraṅgatva*) based on meaning is not being resorted to.
Since it is merely the argument of a partial proponent (*ekadeśin*), there is no fault.

For this very reason, the inclusion of the term *asti* is not for the sake of [forming] an upādi; rather, as you yourself maintain, its purpose is to convey the sense of the possessive suffix (*matup*) following the word *asti*. Having thus established that even the "external status" (*bahiraṅgatva*) does not apply to the *dvigu*, the Siddhāntin states: "A prohibition regarding the *dvigu* must be stated in the sense of the possessive suffix."

For this very reason, in the rule *tadoḥ saḥ sāvanantyayoḥ*, the phrase *anantyayoḥ* (of the two non-final [sounds]) serves a purpose. Otherwise, since the substitution of *atva* for the final sound would be *antaraṅga* (internal) with respect to the general category of suffixes, and the substitution of *satva* for the non-final sound would be established [by default], the [mention of] *anantyayoḥ* would clearly be redundant. This is also the case in the rule *pādaḥ pat*.
The authors of the Bhāṣya and Kaiyaṭa have also indicated that this very [operation] lacks the status of being *antaranga*; let the wise discern this.

Now, if it is argued that in the form *asusravat*, the substitution of *uvaṅ* would not occur because it does not have fewer causes than the *guṇa* substitution for a light penultimate vowel (*laghūpadhaguṇa*), we say no;
for in that case, the status of being *antaranga* exists by virtue of its being an internal operation (*antaḥkāryatva*).
And "being internal" (*antar-aṅgatva*) means having a cause that presents itself first, because the word *aṅga* here refers to the cause.
This quality of being internal is established by worldly logic, as in the case of the statement: "This man, having risen in the morning, performs the bodily functions..."
Then [the cognition arises] of friends, and then of relatives;
furthermore, regarding objects, the sequence of the comprehension of genus, individual, gender, number, and case-role is as conceived by the author of the grammatical treatise.

And since the manifestation of the words that express those [sounds] is postulated according to that very sequence, their effects also follow that same sequence. This is clear from the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *acaḥ parasmin* (P. 1.1.57) regarding the example *paṭvyā*: because of its internal nature (*antaraṅgatva*), the substitution of the preceding *yaṇ* occurs first, while the substitution of the subsequent *yaṇ* is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*) due to its external nature (*bahiraṅgatva*).
Furthermore, that [principle of internal and external status] serves solely to regulate the priority of application when two operations apply simultaneously.
Just as in the case of the analysis of the word *apaṭvyā*,
where [the rule] does not establish the non-validity (*asiddhatā*) of an external factor (*bahiraṅga*) that has already arisen with respect to such an internal factor (*antaraṅga*),
because it is obtained exactly so by the previously mentioned worldly maxim.
This is clear in Kaiyaṭa’s commentary on the sūtra *vāha ūṭh*.

For this very reason, in forms such as *vāyvoḥ*, the elision of *v* (by *lopo vyor vali*) is prevented by treating the semivowel (*yaṇ*) as if it were still present (*sthānivadbhāva*), as stated by the author of the Bhāṣya under the rule *acaḥ parasmin*.

However, when explaining [the rules] according to their sequential order (*krama*), it should be understood that in the aforementioned example, "being internal" (*antarangatva*) consists in operating first, while for the external rule (*bahiraṅga*), "being as if non-existent" (*asiddhatva*)— which takes the form of non-application due to the absence of its cause— is also present. As for the claim that, by this method, even that which has a preceding position is internal, that is to be considered with caution (*cintya*).

In examples such as *srajiṣṭhaḥ*, since the elision of the *ṭi* portion would be superseded by the application of the elision of the suffixes *-vin* and *-mat* (via *vinmator luk*), there would result the futility of the effort made by the author of the Bhāṣya— during the refutation of the purpose of the rule *prakṛtyaikāc*— to prevent that [elision] by resorting to the view that [the suffixes] denote a class (*jāti*).

According to the method you have stated, the elision (*luk*) of the suffixes *vin* and *matup* would be easily avoided by treating it as non-existent due to its being "external" (*bahiraṅga*); furthermore, such a method of relying on the non-existence of external operations is nowhere adopted in the *Bhāṣya*, and because in the Paribhāṣā the word "aṅga" refers to the cause (*nimitta*).

Furthermore, this statement in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *ica ekāco ’m*— which asserts that [the substitution of *am*] does not cause the external element (*bahiraṅga*) residing under the heading of "subsequent member" (*uttarapada*) to be treated as non-existent (*asiddha*)— is an argument of the opponent (*pūrvapakṣin*) and should not be accepted.
In forms such as *parantapaḥ*, there is no non-existence (*asiddhatva*) of the *anusvāra* because the *mum* augment does not apply within the Tripādī (the last three chapters).

Even in the view of the Navyas (the modern grammarians), it is said that by resorting to the *yathoddeśa* (definition-based) position and providing an example of *anyathāsiddha* (otherwise-established), it is necessary for that [rule] to be considered an utterance of that [author].

This is clear from the Bhāṣya on the *asiddhavat* sūtra: "When an internal (*antaraṅga*) rule belonging to the *ābhīya* (belonging to the same section) is present, there is no non-validity (*asiddhatva*) of a co-referential external (*bahiraṅga*) rule belonging to the *ābhīya* by virtue of this [sūtra], because the internal rule is itself non-existent."

Thus, according to the maxim "that which is not otherwise obtained [is superseded]," the fact that there is no internal (antaraṅga) rule in the case of the *sic* affix— which is based on its status as a sublater of the internal— is made clear in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra "ikoguṇavṛddhī" (Pāṇini 1.1.3).

But in that case, in forms such as *akṣadyūḥ*, since the *uṭ* augment is considered "unestablished" (*asiddha*) because it is external, the internal *yaṇ* substitution would not occur; therefore, he says: "When there is immediate sequence of vowels (*aj-ānantarya*), the status of being external is not admitted. (Paribhāṣā 51)
In this regard, the mention of *tug* in the rule *ṣatvatukoḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.86) is an indicator (*jñāpaka*).

Otherwise, in forms such as *adhītya* and *pretya*, since the suffix *lyap* would apply after the compound has been formed, the compound would first come into being; and because *saṃhitā* is obligatory therein, it would be impossible for the word to remain in a non-*saṃhitā* state until the production of *lyap*. Consequently, [the *tug* augment would have to be applied] after the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) [has occurred].

Furthermore, with respect to the suffix *lyap*, since the single substitute (*ekādeśa*) is *asiddha* due to its being *bahiraṅga*—depending on two syllables related to two words—it is quite clear that [the rule] would be useless.

This is because, according to the principle that "that which depends on two syllables related to two words is *bahiraṅga*," the *guṇa* substitution in examples such as *preddhaḥ* is *bahiraṅga*; this is stated in the commentary on the rule *na dhātulopa ārdhadhātuke* regarding the rule *saṃyogāntasya lopaḥ*.
This is clear in both the Sūtra and the Bhāṣya.
As for the fact that the mention of *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ*) is also an indicator (*jñāpaka*),
otherwise, in cases such as "ko 'sicat," [the rule would apply] because it depends upon two syllables related to two distinct words.
[Objection: Since the external single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*), what is the point of that [rule] when the application of *ṣatva* occurs?

[Response: That is not so; because the *iṇ* [sound] is connected with the preceding member, the *ṣatva* likewise depends upon two sounds belonging to two words, and thus both are equal. Furthermore, since the single substitute is treated as having the final letter of the preceding word as its beginning (*aparāditva*), the form *osicat* is considered a word (*pada*); therefore, because it does not begin a word (*padāditva*), there is no prohibition by the rule *sātpadādyoḥ*.
Furthermore, even under the *kāryakāla* view regarding the *traipādika* section, it has already been established that the *bahiraṅgaparibhāṣā* does not apply.

The meaning of the *paribhāṣā*, however, is this: when an *antaraṅga* operation is to be performed based on the immediate sequence of vowels (*ac*), there is the designation of "externality" (*bahiṣṭva*) for a *bahiraṅga* element that has already arisen.
By the word "external" (*bahiḥ*), the *bahiraṅga* is meant.
The state of that [condition] is its being external;
thus, there is neither the application nor the attainment of the status of being "not established" (asiddha) caused by it.

Having stated "that which is external is unestablished" (*asiddhaṃ bahiraṅgam*), the Bhāṣya says, "I shall state [the rule] *nājānantarye*. By this statement, it is indicated that the term *antaraṅga* from that context is to be carried over [into the subsequent rule]. Consequently, there is no fault in cases such as *pacāvedam*, because the internal operation of *etva* (the substitution of *e*) for the vowel *ac* does not have another vowel as its immediate cause.

By the statement "of that which has already arisen and is external," it is established that in examples such as *ajaye indram* and *dhiyati*, the external *guṇa* and *dīrgha* [substitutions] are treated as non-existent (*asiddha*).

For this very reason, statements such as "the *guṇa* of *iṇ*, *niṣ*, and *śī* [is applied] before the *āṬ* suffix, because the *savarṇadīrgha* [substitution] for the *caṅ*-ending [root] is internal (*antaraṅga*)" are logically consistent.
For this very reason, the inclusion of the term *āṅ* in the rule *“omāṅośca”* is purposeful.

For when the form *‘śivaaāaiha’* is established, that [inclusion] serves to prevent the substitution of *vṛddhi* by applying *guṇa*—which, being an operation between a verbal root and a prefix (*dhātūpasargakārya*), is *antaraṅga*—thereby overriding even the subsequent *savarṇadīrgha*.

Now, one might object: in the case of *‘akṣadyūḥ’*, once the *yaṇ* substitution has occurred, the *ūṭh* would be considered *asiddha*, and thus the elision of *val* (the *y*) would result. This need not be said.

The meaning [of the rule] is this: when another internal operation (antaraṅga) conditioned by immediate contiguity (ānantarya-nimittaka) is about to be performed or has already been performed, and another internal operation subsequently presents itself, that [subsequent one] is not considered "asiddha" (non-existent) with respect to the former. If, however, one were to prevent such a case by relying on the non-eternality (anityatva) of the *asiddhaparibhāṣā* itself, then this [present] rule would be rendered useless, since the desired result would already be established by that very [paribhāṣā].
For this very reason, the inclusion of the term *kṛti* in the rule *na lopaḥ sup* (Pāṇini 6.1.68) serves a purposeful function.

Otherwise, in forms such as *vṛtrahabhyām*, the elision of *n* would be established even without that term; for the elision of *n* would be considered *asiddha* (non-existent for the purposes of subsequent operations) due to being *bahiraṅga* (extrinsic), since it depends upon the status of being a *pada* (word) which is caused by the extrinsic suffix *bhyām*. Thus, its [the inclusion of *kṛti*] necessity would be obvious. But in my view...
There is no fault because of the immediate sequence (*jñājānantarya*) of the *kyac* suffix;
and this being so, there is no contradiction with the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the rule "hrasvasya piti" (Pāṇini 6.1.71).
For in that [commentary], regarding the example "grāmaṇiputraḥ,"...

It should not be argued that once the short vowel is applied by the rule *iko hrasvo ’ṅyaḥ*, the insertion of *tuk* is anticipated and resolved by the fact that the short vowel is *asiddha* (non-existent) because it is *bahiraṅga*;
for if the rule *nājānantaryāt* were in force, it would be clearly inconsistent, as that [principle of *bahiraṅga-asiddhatva*] would not apply there.
Because this [Paribhāṣā] is understood to be without scope by that very Bhāṣya;
for it is only logical that the non-eternality (*anityatva*) of the *antaraṅga* Paribhāṣā is established by this indicator (*jñāpaka*).

Precisely for this reason, in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra “*acaḥ parasmin*” (P. 1.1.57), regarding the form *apaṭu ī ā*, the prior substitution of *yaṇ* is established because the subsequent substitution of *yaṇ* is rendered invalid (*asiddha*) by this [Paribhāṣā].
For this very reason, it is not mentioned anywhere else in the Bhāṣya.
Precisely for this reason, after introducing the *antaraṅga* maxim, [the author] states in the rule concerning conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) that there are many purposes for this [maxim],
and for that purpose, this *paribhāṣā* must be formulated.
And it has been stated that "one must provide a remedy for faults" in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *samprasāraṇācca*.

And it has been implied that the counter-argument regarding the scope of the technical definition (*paribhāṣā*) consists precisely in resorting to the principle of non-uniformity (*anityatva*); this suffices.

But in this case, in forms such as *gomatpriyaḥ*, since the elision (*luk*) is dependent on two words, it is "external" (*bahiraṅga*); would this not set aside the "internal" (*antaraṅga*) elision of the *hal-ṅy-ādi* rule [P. 6.1.68] and cause *num* and other operations to apply? To this, he says:
"The external elision (*luk*) sublates even internal rules. (Paribhāṣā 52)
And in this regard, the rule *pratyayottarapadayośca* serves as the indicator (*jñāpaka*).

In forms such as *tvatkṛtam*, since the substitution of *tvam* and *aham* by the rule *tvamāvekavacane*—which is conditioned by the case-ending—is more internal (*antaraṅga*) than the elision (*luk*), that [substitution] is already established; thus, the present rule being otherwise redundant, it indicates that [the elision applies].
Now, one might object: "In *tava putraḥ*..."
If it is argued that [the mention of *apādāna*] is necessary in rules such as *tvatputraḥ* to prevent the subversion of *tava*, *mama*,
and so on, then the author of the Bhāṣya maintains that the continued application (*anuvṛtti*) of the term *apādāna* in this very rule is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) of that fact.
However, the *kviP* suffix for the sense of habitual action (*ācāra*) is not applied after words such as *yuṣmad*;
this is because the entire *sūtra* [Pāṇini 3.1.8] serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) according to the authority of the subsequent *bhāṣya*,
and because, by the authority of the rule prescribing the *nuṭ* augment— "hrasvanadyāpaḥ" (Pāṇini 7.1.54)— the *kviP* suffix for habitual action does not occur after bases ending in consonants.
In the same way, it should be understood that even the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) and the causative suffix (*ṇic*) are not denoted by two stems that have the same meaning.
By this, the argument that the mention of the suffix (*pratyaya-grahaṇa*) there is purposeful for the sake of providing a substitute (*ādeśa*) is refuted.

[Objection: But surely the continued application of the rule up to the word *maparyanta* is also purposeful for the sake of preventing [the substitution] from being a total replacement (*sarvādeśatva*).

If it is argued that the recurrence [of the term *maparyanta*] is redundant because the substitution for everything up to the final *m* is already established by the maxim "exceptions do not supersede general rules" (*na cotsargasamānādeśā apavādāḥ*), as accepted in the Bhāṣya on the rule *asiddhavad atra*— and that this maxim is set aside here because it is contradicted in cases such as *śnam* and *akac*— then [the following is said].

No; for although that [rule] is sublated here by the inclusion of *mit* in the case of *śnam*, by the prior mention of *bahu-c* in the case of *bahuc*, and by the prior mention of *pra-k* in the case of *akac*, this [present rule] remains a general maxim (*utsarga*).
Because there is no intention [to apply] the elision (*tyāga*) [of the suffix],
for this very reason the prescription of the substitutes *yuṣmāka-* and so forth by the rule "tasminnaṇi ca" is purposeful;
otherwise, there would be only the substitute *akaṅ*.

One should prescribe [the substitution]. By the aforementioned reasoning, since the two exceptions—*tavadādyādeśa* and *ākaṅ*—would result in being substitutes for the final letter (*antyādeśatva*), their specific prescription is made;
and this very fact is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) of that [principle].

Although this principle— that sublation occurs only when there is a contradiction— belongs to the view of the Vārttikakāra, the Bhāṣyakāra, however, maintains that sublation can occur even in the absence of a contradiction, provided that [the two rules] are otherwise possible; thus, according to Kaiyaṭa’s interpretation of the sūtra *anabhihite*, this is not an absolute rule.
Nevertheless, since the general rule (*utsarga*)—as indicated by the prescription of substitutes for [stems] ending in *yuṣmad* and so forth—is indeed accepted, there is no fault in the present case.
This very Bhāṣya is also an authority for its acceptance.
And thus, the continued application of the term "ending in *map*" (in Pāṇini’s sūtra) is for the purpose of prescribing substitutes for that which ends in *map*, as in the example *tvatkṛtam*.

In that regard, since the forms *tvam* and *mām* would already be established by virtue of being internal (*antaraṅga*), the rule [Pāṇini 7.2.97] stating "saṃt" is redundant; its purpose is to serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*).

Once this is indicated, however, because the substitutes beginning with *ta-* do not apply in this specific domain, they lack the status of being exceptions (*apavāda*); thus, the rule becomes meaningful for the sake of providing substitutes for the portion ending in *m* (i.e., *maparyanta*). This is the intended meaning.

As for what Haradatta stated—that since the suffix and the subsequent word (*uttarapada*) cannot end in *m* when the internal operation takes effect, the continued application [of the rule] is redundant and therefore serves as an indicator—that is [incorrect].
No; for even internal rules (antaraṅga) are subject to sublation by exceptions (apavāda), and thus they do not apply in the domain of those exceptions.
In fact, this is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) only according to the method of the Vārttika;
however, according to the method of the Bhāṣya, they say that this matter is merely based on explicit statement (*vācanika*).
Some maintain that this [rule] pertains exclusively to the elision (*luk*) governed by the rule *supo dhātu* (Pāṇini 6.1.68).

Others hold, on the authority of the original author of the grammatical treatises as seen in the rules *eṅhrasvātsambuddheḥ* (6.1.69) and *na yāsayoḥ* (6.1.70), that it pertains exclusively to elision (*luk*).
Regarding the first view, the *Bhāṣya* states that in examples such as *ahe trapu*, elision (*luk*) occurs by setting aside the [subsequent] deletion (*lopa*) through this very principle.
It has been stated: in the final stage, every elision (*luk*) subverts even internal rules, not merely the elision of case-endings (*sup-luk*).
For this very reason, in forms such as *sanīsraṃsaḥ*, the elision of the nasal (*na-lopa*) does not occur.

In examples such as *pañcabhiḥ khaṭvābhiḥ krītaḥ* ("bought for five beds") resulting in *pañcakhaṭvaḥ*, Kaiyaṭa has stated that the elision (*luk*) of the feminine suffix *ṭāp* occurs prior to the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*). Otherwise, if the elision were to occur after the single-substitute had been applied, the vowel *a* would not be heard.

In contradiction to this, Kaiyaṭa, in his commentary on the sūtra *tadrājasya*, stated that regarding the example *aty-aṅgaḥ* ("one who has surpassed the Aṅgas"), since the case-ending (*sup*) has been elided, there is an absence of "subsequent plurality" (*bahuvacana-paratva*); thus, he raised the objection that the elision (*luk*) prescribed by *tadrājasya* would not apply. While explaining this portion of the Bhāṣya, he raised the concern that, according to the maxim *antaraṅgān api vidhīn bahiraṅgo lug bādhate*, this [sūtra-based] *luk* might subvert the elision of the case-ending (*sub-luk*). Anticipating this, he established the superior force of the *sub-luk* itself by this [rule].
It should be understood that by this [statement], the superiority of *luk* (elision) is indicated;
for it is impossible to assert that *luk* is stronger than *luṅ* (deletion). Therefore, it is appropriate to state the objection and its resolution [in this way].

By this principle, the strength of *luk*—which destroys the causes of internal operations—as well as the strength of the compounds and other factors that cause it, is made known; a detailed discussion of this may be found elsewhere.

But in that case, since the *guṇa* substitution [of *o* for *au*] would apply by virtue of being internal (*antaraṅga*) in the formation of *saumendra*, the preceding member *pura-* would not exist as part of the word *parendra*; consequently, the prohibition of *vṛddhi* by the rule "not after *indra*" (*nendrasya parasya*) would be redundant.
Furthermore, the treatment of the end of the first member and the beginning of the second as a single unit (*antādivadbhāva*) is prohibited when both are simultaneously relied upon.
Moreover, even *vṛddhi* itself would not apply here.

Even though [the compound] lacks both the status of being like the beginning and the status of being like the end, because the word *indra* is treated as a prior member (*pūrvapada*) within the single-substitute form by virtue of its status as being like the prior limit (*pūrvāntavat*), and because the rule "when relying on both sides, it is neither like the end nor like the beginning" does not apply, or even if one relies on that [rule], since it is without a vowel (*anacka*), the subsequent portion is removed by the obligatory elision of *y* (*yasyeti-lopa*) following the single substitution.

Nor should it be argued that the possibility [of the rule's application] exists because the status of being an "uttarapada" (subsequent member of a compound) could simply belong to the single-substitute (ekādeśa)-qualified form by virtue of its being treated as the subsequent member (*parādivadbhāva*). This is because the *vṛddhi* substitution is prescribed for the initial vowel of the *uttarapada*; in the absence of such an initial vowel, the rule would not apply, as there is no extension (*atideśa*) of that specific form.

Otherwise, as is clear in the Bhāṣya, even in forms such as *khaṭvābhiḥ*, since the final portion would be treated as ending in /ā/ by virtue of being like the preceding part (*pūrvāntavattva*), the substitution of *ais* for *bhis* would result.

For this very reason, in examples such as *pūrveṣukāmaśamaḥ*, it was raised as an objection that, due to its being internal (*antaraṅga*), the *guṇa* substitution would take effect and thus the *vṛddhi* would not occur;
furthermore, because there is no modification of even a single part of that [base].
As it is stated in the Bhāṣya: "In the case of *indra-ekavacana*..."

One [portion] is removed by the elision (*lopa*) of the *yasya* suffix, while the other is removed by the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*); thus, the word *indra* becomes devoid of vowels (*anacka*), and in that case, what occasion is there for *vṛddhi*?

In a *dvandva* compound with Indra as one member, such as *marut-ādibhiḥ* and *indra*, Indra alone is placed first; therefore, it is said: "The single-substitute (*ekādeśa*) does not take effect before the operation conditioned by the preceding or following member, even if that substitute is *antaranga*. (Paribhāṣā 53)

And in this regard, it is clear from the Bhāṣya on the two sūtras "antādivacca" and "vipratiṣedhe param" that the very prohibition "not [the substitution] of Indra" (nendrasya) serves as the indicator (jñāpaka).

But even so, in forms such as *pradhāya* and *prasthāya*, since the operations for doubling (*dvitva*) and so forth are internal (*antaraṅga*), the suffix *lyap* would apply after they have been performed; therefore, he says:
"The suffix *lyap*, though external (*bahiraṅga*), subverts even internal rules" (Paribhāṣā 54).

In the rule *ado jagdhir lyapi*, since the result would already be established by the condition *ti-kiti* alone, the explicit mention of *lyap* serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for this [substitution]; this is clear in the *Bhāṣya* on that very rule.

But even so, in cases such as *iyāya*, once reduplication has occurred, the long vowel substitution (*savarṇadīrgha*) would apply because it is internal (*antaraṅga*), and thus that [result] would not be established; therefore, he says:
"An operation concerning a suffix (*āṅga*) is more powerful than one concerning a phoneme (*vārṇa*). (Paribhāṣā 55)
Therefore, by overriding even the internal *savarṇa*-dīrgha [substitution], the *vṛddhi* [substitution] is established.
The mention of *asavarṇa* in the rule prescribing *iyaṅ*— namely, *abhyāsasyāsavarṇe*— is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) for this.
For that [rule] is indeed intended to exclude *iyaṅ* and so forth in forms such as *īṣatuḥ*.

However, in the absence of this paribhāṣā, [the rule would be] useless because in *īṣatuḥ* and similar forms, the substitution of *savarṇadīrgha* (long vowel of homogeneous quality), being *antaraṅga*, would supersede it;
for *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* are *bahiraṅga* since they are conditioned by their connection with the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*).
The ancients maintain that this [substitution of *iy*] and so forth is not an exception (*apavāda*),

because, according to the maxim "that which applies when another has not yet applied" (*yenāprāptinyāya*), it is determined to be an exception specifically to the *yaṇ* substitution in all its instances, such as in the form *iyati*. However, others argue that in the absence of this paribhāṣā, the very rule "of the reduplication" (*abhyāsasya*) would be rendered useless.
Nor is [the rule] fulfilled in cases such as *iyāya* and *iyeṣa*,

because even for those two, once the doubling has been performed, the previously applied *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* are set aside by the extension of form (*rūpātideśa*) according to the rule "dvirvacaneci"; subsequently, when *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* would again apply, they are superseded by the occurrence of *savarṇadīrgha* (long vowel of homogeneous sounds) due to its being an internal operation (*antaraṅga*).
Nor is that [rule] rendered purposeful by the phrase "in this much" (*iyati*) and so forth;
for if its function were restricted to that alone, one would have simply said "uḥ. The [word] *yv-oh* is understood from the previous context, as in the rule "iṇo yaṇ."
Due to association (*sāhacarya*) and because of the grammatical commentary (*vyākhyāna*), only the root *ṛ* is understood;
therefore, the meaning is that *iy-aṅ* replaces the vowel *i*. This is stated in the rule: "In place of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*), when followed by *ā*."
Alternatively, it is not tenable [to claim] that [the rule] is necessary because of the heaviness [of the suffix] due to the *ārti* (difficulty) of practice;

nor is that sūtra indispensable for the purpose of *iyaṅ* and so forth in the *liṭ* [perfect tense] after the words *e*, *ai*, *o*, and *au* when they have the *kvip* suffix denoting habitual action (*ācāra*).

Likewise, it must be stated that [the rule] is necessary for the purpose of forms such as "uvoṇakīyiṣati," because those [forms] are not expressed according to the authority of the Bhāṣya located at the end of the first section of the sixth book;
furthermore, since in the latter case there is only the second doubling (dvirvacana), the usage you have mentioned is itself difficult to obtain.
And thus, it is logical that the entire sūtra serves as the indicator (*jñāpaka*).

Although, in the Bhāṣya, by the passage beginning "In that he makes this mention of 'non-homogeneous' (*asavarṇa*) in the rule *abhyāsasyāsavarṇe*," it appears that the indicator-status belongs to the mention of "non-homogeneous" alone; [nevertheless, the whole sūtra is intended].

Nevertheless, by the explanatory passage stating, "For without *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*, there is no repetition of a non-homogeneous vowel," the entire sūtra is obtained as the indicator (*jñāpaka*). Furthermore, later on, by the statement, "This is not a [valid] indicator;
this would be for the sake of excessive restriction (*atyarthaṃ*)," the very purposefulness of the sūtra is demonstrated.
If the mention of "non-homogeneous" (*asavarṇa*) were intended solely as an *jñāpaka* (indicatory evidence), then its purpose would indeed be demonstrated by showing what it excludes.

Furthermore, it is not the case that the long vowel substitution (*savarṇadīrgha*) fails to apply in forms such as *iyeṣa* due to the *akṛtavyūha* paribhāṣā; for if the long vowel were not to occur [there], then...

It should not be argued that the entire sūtra serves as an *jñāpaka* (indirect indicator) because the application of the *paribhāṣā* is easily established through the existence of the possibility (*sambhāvanā*) that "there might be a benefit" (*guṇaḥ syāt*); for such a possibility does not exist.

Or, even if it did exist, according to the authority of this very Bhāṣya, [the *paribhāṣā* applies] only in cases where the occurrence of an external rule (*bahiraṅga-vidhi*)—which destroys the cause of the internal operation—takes place precisely after the time when the internal operation (*antaraṅga-kārya*) was ready to occur.
Furthermore, because the application of that very technical designation (*paribhāṣā*) is accepted in that very context.

Nor can it be argued that even in cases such as *iyāya*, where the long vowel is *antaraṅga* (internally conditioned), the rule is rendered purposeful by the prescription of *iyaṅ* for the non-homogeneous vowel before *ṇal*—since the preceding portion (*pūrvāntavat*) constitutes the reduplication (*abhyāsa*), and since the vowel is indeed a phoneme (*ivarṇa*).
Nor is its establishment achieved by the rule *aci śnu*.
It should be stated that this is for the purpose of precluding *vṛddhi*.
For, by virtue of proximity (*pratyāsatti*), the term "non-homogeneous" (*asavarṇa*) refers only to a non-homogeneous vowel belonging to the portion following the reduplicated syllable;
moreover, it is more appropriate to regard [the rule] as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of a *paribhāṣā* than to assume it sublates the grammatical rule (*śāstra*). Thus they say.

And this [application of the rule] arises from the means of knowledge that apprehends the substratum (dharmigrāhakamāna) only when the *aṅga* and the suffix (*vārṇa*) have the same grammatical operation (*samānakāryitva*).

As for the claim that it applies only when there is a common locus (*samānāśrayatva*) in the form of having a common cause (*samānanimittakatva*), that is not correct; for even if that were made known, forms such as *iyāya* and *iyeṣa* would still remain unestablished.
Furthermore, the rule would remain useless (*vaiyarthya*) as it stands.

However, in the case of *syonaḥ*, since this [substitution] does not apply due to its being non-eternal (*anitya*) according to the method to be explained later, the *yaṇ* replacement occurs because it is more internal (*antaraṅga*) than the *guṇa*.
Nor is it the case that even so, *iyaṅ* would be difficult to obtain in forms such as *iyāya*; [for the following reason:]...

In that case, it should not be argued that because [the operation] is to be performed there, the substitution by virtue of being *sthānivadbhāva* is prohibited by the rule "asavarṇe" (Pāṇini 6.1.102);
for precisely by the force of the formulation of the sūtra itself, *sthānivadbhāva* does not apply.
And that [force] pertains to the general case.

In the case of an operation concerning the reduplication (*abhyāsa*), the status as *sthānivadbhāva*—which acts as an obstacle to that operation—is not applicable to the substitute (*ādeśa*) of the subsequent portion (*uttarakhaṇḍa*).

For this very reason, the objection that in forms such as *ārati*, the long vowel (*dīrgha*) prescribed by the rule "ḍhralope" would be difficult to obtain because the substitution of *yaṇ* is *sthānivadbhūta*, is refuted;
furthermore, this is because that [application of *sthānivadbhāva*] is prohibited in the context of rules prescribing a long vowel.

In the case of *ariyiyāt*, the substitution *iyaṅ* indeed occurs by virtue of the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* (as if it were the original), because that *sthānivadbhāva* does not act as an obstacle to the application of the reduplication rule (*abhyāsakārya*).

This is stated in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra "svarito vā" [Pāṇini 8.2.6], which says: "And this [substitution] belonging to the stem (*aṅgasambandhinī*) applies only when the stem itself [is being reduplicated]."
For in that context, the augment *āṬ* is prescribed after the *yaṇ* substitute in forms such as *kumāryai*;
and this [substitution] is non-eternal (*anitya*), because of the mention of *tug* in the rule *chvoḥ*.

Otherwise, since the *tuk* augment would apply first due to its being antaranga, the substitution of *śatṛ* would not be applicable to *tuk*, making the mention of *tug* clearly redundant; thus, the details are explained elsewhere.

If it is objected that, in forms such as *seduṣaḥ*, since the suffix *kvasu* is internal (*antaraṅga*), the augment *iṭ* would apply first; and subsequently, even after the vowel substitution (*samprasāraṇa*), there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of hearing the *iṭ*—to this some reply: "The followers of Pāṇini do not [apply] a grammatical operation when the conditions for another have already been established" (*akṛtavyūhāḥ pāṇinīyāḥ*). (Paribhāṣā 56)
"Those by whom no distinguished deliberation— that is, no certainty— has been made regarding the subject matter of the treatise's application";
the phrase "the destruction of future causes" is to be supplied here.
When the destruction of the cause of an internal rule is subsequently possible due to an external factor, the internal rule does not apply; this is the meaning.
And here, the evidence is the word "samarthānām" in the sūtra "samarthānāṃ prathamāt."
