For that [suffix] is indeed intended for the production of the suffix after forms such as *sūtthita* where the long vowel has already been applied;
otherwise, since the suffix would apply even when the long vowel has already been formed due to its being an internal operation (*antaraṅga*), its purposelessness would be evident.

Nor should it be argued that at the time of the application of the single-substitute (*ekādeśa*), although *vṛddhi* has not yet occurred, once the single substitute has been applied, even though *vṛddhi* would then apply, there is no destruction of its cause;
for the destruction of its cause remains intact precisely because of that very [application].
Nor should it be argued that in the case of *sautthitau*, since *vṛddhi* is *asiddha* due to being *bahiraṅga*, there is no destruction of its cause.
By the inclusion of the term "samartha" (capable), it is indicated that this [paribhāṣā] does not apply even in such a context;
as for the claim that the inclusion of "samartha" merely indicates the non-eternality (anityatva) of the *antaraṅga* paribhāṣā.

That is not so; for the *asiddhaparibhāṣā* teaches that an external (*bahiraṅga*) operation— whether it is simultaneously applicable with an internal one or has already arisen before it— is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) when an internal (*antaraṅga*) operation is to be performed, but it does not teach its non-existence once the internal operation has already taken place, as there is no evidence for such a claim.
And because there is no result [of such a rule];
for in this way, since the single-substitute (ekādeśa) rule is not established by means of a *paribhāṣā*, it is impossible to indicate its non-eternality (*anityatva*).
Furthermore, the principle beginning with "even rules that are *antaraṅga*... is included within this very [category].
And in this case of grammatical application (*pravṛtti*), even the possibility of the destruction of the cause (*nimitta*) serves as a condition for its occurrence.
For this very reason, in examples such as *gomaddaṇḍī*, there is no elision of the *hal* or *ṅī* suffixes (by Pāṇini 6.1.68).

Otherwise, at the time of the elision of the *hal* or *ṅī*, since the elision of the compound (*sāmāsika-luk*) would not yet have applied, and subsequently—due to the absence of anything to be removed—the elision itself would result in being unapplicable.
And here too there exists the possibility: "If elision (*lopa*) were not to occur, then elision by substitution (*luk*) would occur.
However, the inclusion of the *tapara* marker in the rule *alloponaḥ* serves its purpose by making known the non-universality (*anityatva*) of this *paribhāṣā*.
For that [mention of *āna*] is indeed for the purpose of preventing elision in cases such as *āna*.

Otherwise, since there would be a possibility of elision in the absence of lengthening, and because lengthening would not apply by virtue of this paribhāṣā, its redundancy would be quite evident; so they say.

However, Kaiyaṭa, on the sūtra *samarthānām*, states that this paribhāṣā is indicated by the mention of the word *samartha*: "The followers of Pāṇini do not [apply] a grammatical operation (*vyūha*) once it has been completed."

By stating that the augment *iṭ*, although applied earlier than the internal [rule], is nevertheless set aside in cases such as *papuṣaḥ*, he intends the following meaning: "no *vyūha* has been made"—that is, no exceptional reasoning (*viśiṣṭas tarkaḥ*) consisting in the persistence of the effect even upon the destruction of its instrumental cause. This amounts to the principle: "When the cause ceases, the effect produced by it also ceases."

In the rule *sūtthitādiñi* (Pāṇini 7.3.45), when the *vṛddhi* substitution is applied, the long vowel (*dīrgha*) is excluded so that the form *sāvutthitiḥ* does not occur; this is why the condition *samarthānām* ("of those [words] which are semantically connected") is stated.
Furthermore, this matter is established by worldly convention.
For in the world, a cause (*nimitta*) is seen to be of two kinds: one that determines the presence of the effect (*kāryasthito niyāmaka*), and one that does not determine it (*tadaniyāmaka*).
The first case is, for example, in the Nyāya system, where it is accepted that when the enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) is destroyed, duality (*dvitva*) is also destroyed;
and in the Vedānta system, it is well known that *prārabdha* karma acts as the regulator for the persistence of mental distraction (*vikṣepa*).
The second [type] is like a staff and so forth, because it is observed that even upon the destruction of that [staff], the jar is destroyed;
in the treatise, the rule is established in accordance with the observed instances (*lakṣya*).

Regarding the destruction of a future cause, there is no logical principle for its non-arising beforehand, nor is there any commonly accepted example. It should be understood that the intention [of the author] is this: since the purpose of the rule "samarthānām" (Pāṇini 2.1.1) is fulfilled by making known meanings already established in common usage, there is no evidence for it being intended to make known such meanings that are not so established in common usage. Others, however, maintain that in the case of forms like *seduṣaḥ*, when the derivation is performed word-by-word (*padāvadhika*)—where the stage is *ased vas as*—the augment *iṭ* and the vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) apply.

This is clear from Kaiyaṭa’s commentary on the sūtra "samarthānām" [Pāṇini 2.1.1], where it is stated that because the rule for *samprasāraṇa* is prescribed by a specific injunction (*pratipadavidhi*), the *samprasāraṇa* occurs first; consequently, since the condition of being preceded by a *val*-beginning suffix (*valāditva*) is absent, there is no possibility of the augment *iṭ* at all, and thus its establishment [of the desired form] follows.
This is also clearly stated in Kaiyaṭa’s commentary on the sūtra "asiddhavat" [Pāṇini 6.4.22].

Although being prescribed by a subsequent rule (*pratipadavidhitva*) is indeed the seed for sublation only when there is no scope [for the earlier rule], nevertheless, its intention is that it certainly serves as a regulator even when it has scope, provided it applies first.
And this has been explained many times in the *Śabdenduśekhara* and other works.

The inclusion of the term *samartha* (capable) in the rule (*sūtra*) "samarthānām" is intended to prevent the misconception that [sandhi] applies everywhere— since one observes suffixes even in cases like *viṣuṇaḥ* where sandhi has not yet occurred— and thus it restates a meaning established by reasoning (*nyāyasiddha*).
This is indicated in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule "vipratiṣedha," where it is stated that in the case of *vaikṣamaṇiḥ*, the internal factor (*antaraṅga*)...
The example for the technical definition (*paribhāṣā*) has been stated.

Furthermore, in the analytical exposition (*vibhajyānvākhyāna*), when the state "asu utthita as i" is reached, the mention of *samartha* (meaningful connection) is intended to prevent the application of *vṛddhi*— which would otherwise be required by the rule "that which pertains to a phoneme (*vārṇa*) is stronger than that which pertains to a suffix (*āṅga*)"— as is clear in Kaiyaṭa’s commentary on this very point.

For this very reason, it is stated in the Bhāṣya on the *asiddhavat* sūtra: "'The substitution of semivowels (*samprasāraṇa*) for *vasu* must be declared as established (*siddha*) in the rule for the suffix *ac*; [otherwise], in forms such as *papuṣaḥ*, once the semivowel substitution for *vasu* has occurred, the elision of the long *ā* [of the root *pā*] would not take place. If the word were analyzed through a sequential derivation (*vibhajyānvākhyāna*) according to the previously mentioned view of Kaiyaṭa, the semivowel substitution would occur first; since the augment *iṭ* would then not apply, the elision of the long *ā* would be caused solely by the presence of the *u* [of *vasu*]. Consequently, the aforementioned Bhāṣya statement would be inconsistent.
For this very reason, the author of the Vārttika initiated the statement "the prohibition [of doubling] applies to each individual member," and the author of the Bhāṣya did not reject it;
for *pratyaṅgam* means "with respect to each individual member" (*antaraṅgam*).
If this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) were true, its redundancy would be quite evident.

For this very reason, it is stated in the *Bhāṣya* on the sūtra “*chvoḥ*” [Pāṇini 6.4.19]: “An effort must certainly be made here to prevent the occurrence of *tuṅ*; for by virtue of being *antaraṅga*, *tuṅ* would otherwise apply.
If this [technical rule] were present, however, *tuṅ* would not apply at all, and thus the statement regarding the necessity of such an effort would clearly be incoherent.

Nor is it the intention [of the author] that this [statement] is solely for the purpose of making known impermanence (*anityatva*), because that would result in a violation of the natural sense of the words in the phrase "it must necessarily be here" (*avaśyam atra*).

Furthermore, since the rules "pratyayottarapadayoś ca" and "ado jagdhir lyapi kiti" would already have their scope of application through this very [statement], the principle stated in the *Bhāṣya*— that by virtue of such an indicator (*jñāpaka*), the elision (*luk*) and *lyap* override what is internally more powerful (*antaraṅga*)— would be undermined.
Furthermore, this [paribhāṣā] is not seen in the Bhāṣya.

As stated by Kaiyaṭa on the sūtra "asiddhavat": "Because the author of the Bhāṣya does not rely upon the paribhāṣā, 'When the cause [of an operation] disappears, that which was occasioned by it also disappears. In the view of word-formation (*padasaṃskārapakṣa*), once the visarga has been applied in forms such as *hariḥ*, [the rule would apply].
Therefore, in a construction such as "tato gacchati" (he goes from there), only forms like "hariḥ gacchati" (Hari goes) and so forth are grammatically correct;
or, in that regard, one may simply not resort to the view of word-level phonological refinement (*pada-saṃskāra-pakṣa*). This is the general direction [of the argument].
“An exception (apavāda) is stronger even than that which is internal (antaraṅga). Regarding this, he states the meaning of the term *apavāda*:
“That rule which is commenced when another has not yet taken effect is the sublater of that [other]. (Paribhāṣā 57)
The suffix *kta* in *prāpta* is used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*); thus, the phrase *yena nāprāptaḥ* means "by which there is an inevitable attainment.
This is because the double negative (*nañ-dvaya*) conveys the strengthening of the primary meaning.

And thus, there is sublation (*bādha*) of a general rule (*sāmānya-śāstra*)— which has as its object that which is delimited by a general property residing in that which is delimited by the specific property intended by a specific rule (*viśeṣa-śāstra*)— by that specific rule.
For the seed of this [specific rule's] power to sublate is its lack of purposeful application (*acāritārthyam*) with respect to that which is not a locus for the application of the former.

For this very reason, in the rule *āyādayaḥ*, one might raise the objection that in forms such as *agopāyiṣyati*, the suffixes beginning with *sy* (the third-person endings) would apply by virtue of being subsequent, thereby subverting the application of the *āy* and other substitutes; to this, it is replied: "The *āy* and other substitutes are without scope [elsewhere]. However, even in cases such as *gopāyati*, the suffix *śap* would still apply. And there is no difference whether *śap* is present or absent.
Now this is stated: there is no distinction.

As it was said [in the Bhāṣya]: "There is no scope for *āt* and the others that is not pervaded by *syat* and the others; such a scope does not exist. Thus, even though [the suffixes] have fulfilled their purpose after the application of those [others], it is exactly the same in that there is no scope unpervaded by them.
Furthermore, even after its operation, there must be the cognition of its sublation once its purpose has been fulfilled;
otherwise, since sublation would already be established by the very fact that [the subsequent rule] finds no scope [to operate], this statement would result in redundancy,
and the demonstration of the "curd-Kauṇḍinya" maxim (*takrakauṇḍinyanyāya*) would likewise result in redundancy.

Likewise, there is the sublation (*bādha*) of the first doubling by the second doubling, which occurs subsequently and possesses its own scope; or just as the rule *ādeḥ parasya* (P. 1.1.54), which has already fulfilled its purpose through its application even to the initial sound, sublates the rule *alo 'ntyasya* (P. 1.1.52).
As it has been stated in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *midaco 'ntyāt*: "Even when [two rules] are both possible, there is sublation (*bādhana*).
Otherwise, in the case of the example "Let curd be given to the Brāhmaṇas; but buttermilk to Kauṇḍinya," the giving of curd would not be sublated by the giving of buttermilk.
Because it is possible for that *dān* [suffix] to have its purpose fulfilled either subsequent to or prior to that [application of the rule];
for this very reason, even when the domains differ, it functions as an exception (*apavāda*).

For this same reason, anticipating an objection that the *nuṭ* augment would be sublated by the substitution of *aciḥ* (the *aci-ādeśa*), the *Bhāṣya* on the *sūtra* "tṛjvat" resolves it by means of the indicator (*jñāpaka*) "na tisṛ."
Regarding this, some maintain that it is understood from this that there is an absence of *apavāda* (exception) status even when there is a difference in scope;
however, that is not correct, because by the elision (*luk*) of the suffixes *-vin* and *-mat*, there would result in no sublation of the mere *ṭi*-elision. (Note:
In certain editions, although the maxim “an exception is stronger than even what is internal” (*antaraṅgād apy apavādo balīyān*) has been accepted as a *paribhāṣā* [technical rule],...)

However, because this is already covered by the principle "among rules that are [respectively] subsequent, permanent, internal, or exceptions, each succeeding one is stronger," and because of the natural inclination of Nāgeśa’s writing,
and because it is recited in the list of Paribhāṣās;
Because it has been upheld by Candrikākāra, and because it has also been accepted by Bhaṭṭoji Dīkṣita in the Siddhāntakaumudī,
[the principle applies that] "that rule which is commenced when something else is not already established..."
"In this context, it is recited as a technical rule (paribhāṣā) precisely in the form: 'it becomes its sublater'."
As for what Kaiyaṭa stated in the commentary on the sūtra "dayater digi" regarding the purposeful application of the substitute *digi* after reduplication—
that was said with boldness (prauḍhi); and that its status is indeed such has been indicated by him himself in the subsequent passage.

The view of the *Vārttika*—namely, that "impossibility itself constitutes the sublation [of a rule], because contradiction is its seed"—is not useful for establishing the intended definition (*lakṣya*), since it has been refuted by the author of the *Bhāṣya*. Furthermore, the maxim of "the curd for Kauṇḍinya" (*takrakauṇḍinya-nyāya*) concerns a domain where the [general rule] does not apply and where its purpose is not yet fulfilled; thus, it applies only to the domain of what is to be enjoined (*vidheya*). This is clear from the *Bhāṣya* on such rules as "taddhiteṣvacāmādeḥ" (P. 7.2.117) and "dhātorekācaḥ" (P. 3.1.22).
In some cases, however, it functions as a sublater precisely because there is no possibility [for the other rule] at all;
for example, the substitution of *ām* for *ṅe* is a sublater of *yāṭ* and so forth.
For once *yāṭ* and the others have been applied, the substitution of *ām* for *ṅe* does not occur.
Because there is an intervention for that which is being pointed out;
in that case, their sublation occurs simply because its own [application] takes place first. Once the sublater has operated, if the general rule (utsarga) applies, then it certainly does so.
Just as in that very same case there is the introduction of the augment *yāṭ*,
but not when [the rule] is not applicable;
for example, in forms such as *apaceyuḥ*, because the substitution *iy*— which has no other scope (*niravakāśa*)— subverts the long vowel, the long vowel does not occur.
This is recited: "In some cases, even in the domain of an exception (apavāda), a general rule (utsarga) applies. (Paribhāṣā 58)
In this context, the word *apavāda* refers to an exception (*bādhaka*).
As it is stated in the Bhāṣya on the rule *guṇo yaṅlukoḥ*:
"Among the modifications of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*), exceptions do not supersede general rules."
In *ajīgaṇat*,
the substitution of *ī* for the root *gaṇ* (by Pāṇini 7.4.95) takes precedence over *halādiśeṣaḥ* (Pāṇini 7.4.60) because it is an exception (*apavāda*).
The substitution of *ī* for *gaṇ* does not take precedence over *halādiśeṣaḥ* because [in this specific case] it is an exception.

What then? By the text "because there is no scope," it is meant that the substitution of *ī* for the final *ṇ* of a reduplicated form consisting of a cluster [of consonants] would have no scope once the rule *halādiḥ śeṣaḥ* has applied and eliminated those [consonants]; however, when the substitution of *ī* has been performed, its application occurs because the final consonant (*hal*) no longer exists.
And it has been established that among the various modifications resulting from repetition, there is an absence of the relationship between the sublated and the sublator;
and since that [relationship] exists, when the elision (*lopa*) is performed, the substitution of *it* (the short *i*) applies by implication to the remaining final [element], so there is no fault.
Nor can its status as an exception (*apavāda*) be easily asserted on the basis of the principle of "that which was not previously applicable" (*yena nāprāpti*).
This is because it has already been stated that its scope consists of cases where the purpose [of the rule] has been fulfilled.
This point is also suggested in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *iko jhal*.

For in that context, when the long vowel in *ajjhana* has superseded the *guṇa* substitution, the *guṇa* would apply again after the lengthening—since it would otherwise be of no occasion (*anavakāśatva*) due to the absence of a result—were it not for this principle.

Regarding the rule for the lengthening [of the vowel] in *dīrghavidhānam*, once the lengthening has been applied, it is stated that the mention of *mī* in the rule *“sani mīmā”* (Pāṇini 7.4.54) serves a purpose because it includes the root *mā*; there, the subsequent application of the rule *“iko jhal”* (Pāṇini 1.2.9), which causes the suffix to be *kit*, is intended to block the *guṇa* substitution that would otherwise apply.

Otherwise, if the blocking were due to the status of an exception (*apavāda*), the general rule (*utsarga*) would not apply within the scope of that exception, and the inconsistency of both the *Bhāṣya* and the *Sūtra* would be evident.

As for the claim that in cases such as *kāñcanī*, the suffix *ayaṇ* occurs even in the domain of the exception (*apavāda*) *mayaṭ*— on the basis of the maxim "in some cases, [the general rule applies] even in the domain of an exception"— that is not correct; for it contradicts the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *aṇaḥ karmaṇi ca*.

For in that context, it has been stated—such as in "godāyo vrajati"—that the re-enunciation of the suffix *aṇ* is for the purpose of preventing its non-application in the domain of exceptions (*apavāda*).
In examples such as "kāñcanī," one should understand that the secondary (*śaiṣika*) suffix *aṇ* occurs in the sense of "constructed with gold" (*kāñcanena nirmitā*).
Here, this should be understood: if, in the rule *yenanāprāpte*, the word *yena* means "by something other than itself" (*svetareṇa*), [then the following applies].
In that case, whatever else one obtains within its own domain is sublated, because there is no scope for it that has not already been occupied by another injunction;
this very process is designated as the "general consideration of what is sublated."
Even if there is sublation by way of lack of scope (*anavakāśatva*), this [objection] can still be raised provided there is an example [of such a case],
because of the absence of a decisive criterion (*vinigamanāviraha*).
However, if the meaning of "by which" (*yena*) is "by which rule" (*lakṣaṇena*), [then the objection does not apply].
Alternatively, the meaning may be "by way of its function. In that case, there arises an inquiry into the specific nature of the sublation:

whether the meaningfulness [of the weaker rule] lies in the sublation of this [weaker rule], or rather in the sublation of that [stronger rule], even though the sublation occurs by virtue of [the stronger rule's] having no other occasion for application (*anavakāśatva*). Thus, an inquiry into the specific details is possible.
If there is an example.

In this context, regarding the meaning "by the effect," when it is not yet determined that the *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) which is about to be initiated—being delimited by the form of the subsequent element (*pararūpa*)—is a sublater of that [subsequent rule], he speaks while considering its specific nature, namely: "Is it that which is prescribed by a rule?
[The answer is: *Parastādapavādā anantarān vidhīn bādhante, nottarān* (Pariśiṣṭa 59): "Exceptions (*apavāda*) sublate the immediately preceding rules, but not those that follow."

The underlying rationale for this is as follows: when both one's own [rule] and another must necessarily be set aside, once the purpose is fulfilled by setting aside the immediately preceding rule that presents itself first, there is no evidence for setting aside a subsequent rule that presents itself later;
furthermore, since the requirement (*ākāṅkṣā*) has ceased, there is no evidence for setting aside a rule based on conflict (*vipratiṣedha*). This is the seed of the argument.

Having determined that, in the case of the portion beginning with "oṣṭha" in the rule *nāsikodarauṣṭhajaṅghādante*, there is a sublation (*bādhakatva*) delimited by the prohibition of the suffix *ṅīṣ*, he states— when the inquiry arises as to what is being set aside— that "exceptions (*apavāda*) sublate preceding rules."
Nor those from the north. // Paribhāṣā 60 //

Therefore, in the case of the five [suffixes] beginning with *auṣṭha*, it is precisely the prohibition [stated in Pāṇini 4.1.54], "not after a word ending in a conjunct consonant or having a penultimate vowel," that is set aside, and not the rule characterized by the presence of the prefix *sa-* or the word *nañ* (i.e., Pāṇini 4.1.57); this is clear from the *Bhāṣya* on the rule "nāsikodara" (Pāṇini 4.1.55).
The seed of this [independence] is the absence of expectancy due to the sublation of what was previously presented.
But surely, by the rule “vā chandasi,” there would be an option for *hi* as well— just as there is for the immediately preceding *apit* (the affix *si*) by the rule “serhyapicca”—

and likewise, by the prohibition “noṭa,” the prohibition would apply to the *vṛddhi* of both *sic* and *mṛji* characterized by the immediately preceding [rule] regarding the *halanta* [root], just as it does to the *vṛddhi* of *sic*. Therefore,
he states [his view] based precisely on the aforementioned reasoning:
A rule or a prohibition applies to what immediately precedes. // Paribhāṣā 61 //

For this very reason, the inclusion of the term *ṅīp* in the rule "saṃkhyāvyayādeḥ" is purposeful; for it serves to prevent the application of *ṅīṣ* to words ending in *an*. Likewise, the inclusion of the long vowel (*dīrgha*) in the rule "na ktici" is also purposeful.
For that [prohibition] is intended precisely to prevent the prohibition of the immediately preceding rule, "anudāttopadeśa-...
Kaiyaṭa, on the sūtra "aṣṭābhyaḥ," states that the maxim "the immediately preceding [is affected]" is stronger than the maxim regarding intermediate exceptions (*madhye 'pavādanyāya*).
This [maxim] is based on proximity (*pratyāsatti*).
There is also another position: that this rule is determined according to the requirements of the specific instances (*lakṣya*).
In various places, this principle is either set aside by the declaration of the *svarita* accent or by the force of the context (*sāmarthya*).
Just as by the rule *ṭiḍḍhāṇañ* there is the prescription of *ṅīp* even when it is separated by *ḍāp*,
and by the rule *na ṣaṭ* etc., there is the prohibition of both *ṭāp* and *ṅīp*;
and this [principle] is clear in the Bhāṣya on [sūtras] such as *śi sarvanāmasthānam*, with further details elsewhere.

[Objection: But in cases such as *dadhati*, since the substitution of *at* for the final [phoneme] is internal (*antaraṅga*), there would be no status as a substitute (*sthānivadbhāva*) because it is an operation concerning an *al* (a phoneme), and thus the substitute would not apply; consequently, that [rule] would result in being useless. To this, he says:
"For exceptions (*apavāda*) take effect first, and general rules (*utsarga*) afterwards. (Paribhāṣā 62)

For one whose sole eye is the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), having thoroughly examined the scope of negation (*apavāda*) and ascertained the absence of that [negation] within its own scope, one generally refines each respective object of definition (*lakṣya*).
Otherwise, there would be the consequence of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*); such is the meaning.
The phrase "they become attached" means that they become established upon the intellect (*buddhi*).

However, the maxim "if an exception finds its scope elsewhere" does not apply here, because there is no scope for it to find its application within the domain where the substitution of the final letter (antādeśa) would otherwise occur.

One whose sole eye is the linguistic object (*lakṣya*), however, even without a thorough investigation of that treatise (*śāstra*), refines the linguistic object by means of the general rule (*utsarga*), having set aside the domain of exceptions (*apavāda*).
For even for such a person, merit (*dharma*) arises only from usage preceded by the recollection of the grammatical procedure (*prakriyā*) of the treatise. Thus it is said:
"Having mentally excluded the domain of exceptions, the general rule then applies" (Paribhāṣā 63).
The meaning of “tataḥ” (then) is “even before the consideration of the rules that constitute exceptions. The meaning of “prakalpya” (having postulated) is “having set aside.

For this very reason, in the Bhāṣya on the *Pāṇinīya-sūtra* defining the meaning of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), it is said: “Having stated both of these, the general rule (*utsarga*) never [applies] at all.”
This was said for the purpose of awaiting an objection.
It is precisely on this basis that the moderns recite:
"An exception (*apavāda*), even when its cause is yet to arise, subverts a general rule (*utsarga*), even when the latter's cause has already arisen. (Paribhāṣā 64)

As for what Kaiyaṭa has stated in his commentary on the *Abhyastasūtra*, taking up the phrase "and having postulated" (*prakalpya ca*), namely: "Just as in the case of 'no *samprasāraṇa*' [the *samprasāraṇa* occurs first for the subsequent semi-vowel (*yaṇ*),

while the prohibition applies to the preceding one because it is caused by that]," this, however, is inconsistent with the literal meaning of the words beginning with "an exception (*utsarga*) from that."

As for the claim that the meaning of the general rule (utsarga) cannot be established without the meaning of the exception (apavāda), that is not correct; for it would result in a violation of the natural sense of the words in the passage beginning with "he enters the domain of the exception."
Furthermore, because there is an absence of the comprehension of the sentence meaning when there is an apprehension of word-meanings produced by words [but no syntactic connection],
whereas in cases where an exception (*apavāda*) is prohibited, the general rule (*utsarga*) indeed operates even within the scope of that exception.

Just as in the case of *vṛkṣau*, because the rule *nādici* prohibits the long vowel of the same quality (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*), the [subsequent] *vṛddhi* substitution proceeds without being obstructed by that [prohibition], since it does not apply [in that specific context]. For this very reason, forms such as *tau sat* are consistent. Precisely because of this indication, the maxim of "the lost opportunity" (*bhraṣṭāvasaranyāya*) is not resorted to in this grammatical system.
This has been explained in the *Bhāṣyapradīpodyota* on the *Bhāṣya* to the rule "iko guṇavṛddhī" (Pāṇini 1.1.3), where it is stated that the maxim—
"when the killer of Devadatta is killed, there is no resurrection of Devadatta"— does not apply here at all;
for when Devadatta himself is killed, there is no resurrection, nor is there one for the one who was intent on killing Devadatta.
In the case of killing, however, there is indeed an emergence [of the original state].
In the present case as well, it is not the case that the *vṛddhi* [vowel] is killed by the long vowel of the same quality (*pūrvasavarṇadīrgha*);
rather, there is merely a contingency (*prasakti*) that is of the same nature as the attempt to kill.
For it is only that which is applicable (*prasakta*) which is negated.
Furthermore, even the status of being explicitly stated (*pratipadoktatva*) is a cause for sublation (*bādha*) only when there is no other scope (*niravakāśatva*).
This is clearly stated in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule “*śeṣādvibhāṣā*” (Pāṇini 5.4.154).

For in that context, having raised the objection that "the inclusion of the word *śeṣa* (remainder) is purposeless, since those [suffixes] which are prescribed for specific words (*pratipadam*) will be the sublaters," it was stated: "Prescriptions are indeed sublaters when they have no other scope (*anavakāśa*), and the compound-final suffixes (*samāsānta*) do have scope in the absence of the suffix *kap*."

In some cases, even when there is no lack of scope (*anavakāśatva*), strength (*balavatva*)—which causes priority of application due to its quick presentation—is established by the status of being a *pratipadavidhi* (a rule prescribing a specific form) when there is a conflict with rules that are subsequent (*para*), permanent (*nitya*), and so forth. This is because Kaiyaṭa, in his commentary on the sūtra "pratyayottarapadayośca," records the reading: "When subsequent (*para*), permanent (*nitya*), internal (*antaraṅga*), and *pratipada* rules meet in conflict, they possess mutual relative strength. For this very reason, regarding forms such as *rame*, one might raise the objection that since the *etva* (the substitution of *e* for *ay*) is prescribed by a *pratipadavidhi*, it would apply first; consequently, due to the elision of the vowel *ā* (via *praśleṣa*), the elision of the consonant and following elements (*halṅyādilopa*) would not occur. Anticipating this, the objection is resolved by the elision according to the rule "eṅhrasvāt" (Pāṇini 6.1.69).

But surely, in examples such as *ayaje indram*, even though it is internal (*antaraṅga*), the *guṇa* substitution would be superseded by the long vowel resulting from the coalescence of similar vowels (*savarṇadīrgha*) because of the latter being an exception (*apavāda*). To this, he says:
"If an exception (*apavāda*) has its utility elsewhere, then it is superseded by what is internal (*antaraṅga*). (Paribhāṣā 65)
This is because there is an absence of the seed of sublation (*bādhakatva-bīja*), which consists in having no scope (*niravakāśatva*).

And thus, in the present case, the *savarṇadīrgha* (long vowel by homogeneous merger), which has already found its application within the same domain as the internal (*antaraṅga*) *guṇa*, also sublates the *yaṇ* [substitution], even though that *yaṇ* is an exception (*apavāda*) to the *guṇa*.
This refers to the domain of internality (*antaraṅgatva*) characterized by having a cause that presents itself earlier.
As for the fact that there is no relationship of sublation and being sublated between scripture and direct perception, it is because their results are different;
for this very reason, [it is said]: "Let curd be given to the Brahmins..."
In examples such as "kambalaḥ kauṇḍinyāya," Kaiyaṭa maintains on the basis of the sūtra "chvoḥ" that the gift of a blanket does not preclude the gift of curds.
This is incorrect, because it contradicts the Bhāṣya on the sūtra "dīrgho 'kitaḥ," which states: "The augment *nu* is an exception (*apavāda*) to the lengthening [of the vowel]."

Now, one might object that in forms such as *ajīgaṇat*, the substitution of *ī* for the vowel of the root *gaṇ* would, due to its lack of scope (*niravakāśatva*), supersede the rule of *halādiḥśeṣa* (the retention of the first consonant). To this, he says:
"In the case of modifications of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa*), there is no relationship of sublation and sublated. (Paribhāṣā 66)
The mention of *akic* (a suffix that is not *kit*) in the rule *dīrgho 'kitaḥ* is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) for this [paribhāṣā].

Otherwise, in the case of *ayaṃyayamyate*, once *nuṭ* has been applied, lengthening would not apply because the stem would no longer end in *an*; thus, the purpose of that [mention of *akic*] would be clearly redundant.
This [paribhāṣā] indicates that it is not sublated even by those [rules] that are otherwise sublaters of *antaraṅga* operations and the like.
By this, forms such as *acīkarat* and *mīmāṃsate* are established.
In the first case (*acīkarat*), the substitution of *sanvadbhāva* would be superseded by the lengthening [of the penultimate vowel], because the latter applies later in the order of rules.
In the second case (*mīmāṃsate*), the lengthening prescribed by the rule *mānbadha-* would supersede this [substitution of *sanvadbhāva*], because it is more internal (*antaraṅga*).

As for Kaiyaṭa’s statement on the sūtra "eka" that this [rule] applies only where all [substitutions] occur even after each individual [substitution] has taken place—that is not correct; for once *nuṭ* has been applied, the substitution of *it* would not apply, which would result in the inconsistency of the examples cited in the Bhāṣya under the sūtra "guṇo yaṅlukoḥ. This is explained in detail elsewhere.
But would not the suffix *ṇvul* also apply in the domain of *tṛn* when it signifies "one who habitually performs that action" (*tacchīla*) and so forth?
Nor can it be argued that *ṇvul* is an exception (*apavāda*) to *tṛn*, because an exception that is not of a dissimilar form (*asarūpa*) only subverts the general rule optionally. Therefore, he says:
The rule of non-identity of forms (*vāsarūpavidhi*) does not apply in the case of suffixes expressing habitual action (*tācchīlika*).

Since the suffix *ṇvul* is already established [by Pāṇini 3.1.133], the prescription of *vuñ* by the rule "nindahiṃsā... (Pāṇini 3.2.146) for roots ending in a single vowel (*ekāc*) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*).
This is because there is no difference in accent between *ṇvul* and *vuñ* in that context.
The locative case in "tācchīlikeṣu" is a locative of scope (*viṣaya-saptamī*).

Therefore, it should be understood that the rule of *vāsarūpa* (the optionality of alternative suffixes) does not apply with respect to suffixes that denote a habitual action (*tācchīlika*) or those that do not.

Now, an objection might be raised: "If this were so, forms such as *kamrā* and *kamanā* would be unestablished; for by the rule *namikampi-* [Pāṇini 3.2.167], the suffix *ra* would supersede the suffix *yuc* prescribed by the rule *anudāttetaśca halādeḥ* [Pāṇini 3.2.149]."
No; for by the rule "sūda-dīpa-dīkṣaś-ca," the prohibition of the *yuk* suffix after the root *dīp* indicates that the stated meaning is not universally obligatory (*anitya*).
Now, one might object: "In cases such as *hasitaṃ chātrasya hasanam* ('the laughing of the student'), the suffix *ghañ* would apply;
in *icchati bhoktum* ('he wishes to eat'), the optative (*liṅ*) and imperative (*loṭ*) suffixes would apply;
and in *īṣatpānaḥ somo bhavatā* ('Soma is easily drunk by you'), the suffix *khal* would apply. To this, he says:
In the case of the suffixes kta, lyuṭ, tumun, and those having the sense of khala, the rule of non-identity of form (vāsarūpavidhi) does not apply.
And this [form] is established because the rule regarding optional forms (*vāsarūpavidhi*) is not universally obligatory.
The evidence for its non-obligatoriness is the rule *arhe kṛtyatṛcaśca*.

For in that rule, the mention of the *kṛtya* suffixes and the *tṛc* suffix is made so that the *liṅ* suffix—conjoined by the particle *ca*—should not supersede them; this is explained in detail elsewhere.
This is clear in the Bhāṣya on the "vāsarūpa" sūtra.

[Objection: But in the case of "śvaḥ paktā" (he will cook tomorrow), by the rule of non-identity of form (*vāsarūpavidhi*), the suffix *lṛṭ* would also be applicable; since a difference in form arises once the substitute has been applied, [the author] says:
"Among the substitutes for *la*, the rule of non-identity of form does not apply. (Paribhāṣā 69)
The meaning is that it [the *liṭ*] does not exist in those *lakāra*s that have undergone morphological alteration (*vairūpya*) due to grammatical substitution (*ādeśa*).
And here, the prescription of the *laṅ* by the rule “*haśaśvatorlaṅ ca*” serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*).

Otherwise, since the co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of the *liṭ* with the *laṅ* would already be established by the rule “*parokṣe liṭ*” due to their dissimilarity (*asārūpya*), what would be the purpose of prescribing the *laṅ*?

In order to ensure the co-occurrence (*samāveśa*) of the *śatṛ* suffix with the *tiṅ* suffixes, the word "optionally" (*vibhāṣā*) is carried over into the rule prescribing the *śatṛ*, and the word "or" (*vā*) is included in the rule "liṭaḥ kānac vā" (A 3.2.106).

This indicates that, according to Kaiyaṭa and others, in the "vāsarūpa" sūtra (A 3.1.94), only a suffix that is not subsumed under the category of a substitute (*ādeśa*) is understood as being subject to the option. The result of this is that after roots such as *sad*, when expressing general past time, only the *kvus* suffix occurs in place of the *liṭ*.
However, it should be understood that [the suffix] *tiṅ* does not occur in the sense of a *pakṣa*.

Now, one might raise the objection: in rules such as "ṅamo hrasvāt," there would arise a doubt as to whether it means "of a *ṅam* [suffix] following [a vowel]" or "when a vowel follows a *ṅam*. Therefore, he says:
"When both [case-endings] are indicated, the indication by the fifth case (ablative) is more powerful. (Paribhāṣā 70)

Because the instruction in the locative case in *aci* finds its application later in the rule *mayauñaḥ*, the instruction in the ablative case [in *aci*] would have no scope; therefore, only the rule *tasmād ity uttarasya* operates.

However, where both [the locative and ablative instructions] lack application, as in *ḍaḥ si dhuṭ* and similar rules, the determination is made by that very rule (*tasmād ity uttarasya*) because it is subsequent to the rule *tasmin*.
Thus, even though both [rules] have their purpose fulfilled—
as in the case of "āmi sarvanāmnaḥ suṭ" and so forth—
therein, the locative case in "āmi" has its purpose fulfilled in the rule "trestrayaḥ."
It is clear from both the *Bhāṣya* and Kaiyaṭa’s commentary on the rule *tasminn iti* that the fifth [vowel] in *āditi* (i.e., the long *ī*) has its purpose fulfilled by the rule *āj-ja-ser asuk*.
Thus ends the second section, titled "The Seed of Sublation," in the *Paribhāṣenduśekhara* composed by the illustrious Nāgeśabhaṭṭa.
Now begins the third chapter, titled "The Remainder of the Treatise."
But would not the substitution of *s* by the rule “*ataḥ kṛkami*” fail to apply in the case of *ayaskumbhī*, since only the word *kumbha* is mentioned [in that rule]? To this, he says:
“When there is the mention of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), there is also the inclusion of that which is qualified by gender. (Paribhāṣā 71)

When there is the mention of a word that denotes a nominal stem (prātipadika) either in its general form or its specific form, it should be understood that this also includes [the same word] qualified by a suffix denoting gender;
the word "also" (api) implies that it includes the bare stem as well.

The indicator (jñāpaka) for this rule is the inclusion of feminine words such as *śramaṇā* in the sūtra “kumāra-śramaṇādibhiḥ,” which falls under the section governing grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

Furthermore, in cases such as *śramaṇā-kumārī* (a female ascetic maiden), the word *kumārī* alone stands in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with words characterized by feminine suffixes, and not the word *kumāra*; this, therefore, serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*).
And this [indicator] applies in the context of rules concerning secondary members (*upapada*), such as in the rule “*dviṣat-parayoḥ*” and so forth.
In the rule for the formation of compound endings, in the case of the substitution of *mahat* for *mahat*, and in the accentuation of suffixes marked with *ñ* or *ṇ*.

It is clear from the Bhāṣya on the *ṅyāpprātipadika* rule that [the term *prātipadika*] does not apply in cases such as *rājasva-re brāhmaṇakumārayoḥ* and *baho-r-nañvad-uttarapada-bhūmni*, nor in instances where a compound aggregate (*saṃghāta*) is intended to be included.
Furthermore, it is stated in that very same place that it does not apply in operations conditioned by case-endings (*vibhakti*).

In that regard, regarding the rule for adding suffixes to compounds (*samāsānta*), there is no application [of the term "compound"] when referring only to its constituent parts; however, it certainly applies when referring to the compound as a whole,
because the fault mentioned therein occurs specifically in the context of rules governing accent (*svara*) where the compound as a whole is intended.

And from the Bhāṣya on the sūtra "bahuvrīherūdhaso 'naṅ," because of the statement in the Bhāṣya: "The [suffix] does not apply in these very cases due to its non-eternality; moreover, the faults have indeed been enumerated in their entirety."
But in that case, there would be an inconsistency with the Bhāṣya on the sūtra "bahuvrīherūdhaso ṅīṣ.

For in that context, regarding the form "kuṇḍodhnī," the suffix *kap* is introduced by the rule "nadyṛtaśca" because the meaning is "from a bahuvrīhi ending in a feminine noun (*nadī*)," yet since [the word *kuṇḍodhnī*] lacks the status of being a bahuvrīhi while ending in a feminine noun, that [Bhāṣya] would be inconsistent.
This has already been resolved by the meaning "that compound which ends in a word ending in *nadī*.

If it is argued that [the rule refers to] a compound whose final member is a *subanta* (inflected nominal) having as its base (*prakṛti*) a word ending in *nadī*, we say no; for by this *paribhāṣā*, when there is co-occurrence with a feminine suffix (*strīpratyaya*), the status of being a *prātipadika* and those properties subsumed under it—which were observed in the form devoid of that suffix—are extended (*atideśa*) to the qualified form as well.
But if this were so, then just as in "yūnaḥ paśya," there would also be vocalization (samprasāraṇa) by the rule "śvayuvonām" in "yuvatiḥ paśya.
To this, he says:
"When a case-ending follows, that which is qualified by gender is not taken [as the basis for grammatical operations]. (Paribhāṣā 72).
And this [point] is clear in the Bhāṣya on the rule *yuvo‘nākau*;
others hold that it is based on that [Bhāṣya], because the mention of *ghaṭa* and *ghaṭī* indicates that the *liṅgaviśiṣṭaparibhāṣā* is not universally valid (*anitya*).

But surely, because the rule "tasyāpatyam" (his offspring) is indicated by the singular number and the neuter gender, [the forms] "gārgyaḥ" and "gārgyau" and so forth have been stated; therefore, he says: "In the Sūtra, gender and number are not restrictive. (Paribhāṣā 73)
The mention of the neuter gender in the rule *ardhaṃ napuṃsakam* serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*).
However, it has been explained elsewhere that this is not for the sake of establishing its status as a permanent neuter (*nityanapuṃsaka*);

rather, those two [the masculine and feminine forms] are mentioned as being invariably concomitant (*nāntarīyaka*), according to the maxim of grain and chaff. This is clear from the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *tasyāpatyam*.
For this very reason, in the *Ākaḍāra* sūtra, the word "eka" (one) is rendered meaningful; the details are explained elsewhere.

But would not the suffix *ky-aṅ*, which is prescribed by rules such as “*bhṛśādibhyo bhuvyacveḥ*,” also apply here in the sentence “*kva divā bhṛśā bhavanti*” (Where do they become intense by day)? To this he says:

*Nañ-iva-yuktam anyasadṛśādhikaraṇe tathā hy arthagatiḥ //* (Paribhāṣā 74) [The negative particle *nañ* and the word *iva*] when joined [to a term] refer to something other than that [term] which is similar to it; for such is the comprehension of the meaning.
Whatever is seen to be conjoined with a negative particle (*nañ*) is understood as having its effect upon a substance (*dravya*) that is distinct from, yet similar to, that [which is conjoined];
for such is the comprehension of the meaning.
Indeed, when it is said, "Bring a non-Brahmin" (*abrahmaṇam ānaya*), one does not consider his task accomplished by bringing a clod of earth.

Therefore, since *kyaṅ* applies to that which ends in a *cv*-suffix, which is similar to a *cv*-suffix, and which concerns the transformation of something into what it was not, the aforementioned fault does not arise.

In rules such as "and [the substitution of *o* for *au*] in a word beginning with *oṣadhi*, when a case-ending (*vibhakti*) other than the first follows," the mention of "case-ending" (*vibhakti*) is merely a restatement for the sake of maintaining the principle established by this very logic.
By this, those who claim that the mention of "in a case-ending" (*vibhaktau*) and so forth serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the non-universality (*anityatva*) of that rule are refuted.
Because there is no fruit [of the suffix] in the case of impermanence (anityatva), as agreed upon in the Bhāṣya;
for this very reason, it should be understood that in the sūtra "akartari ca," the mention of *kāraka* was rejected in the Bhāṣya.
And this is clear in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra "bhṛśādibhyaḥ."
By stating "similar to something else" (*anyasadṛśa*) here, he indicates that similarity is not constituted by difference;
this has been explained in the *Mañjūṣā*.

Now, an objection might be raised: in cases such as *vyāghrī* ("tigress") and *kaccapī* ("tortoise"), since these are compounds with a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*), the feminine suffix *ṭāp* would apply even more internally (as an *antaraṅga* operation) than the suffix *ṅīṣ*, which is prescribed for feminine nouns denoting a genus (*jāti*) when the stem ends in short *a*. Consequently, because the stem would no longer end in short *a*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* would not occur. To this, he says:
"The rule regarding the compounding of *gati*s, *kāraka*s, and *upapada*s with *kṛt*-derived words [is intended to ensure that the resulting form ends in short *a*]."
Prior to the production of the suffix *su*. (Paribhāṣā 75)

By the inclusion of the term *atiṅ* (not a finite verb) in the rule *upapadam*, and by the extraction (*apakarṣaṇa*) of that same term into the rule *kugatiprādayaḥ*, the meaning is that a compound consisting of a non-finite-verb-ending element [with another word] is formed; thus, through partial acceptance (*ekadeśānumati*) of the rule *sup-supā* in these two rules, this [formation] is established even in the case of a *kāraka* relationship.
Consequently, the form *aśvakrītī* is established.

Otherwise, since it would not have ended in *ṭāp* or a short vowel (*adanta*) prior to compounding, the suffix *ṅīṣ* would not apply by the rule "after a word ending in *krīta*, when preceded by an instrument [expressed in the third case]. Because this rule is not universally obligatory (*anitya*), in some cases compounding occurs even after the formation of the case-ending (*sub*), as in:
*sā hi tasya dhanakrītā* ("for she was bought by him with wealth").
Others, however, say that there is no evidence for [the suffix] *ṭāp* in the case of *anityatva*, because the rule *ajādy-ṭāp* does not apply there;
for this very reason, in forms such as *kumbhakāraḥ*, even the genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*) occurs only prior to the derivation of the nominal suffix (*sub*).

It is clear from the Bhāṣya that when a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) is absent, the unification of meaning (*ekārthībhāva*) is brought about by the upapada compound; therefore, there is no sentence (*vākya*) in that case.
For in that context, there is the Vārttika: "The upapada compound takes precedence over the genitive compound by way of conflict (*vipratiṣedha*).
Alternatively, there is the rejection (*pratyākhyāna*) of that [Vārttika] as follows: "The genitive compound is optional; when it does not occur, then the upapada compound occurs."

Although the author of the Vārttika stated— intending that the *upapada* compound is *antaraṅga* (internal)— "Or rather, there is no *upapada* compound because of the absence of a genitive compound," nevertheless, that statement is intended as a refutation of both [the *antaraṅga* argument and the genitive compound].

This is because the Bhāṣya passage beginning with "Or else" (*athavā*) establishes, through the general mention of a *kāraka* in the Paribhāṣā, that all compounds of roots with *kṛt*-suffixes ending in a *kāraka*-case suffix occur precisely prior to the arising of the case-ending (*sub*).
By this, the claim that "this [principle] applies only to the inclusion of the agent and its specific attributes" is refuted;

for, since it lacks syntactic unity with an injunction (*vidhi*), it cannot— like a rule concerning conflict (*vipratiṣedha*) and so forth— be understood to mean "it applies only to inclusion" by way of determining the application of grammatical operations.

Now, an objection is raised: since the rule *ugidacām* [Pāṇini 7.1.70] would apply to a verbal root (*dhātu*) only if it possesses the *ugit* designation, and by the restriction that this applies only to the root *añc*, the addition of the augment *num* is already established for non-verbal bases; therefore, the explicit mention of "non-verbal" (*adhātu*) is redundant. To this, he replies: **Paribhāṣā 76:** In the absence of a present state, there is recourse to what was previously so. This means that even if a base is not currently a verbal root, the grammatical operation is still applied on the basis of its having been a verbal root in the past. Thus, the mention of *adhātu* is not purposeless.
This [application] of the capacity of those respective statements is established by logic (*nyāya*).

By virtue of that capacity, the meaning being "even for that which was previously not a verbal root," the addition of *num* is established in forms such as *gomān* from *gomat-yati* with the suffix *kvip*.
This is clear in the *Bhāṣya* on the rules beginning with "nāmi."
In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, there is also the cognition of its quality (*tadguṇasaṃvijñāna*).

Furthermore, there is the *atadguṇasaṃvijñāna* [bahuvrīhi]. Its meaning is that there is no "cognition of those qualities"— that is, no connection with the specific qualities which are the meanings of the constituent members— where the external referent (*anyapadārtha*) is related by way of the relation of inherence (*samavāya*).
In those cases, it is generally a *tadguṇasaṃvijñāna* [bahuvrīhi]; elsewhere, it is generally otherwise,
as in the examples "long-eared" (*ālambakarṇa*) and "Citragu" (the one whose cows are variegated).
The examples "sarvādīni" and "jakṣatyādayaḥ" are clearly explained in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra defining the technical term *sarvanāman*.
But surely, since the suffix *yat* is drawn over by the rule “*vadaḥ supi kyap ca*,” it would also carry over into the rule “*bhuvo bhāve*” (Pāṇini 3.3.18); therefore, he says:
“That which is drawn over by *ca* does not apply to what follows” (Paribhāṣā 78).
While the suffix *ṇamul* is still in effect, the repeated mention of *ṇamul* in the rule “*avyaye ’yathābhiprete*” (Pāṇini 1.4.61) is an indicator (*jñāpaka*) [of this].
Otherwise, he would have said “*ktvā ca*”.
For that [mention of *ktvā*] is intended for the purpose of connecting both [suffixes] with the subsequent rules.
The examples are clear.
This [word] is *anitya* (non-eternal).

For this very reason, in the rule “*tṛtīyā ca hoḥ*,” there is a connection with the second case (*dvitīyā*), even though it was not explicitly drawn over (*anukṛṣṭā*) from that rule, in the rule “*antarāntareṇa*.”
This [interpretation] is contradicted by the rejection of all the *ca* particles used for the purpose of *anuvṛtti* (carrying over) found in the rule *“luṭi ca kṛpaḥ”* (*Pāṇini 1.3.93*),
the intention of which is that the carrying over or cessation of a term is managed through interpretation alone (*vyākhyāna*).
Furthermore, it is also contradicted by the *bhāṣya* on the rule *“kulijāllukkhau ca”* (*Pāṇini 5.1.125*).

For in that context, the suffix *ṣṭhan* [is applied] by the rule "dvigoḥ ṣṭhaṃśca"; and having accepted the recurrence (*anuvṛtti*) of both that [rule] and of the rule "kho ’nyatarasyām" which is drawn in by the word "ca," the option for *luk* and *kha* was rejected in the Bhāṣya.

Now, it might be argued that what is prescribed for words beginning with an unaccented vowel (*anudātta*) or ending in a final acute accent (*antodātta*) would not apply to words beginning with a consonant or ending in a consonant; therefore, it is said:
"In rules concerning accents, a consonant is as if non-existent" (Paribhāṣā 79).
The meaning is: "in a rule [governing] a suffix whose udātta accent is intended.

The exclusion of *pṛthivī* and others in the sūtra—"Not when the following word begins with an anudātta vowel, except in the case of *pṛthivī*, *rudra*, *pūṣan*, and *manthin*"—is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) of this [principle].
Otherwise, since words such as *pṛthivī* do not begin with an anudātta vowel, the rule would not apply to them anyway; thus, their exclusion would clearly be redundant.
And this [rule] has as its object that which has a vowel (*svara*) as its designatum, precisely because of the very means of cognition (*māna*) that apprehends the substratum (*dharmin*).

For this very reason, [the rules] "after *śatṛ*, *an*, *ūṅ*, *nadī*, and those beginning with *yaj*, [the acute accent is on the final syllable]" and "after a vowel, when *yaK* follows the agent" [are established].
In such cases as these, the rule *acaḥ* (Pāṇini 6.4.138) and others find their proper application.

For this very reason, in examples such as *rājavatī*, because the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*), the word retains its status as ending in *anvatī*; consequently, the accent prescribed by the rule *anto ’vatyāḥ* (Pāṇini 6.1.220) does not apply.

Regarding the term *udaśvitvān*, the grammatical treatises (*ākara*) state that the acute accent on the suffix *matup*— which would otherwise apply by the rule *hrasvanuḍbhyām*— does not occur here. This is also clearly explained in the *Bhāṣya* on the sūtra *samāsasya*.

Regarding the sūtra "uccairudāttaḥ," Kaiyaṭa, however, says: "This [distinction] is not necessary, because even a consonant (hal) appears as if it were udātta and so forth through the coloring (uparāga) of the adjacent vowels (samih), and thus its [status as udātta] is established.
This has also been indicated in the Bhāṣya on that point.

But even so, in cases such as *rājadṛṣat*, the final acute accent (*antodāttatva*) prescribed by the rule "of a compound" (*samāsasya*) would not apply to the vowel *a* of the letter *ṣ*; therefore, he says: "A consonant is treated as non-existent when an accent is to be applied to a vowel. (Paribhāṣā 80)
And regarding this, in the sūtra “yato nāvaḥ,” the negation *anau* serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*).

In the word *nāvyam*, the initial *n-* is not capable of being combined with a vowel; and that vowel which is capable of such combination is not the initial [of the word]. Therefore, that negation would be purposeless.
Nor should it be argued that the initial *m* itself could be the closest substitute (*antaratama*) characterized by the quality of acute (*udātta*);

for if that were the case, the condition of being "biforcated" (*dvayackatva*), which serves as the cause [for the application of the rule], would be destroyed, and consequently, due to the contradiction with what is depended upon (*upajīvya-virodha*), the acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyudāttatva*) would not apply.
This is explained in detail elsewhere.
And this [point] is clear in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra "samāsasya."

[Objection: But would not the prohibition [stated in Pāṇini 6.3.34] "pūraṇa-guṇa... apply even to the suffix *tavyat*; would not the substitution of *au* for the root *div-* [stated in 7.1.84] "diva aut" apply even when the suffix *kvip* follows; and likewise, would not the accent [stated in 6.1.213] "yato 'nāvaḥ" apply even to the suffix *ṇyat*; and would not the rule "ṛdṛśo 'ṅi guṇaḥ" [stated in 7.4.16] apply even to the suffix *caṅ*? To this, he says:
**Paribhāṣā 81:** When there is a mention of a base without an *anubandha*, it does not include a base with an *anubandha*.
When that which possesses a specific suffixal marker (tadanubandhaka) is mentioned, there is no application of that which lacks such a marker (atadanubandhaka).
In the sūtra "vāmadevāḍḍyaḍḍyau," the fact that the suffixes *ḍya* and *ḍḍa* are marked with the indicatory letter *ṭ* (ḍitva) is not an indicator [of the desired point];
for that [ṭ] is intended to prevent the inclusion of those two [suffixes] in the rule "yayatoścātadarthe."
The meaning of that [rule] is that the final syllable of a subsequent member ending in *ya* or *yat* is acute when preceded by *nañ*.
In this way, in the case of *āvāmadevya*, there occurs only the original accent (*prakṛtisvara*) of the indeclinable (*avyaya*) as the prior member.
The meaning of the final [part of the rule] is that there is no mention of that which has both a *tanmātra* (the mere phoneme) and an *anubandha* (indicatory letter) as its suffix;
for these [suffixes] are common to both suffixes (*pratyaya*) and non-suffixes (*apratyaya*),
since they have been applied [to both] in such rules as "diva aut" (Pāṇini 7.1.84).
Furthermore, it is clear from the *Bhāṣya* on the rule "auṅa āpaḥ" that these two [rules] do not apply when there is the elision of a phoneme (*varṇalopa*).

This is because, according to the authoritative evidence establishing the nature of the grammatical elements (*dharmigrāhakamāna*), this [non-application] occurs only when that very marker (anubandha) by which a form possesses a marker— whether it be having one marker or two markers— is not uttered.

Therefore, regarding the rule *jaśśasoḥ*, one should not suspect that because it lacks an anubandha (marker), only the *taddhita* suffix *śatṛ* would be included here; for the same logic applies when either of the final two anubandhas is uttered. Consequently, in rules such as *vano ra ca*, the non-inclusion of *ṅvanip* and *kvanip* is established.
The claim that the inclusion of the term *ekānubandhaka* is possible [as a restrictive condition] does not accord with the Bhāṣya and other authorities; the details are found elsewhere.

Now, one might object: in cases such as *kuṭīraḥ*, since these suffixes are *svārthika* (having the same meaning as the base), and because it is a logical principle that *svārthika* suffixes follow the gender and number of their base, the occurrence of the masculine gender is untenable;
furthermore, in the case of *apkalpam*, the neuter gender and singular number would be untenable. To this, he says:
"In some cases, *svārthika* suffixes deviate from the gender and number of their base. (Paribhāṣā 83)
The mention of "in the feminine" (*striyām*) in the rule *ṇacaḥ striyām* is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) of this [principle].

Otherwise, since [the suffix] *ṇac* would be prescribed only for the feminine by the rule *karmavyatihāre ṇac striyām*, what would be the purpose of that [mention]? And this [principle] is clear in the Bhāṣya on the rule prescribing the suffix *bahu*.
Now, one might object: in the example "supathī nagarī" cited in the Bhāṣya on the rule "yuvoranākau," the suffix *kap* would apply by the rule "inaḥ striyām. To this, he says:
"The rule for compound-final suffixes (*samāsāntavidhi*) is not universally obligatory (*anitya*). (Paribhāṣā 84)

The inclusion of the word *rājame* among the words beginning with *aśva* in the list of *aśvādi* (Pāṇini 6.2.190) is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the fact that the final syllable is udātta according to the rule "prateraṃśvādayastatpuruṣe.
Otherwise, since the final udātta would already be established by the suffix *ṭac*, what would be the purpose of that [inclusion]?
This is clear from the Bhāṣya on the rule prescribing accent, "dvitribhyāṃ pāddanmūrddhasu" (Pāṇini 5.4.140).
But surely, in cases such as *śatāni*, once the augment *num* has been applied, the designation *ṣaṭ* would apply, and consequently, there would be elision (*luk*);
likewise in *upādāsta*.

In this case, once *āt* has been applied, the substitution of *it* [for the final vowel] as prescribed by the rule *sthaghvoricca* would follow; therefore, he says: "A grammatical operation conditioned by a specific combination [of sounds] is not the cause for the destruction of that very combination. (Paribhāṣā 85)
Conjunction (*sannipāta*) is the connection of two things;
a rule caused by that conjunction is "non-causal" (*animitta*) for anything that destroys that conjunction.
This [rule] is based on the principle that it is improper for something to contradict its own basis of subsistence (*upajīvya*).

For this very reason, the term *sannipāta* here does not refer merely to the connection between the preceding and the following elements, but also includes the relationship between a qualifier and a qualified (*viśe�ṣaṇa-viśeṣya-sannipāta*).
For this very reason, in examples such as *grāmaṇikulam*, even though the neuter short vowel [of the suffix] occurs, the *tuk* augment prescribed by the rule “*piti kṛti*” does not apply.
This is because the short vowel arises through the conjunction (*sannipāta*) with the final letter of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), and therefore it cannot be the cause for its own prescription.
The obstruction of the status of being a final letter of the stem caused by the *tuk* augment is indeed evident.

Nor can it be argued that the short vowel is *asiddha* due to being *bahiraṅga* by virtue of depending on meaning, because it has already been stated that one does not rely on *bahiraṅga* status based on meaning.

Furthermore, by the force of the rule “*ṣatvatukorasiddhaḥ*” and because of the inclusion of the term *kṛti* in the rule for *tuṅ*, the *bahiraṅga-paribhāṣā* does not apply in the prescription of *tuṅ*.

Precisely because of the inclusion of the term "all types" (*sarvavidha*) [in the definition of *sannipāta*], the author of the Vārttika stated during the examination of the fault regarding this paribhāṣā— "A suffix (*pratyaya*) that depends on a phoneme (*varṇa*) shall not be the cause for the displacement of that phoneme"— [adding]:
"For a suffix does not have as its cause a preceding or following *sannipāta*."

Considering that this very [conjunction] is what is grasped by the term *sannipāta*, and thus anticipating the objection that "the suffix (*pratyaya*) is not caused by *sannipāta*," the proponent of a partial view (ekadeśin) stated—accepting that premise for the sake of argument—that "in that case, the designation of a stem (*aṅga-saṃjñā*) would be without cause.
Therefore, there is no contradiction with that Bhāṣya.
Furthermore, in this way, [the form] *śaivaḥ*...

In cases such as *gārgāyaḥ* and *vainateyaḥ*, since the designation of the *aṅga* (base) would not result in being a cause for elision (*lopa*), the condition "depending on a phoneme" (*varṇāśraya*) would be rendered meaningless.
[Furthermore,] in cases such as *grāmaṇikulam* and *grāmaṇiputraḥ*, regarding the shortening (*hrasvatva*) conditioned by the subsequent member (*uttarapada*), in some way or another...

Since prevention [of the *tug* augment] is also possible by means of the *bahiranga-paribhāṣā*, the *tug* was barred by that *paribhāṣā* in the *bhāṣya* on the rule “*kṛnmejantaḥ*” and on the rule “*hrasvasya piti*,” according to the proponent of that [view].
For this very reason, some maintain that this was stated by the author of the Vārttika in the sūtra *kṛnmejantaḥ* as a result of the paribhāṣā.
The evidence for its status as a rule characterized by immediate contiguity (*sannipātalakṣaṇavidhi*) is as follows:
that contiguity which constitutes its own cause prior to its own operation [is not destroyed by it].
It follows that a rule other than itself (*svātirikta-śāstra*) which destroys that [application] cannot itself be its cause.

But if this were so, in forms such as *rāmāya*, the long vowel would not result from the rule "supi ca," because the substitution of *y* (the *yādeśa*), having arisen through the conjunction of the stem ending in *a* (*adanta-aṅga-sannipātena*), would destroy that very conjunction.

Nor should it be argued that because the long vowel [produced by the rule] *yaṇ-ādittva-sāpekṣa-dīrgha* is *asiddha* due to its being *bahiraṅga*, there is no violation of the *sannipāta* condition here;
for even if the *asiddhatva* is merely superimposed (*āropita*), the actual violation of the condition does occur in reality, and thus this [rule] applies.

Furthermore, although a *bahiraṅga* operation is *asiddha* when an *antaraṅga* operation is to be performed, there is no evidence for its *asiddhatva* once that [antaraṅga] operation has already taken place.

Furthermore, if this [paribhāṣā] were not to apply on the grounds that there is no destruction of a *sannipāta* (a phonological combination) resulting from an extended application (*atideśika*), then in cases such as *gauri*, even though the vocative suffix (*sambuddhi*) is elided, there would be no destruction of the *sannipāta* caused by a short vowel due to the status of the substitute being "as if it were the original" (*sthānivadbhāva*).
Consequently, the Bhāṣya on the rule “*kṛnmejantaḥ*” (P. 1.1.39), which addresses the over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of this [paribhāṣā] in such instances, would be inconsistent.
If it is argued that because the *sannipāta* is not based on the grammatical system (*aśāstrīya*), the status of being "as if the original" (*sthānivattva*) does not apply here—[we reply:]...
If it is then asked how non-validity (*asiddhatva*) can also apply here,

[the answer is that] Kaiyaṭa has clearly stated in his commentary on the sūtra *īdūded dvivacanaṃ pragṛhyam* that "non-validity does not apply to what is not prescribed by the grammatical system" (*aśāstrīye 'siddhatvāpravṛtteḥ*).
And if it is argued that, in this way, this paribhāṣā indeed applies even to an operation that is itself subject to the rule *pūrvatrāsiddham*, [we reply as follows:]

No; because this [rule] is considered non-eternal (anitya) due to the specific mention of "for the sake of difficulty" (*kaṣṭāya*). However, there is no insistence that the two elements whose conjunction is obstructed by a grammatical rule must necessarily be included in a rule caused by their conjunction.

For this very reason, in the case of *dākṣiḥ*, there is a concern that the elision of the final vowel (*al-lopa*) might not serve as the cause [for the application of a grammatical operation] because of the paribhāṣā stating that "the designation of a stem (*aṅga-saṃjñā*) is caused by the conjunction of the base ending in *ā* with the suffix *in*. This concern is resolved by [the principle of] non-universality (*anityatva*), as stated in the Bhāṣya on the rule *kṛnmejantaḥ*: "For there is no such thing as a stem-designation for that which ends in *ā* when the stem-designation is being applied."

Furthermore, there is no inconsistency with the Bhāṣya— which states that the designation of indeclinability (*avyayasaṃjñā*) in examples such as *kumbhakārebhyaḥ* and *ādhaye* is prevented by this Paribhāṣā—
on the grounds that "by this Paribhāṣā, let there not be elision (*luk*)."
However, the status of being an indeclinable (avyayatva) would certainly still occur; for it is by the elision (luk) that the conjunction of those [factors] is obstructed,
not by the technical designation (saṃjñā) "indeclinable."
It should be stated that *akac* would indeed occur as the result of *saṃjñā*;

however, there is no fault [in our position], because according to the authority of the Bhāṣya which provides this example, the principle holds that "that which, directly or indirectly, destroys the combination of elements that is its own cause, is itself not an occasion for its own application.
By this, the claim that *akac* would occur here is refuted.

Nor should it be argued that, under the *kāryakāla* view, although the technical name (*saṃjñā*) associated with the single sentence containing *luk* might be sublated, the [technical name] associated with the single sentence containing *akac* would not likewise be sublated;
for while the technical name associated with that [sentence containing *akac*] is *antaraṅga*, the *guṇa* substitution and other operations are *asiddha* [with respect to it],
whereas the [technical name] associated with the single sentence containing *luk* is not *antaraṅga* relative to the *guṇa* and other such operations.
Because both [the suffixes] are, by their very form, based on a *su*-stem;
furthermore, the grammatical rule "nayāsayoḥ" indicates that these [suffixes] are optional.
Therefore, there is no over-extension of the rule.
This [principle] is clearly stated in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *kṛnmejantaḥ*.

The results of its non-eternality (*anityatva*) are enumerated in the Bhāṣya: that which depends on a phoneme (*varṇāśraya*), a suffix (*pratyaya*), and that which is not a cause for the displacement of a phoneme (*varṇavicālasyānimitta*).

‘Dākṣiḥ’ [is an example where the substitution of *ā* occurs] prior to the application of the augment *puṅ*. ‘Krāpayati’ [is an example where the substitution of *ā* occurs] prior to the application of the augment *puṅ*. ‘Adītapat’ [is an example where the substitution of *ā* occurs] prior to the shortening of the vowel.
‘Yā sā’ [is an example where the substitution of *a* occurs] prior to the application of the feminine suffix *ṭāp* for the pronouns beginning with *tyad*.
This is a rule for the elision of the vowel *ā*: *papivān*.

[In the case of] *agnimān* and *paramavācā*, the acute accent (*udātta*) on the suffix *matup* and the case ending is due to the rules "after a short vowel and after *nuṭ*" and "from a final-accented second member," which result in the suppression of the preceding accent (*pūrvanighāta*).
The shortening of a feminine noun ending in *nadī* occurs due to the elision of the *saṃbuddhi* [vocative] suffix— as in "nadi," "kumāri," and so forth.
The substitution of *y* occurs due to lengthening— as in...
It leads to hardship; otherwise, there would be mere proliferation.
As for the statement in the Bhāṣya, "Indeed, the defects have been enumerated in their entirety," the detailed explanation is found elsewhere.

But is it not the case that in examples such as *pañcendraḥ*—derived from *pañcendrāṇyo devatā asya* ("the five Indrāṇīs are its deities")—where the suffix *aṇ* is elided by the rule "elision after a *dvigu*" (*dvigor luk*), the feminine suffix would also be elided by the rule "when a *taddhita* suffix is elided" (*luk taddhite*), resulting in the undesirable consequence of hearing the *ānuk* augment? To this, he says:
"When those prescribed in conjunction with one another are subject to the elision of either one, there is the elision of both. (Paribhāṣā 86)
And here, the mention of *cha* in the rule “*bilvakādibhyaśchasya luk*” (Pāṇini 4.2.87) serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*).
For that [mention] is intended so that there may be no removal (*anivṛtti*) of *kuk*, by means of teaching the elision (*luk*) of *cha* in its entirety.
In that rule, the words *bilvaka* and others—which already possess the augment *kuk* and are included within the group beginning with *anaḍuh*—are specifically indicated by the term *bilvakādi*.
Nor is the inclusion of the letter *cha* redundant even in this case;
for its non-exclusion is established by the very force of restating the augment *kuk*,
otherwise one would have simply said "from *bilva* and so forth."

It should not be argued that there is no over-extension because the elision (*luk*) is prescribed only for a suffix enjoined with *bilva* and others as the immediate antecedent, according to the technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) "that which is taught by its specific form" (*lakṣaṇapratipadokta*).

Even so, since that [suffix] is also taught by its specific form, the mention of *ku* (in the rule *kugati-prādayaḥ*) must be purposeful in order to prevent the undesired elision of the suffix *aṇ*—enjoined by the rule *bilvādibhyo ṇ*—which would otherwise apply in the sense of a derivative (*vikāra*) and the like.

However, when joined with the particle *ca* in the sense of conjunction, this [principle] is established by logic (*nyāyasiddha*), due to the rule that the two things to be enjoined must be simultaneous and occupy the same locus.

As for the rule "ṇāviṣṭavat" (Pāṇini 6.4.155), which prescribes the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvat*), this is for the purpose of indicating that [the application of] this rule is not invariably obligatory (*anitya*).

Otherwise, in forms such as *etayati*, since the feminine suffix *ṅīp* would be removed by the elision of the *ṭi*-portion (*ṭilopa*) itself, the feminine marker would also be removed by the *sanniyogaśiṣṭa* maxim (the rule that when two things are taught together, they are removed together). Consequently, the establishment of forms like *etayati* would be achieved even without it, making the prescription of *puṃvat* clearly redundant. Thus, regarding the sūtra "ṭeḥ" (Pāṇini 6.4.143)...

Kaiyaṭa says: "That is not so; for in cases such as *aiḍabiḍayati* (he treats [him] like Aiḍabiḍa), the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvat*) is necessary. As for forms such as *aineyaḥ* and *śyaineyaḥ*, they are established by the principle of *sthānivadbhāva* (the substitute being treated like the original); this is explained in detail elsewhere."

Now, an objection is raised: in examples such as "she whose habit is stealing is a *caurī*," since the suffix *ṇa* is applied by the rule "after *chatra* and others, *ṇa*" (*Pāṇini 4.4.62*), the feminine suffix *ṅīp* would not be applicable.
To this, he says:
"In the case of a *ṇa* suffix added in the sense of a habitual trait (*tācchīlika*), the operations of *aṇ* take place. (Paribhāṣā 87)
The rule "kārmastācchīlye" (Pāṇini 6.1.159) is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) for this [paribhāṣā], as its purpose is to override the *prakṛtibhāva* prescribed by the rule "an" (Pāṇini 6.4.167).

Furthermore, the modern scholars (*navyāḥ*) maintain that another purpose of this [paribhāṣā] is the establishment of the suffix *phiñ* by the rule "aṇo dvyacaḥ" (Pāṇini 4.1.153), following a suffix ending in *aṇ* that conveys a habitual disposition (*tācchīlika*).
This is because the term "tācchīlika" is used [in the rule]. [Thus, the suffix *phiñ* is applied] to [the word] "tadasyāṃ... [etc.].
Regarding the word *praharaṇa*, by [the application of] the suffix *ṇa*, the form is simply *adāṇḍā*;
this is clear in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra *kārmaḥ*.
But is it not the case that in rules such as “*kasaparimṛḍbhyām*,” the substitution of *vṛddhi* for the root *mṛj* would be difficult to avoid? To this he says:
"An operation stated with respect to a verbal root applies to its suffix. (Paribhāṣā 88)
The dropping of the *t* in *bhrauṇahatye* is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) for this [rule].

However, the reading "when there is a grammatical operation based on the actual form of a root, that operation is understood to apply to its derivative suffix" has been refuted in the Bhāṣya by means of deriving the augment *ām* in forms such as *prasṛḍbhiḥ* via the rule "and for a root with a low-pitched vowel and a reduplicated penultimate.
This [rule] serves as a regulator only for those operations which are conditioned by a suffix.

Therefore, the substitution of *k* (kutva) based on the fact that [the suffix] occurs at the end of a word— as in the rule "naśervā"— does indeed apply in cases such as *praṇagbhyām*. However, this [principle of *padāntatva*] does not apply in the rules for *iyaṅ* and so forth,
because it is non-universal (*anitya*) due to the prohibition in the rule "na bhūsudhiyoḥ."
This is clear in the Bhāṣya on the rule "mṛjer vṛddhiḥ."
But would not the designations "pronominal" (*sarvanāman*) and "indeclinable" (*avyaya*) fail to apply in cases such as *sarvake* and *iccakaiḥ*? To this he says:
"That which falls within [a group] is included by the mention of that group. (Paribhāṣā 89)
The prohibition "akoḥ" in the sūtra "nedamadasorakoḥ" is the indicator (jñāpaka) for this [principle].
The reading in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra "yena vidhiḥ" is: "That which constitutes a part of something is included by the mention of that whole."

But surely, by the rule “*gāti-sthā-ghu-pā-bhū-bhyaḥ*,” there would be elision (*luk*) of *sic* after the root *pā-* as well in forms such as *apāsīta*; therefore, he says: “Between a root with an elided *vikaraṇa* suffix and one with a non-elided *vikaraṇa* suffix, the latter [takes precedence]. (Paribhāṣā 90).

And regarding this, Kaiyaṭa maintains that the indicator (*jñāpaka*) is the separate mention of *sūti* and *sūyati* in the rule *svarati-sūti-*, when it would have been sufficient simply to say *sūṅ*. That is not correct;

for since, by virtue of association (*sāhacarya*), only the root with the *aluk*-suffix (*sū*) would be expected to be understood, the separate mention cannot serve as an indicator for that [proposed] point.
This technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) has been implied in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule "yasya vibhāṣā" (Pāṇini 7.2.15).

For there, having raised the objection regarding the prohibition [of the augment *iṭ*] in the usage of the form *viditaḥ*, it is stated under the rule "vibhāṣā gamahanavidaviśām" (Pāṇini 1.2.4) that "the mention of the root *gam-* in the rule refers to that which takes the *śap* verbal suffix, whereas this [root *vid-*, as in *viditaḥ*] takes the *luk* suffix. Thus, the prohibition applies only to those roots for which the optionality was prescribed in connection with the *śap* suffix.
In this context, the particle *ca* has the sense of "because": because this [root] lacks a vikaraṇa suffix,
therefore, by virtue of its association with *viśi*, there is the inclusion of that which possesses the *śap* vikaraṇa.
