However, its [the *han* root's] inclusion [in the rule] is not due to association with *han*, because that would contradict this very Paribhāṣā; such is the intention [of the author].
For this very reason, it was not stated in the Paribhāṣā that "only that which has a *luk*-vikaraṇa" [is meant].
However, this has not been stated explicitly anywhere in the Bhāṣya.

Regarding the sūtra *gāti-sthā-*, the author of the Vārttika stated, "The root *pibati* must be included," and the author of the Bhāṣya stated, "In every instance where *pā* is mentioned, it is the root with the *luṅ*-vikaraṇa that is intended.
Furthermore, Kaiyaṭa clearly stated this in his commentary on the sūtra *svarati-sūti-*.

But surely, in forms such as *prajighāyayiṣati*, the substitution of *k* for *h* (kutva) prescribed by the rule "heracaṅi" would not apply; therefore, he says: "When there is the mention of a base, that which has an additional *ṇi* affix is also included. (Paribhāṣā 91).
The very prohibition "not before *acaṅ*" is the indicator (*jñāpaka*) for this [rule].
And this [prohibition] applies only to the domain of *kutva*.
This is stated in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra "heracaṅi" (Pāṇini 7.3.56).
This is clear.

Now, in forms such as *yuṣmabhyam*, if one were to divide the rule *bhyasaḥ* as *bhyam-aḥ*, then after *bhyas* is replaced by *bhyam*, the elision of the final letter would apply, and consequently, the substitution of *e* (by *ato guṇe*) would occur; therefore, he says:
"When a grammatical operation has already taken effect upon a base (*aṅga*), that base does not undergo another operation [based on the same cause]. (Paribhāṣā 92)

The meaning is that when an operation (*kārya*) produced by a rule (*vṛtta*) concerning a specific grammatical element (*aṅga*) has already taken place, there is no further application (*avidhāna*) of another operation concerning that same element once it has occurred.
And this [principle] is indicated by the formulation of the rule “*jyādādīyasaḥ*” (Pāṇini 6.4.160) and others.

Otherwise, since the desired form would already be established by the elision of the vowel *i* (in *pibati*) and by the rule "akṛtsārvadhātuka... which prescribes lengthening, the [prohibition] would clearly be redundant.

For this very reason, after having taught this [prohibition] in the two rules "jñājanorjā" and "jyādādīyasaḥ," when the question is asked as to what purpose it serves, the prohibition of *guṇa* for the root *pā* (to drink) is stated;
however, that [prohibition] need not have been stated.
Thus, only the purpose has been stated, but not the establishment of the technical term (*lakṣya*).
As it was said regarding the rule *abhyaso bhyam*: the division [of the sūtra] is *abhyam*.

Regarding the rule *śeṣe lopaḥ*, it is established that there is only the elision of the final [element], and by means of the *pararūpa* substitution according to *ato guṇe*, the form *yuṣmabhyam* is achieved; this has been explained elsewhere.

Thus, they say that the Bhāṣya situated within these two rules is intended as an explanatory indication (*jñāpaka*), whereas the Bhāṣya on the rule *bhyaso bhyam* is merely the statement of a partial view (*ekadeśyukti*).

As for the fact that, although one could have simply said "of *o*" (*oroḥ*), the term "guṇa" is used in the rule "guṇaḥ of *o*" (*orguṇaḥ*)—this indicates that a grammatical operation conditioned by a technical name (*saṃjñāpūrvakavidhi*) is not universally obligatory (*anityatva*). (Paribhāṣā 93)
And this [application] occurs only when the status of being preceded by a technical name (*saṃjñāpūrvakatva*) is part of what is to be enjoined;
thus, forms such as *svāyambhuvam* are established.

Thus, since the form *nilīyate* is already established by the rule itself, the specific mention of *āni* indicates that the rules concerning augments (*āgama-śāstra*) are not invariably obligatory (*anitya*). (Paribhāṣā 94)
By this, the statement "of one desiring to cross the ocean," and so forth, is established.

Since [the form *tanoti*] is established by the very recitation of the root *tan* in the list beginning with "tanādi," the inclusion of *kṛñ* in the rule "tanādikṛñbhyaḥ" indicates that an operation based on a specific class (gaṇakārya) is not invariably obligatory. (Paribhāṣā 95)
By this, the principle that "one should not trust the untrustworthy" and so forth is established.
Likewise, because the root *cakṣiṅ* is marked with the indicatory letter *ṅ*, it is established that the ātmanepada characterized by having an anudātta initial vowel is not obligatory. (Paribhāṣā 96)
By this, the statement "the sloughing skin is expanding," and so forth, is established.

Likewise, even though the rule "anudāttam padamanekam" (P. 6.2.49) would already be established by a compound with the negative particle *nañ* without the word *artha*, the inclusion of the term *varja* indicates that a compound containing *nañ* is not universally obligatory (*anitya*). (Paribhāṣā 97)
As for the claim that "he subhru" is established because the rule "neyaṅuvaṅ" is considered optional (*anitya*),
that is not correct; for it is observed in the *Bhāṣya*,
and there is no evidence that an meaning indicated by a rule not mentioned in the *Bhāṣya* can serve as a regulator of grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*).

For it is more appropriate to assume that the mere unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) is the purpose of reciting the words of the Sūtras when their specific purpose has not been examined in the Bhāṣya. Furthermore, even if [the meaning] were made known, there would be no point in [the use of] *āni*, because a usage devoid of the augment *āṬ* is unestablished.

It should be understood that the inclusion of *āṭ* is like the inclusion of the imperative (*loṭ*). For this very reason, the option (*vā*) in the rule "ghorlopo liṭi vā" has been rejected; even if there were elision (*lopa*), in the alternative case where *āṭ* is present, the hearing of *āṭ* will occur—as in "dadhāt."

Regarding the form *aṭi dadhat* (with the augment *aṭ*), if the rule for augments (*āgamaśāstra*) were not considered optional (*anitya*), then *āṭ* would not apply and the form *dadhāt* would remain unestablished; consequently, since the inclusion of the word "optionally" (*vā*) would be indispensable, its rejection (*pratyākhyāna*) would clearly be inconsistent.
By this, Kaiyaṭa’s statement beginning with "some" (*kecit*) and so forth—which asserts that this very mention of "optionally" (*vā*) indicates the non-optional nature of that [rule]—is explained.
That too is to be considered,
because it contradicts the Bhāṣya’s rejection [of that view], and because the mention of the root *kṛ* in the sūtra beginning with *tan-* was rejected in the Bhāṣya.
And because the letter *ṅ* in the root *cakṣiṅ* has its purpose fulfilled by ensuring that [the final *i*] does not become an *it*.
In the same way—what is extended by analogy is non-eternal. (Paribhāṣā 98)
The rule for elision and the rule for the augment iṭ are stronger than all other rules.
Such points not mentioned in the Bhāṣya are to be understood; furthermore,
forms such as *svāyamabhuvam* are indeed incorrect in common usage,
as explained at length elsewhere.
Furthermore—[an objection: surely, when the suffix *yaṅ* is elided (*yaṅluk*), the substitute *vadh* would not apply to the root *han* in the optative (*āśīr-liṅ*)? To this, he says:
"When there is a mention of a base form (*prakṛti*), that which ends in *yaṅluk* is also included. (Paribhāṣā 100).

This [argument] is established by logic (*nyāyasiddha*), because the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) regarding the doubling of the sixteenth [syllable] teaches that the composite whole consisting of two applications possesses the nature of the original base (*prakṛti*) through the principle of "doubling the application.
For this very reason, it is said that when doubling is performed in forms such as *juhudhi*, the doubling of the *dh* sound is accomplished.
But even that is not correct, because it is not observed in the *Bhāṣya*.

Furthermore, even if that established doctrine (*siddhānta*) were to bring about the realization of the true nature (*tattva*) of each of the two individually, there is no evidence for the realization of the true nature of the aggregate.

For this very reason, in the rule *dayater digi*, having raised the objection that—since the doubling (*dvitva*) occurs because [the root] *as* follows [the prefix], when the substitution of *bhū* for the subsequent *as* has taken place, the hearing of the original form of the preceding one would result—the objection is resolved by resorting to the locative case of the "domain" (*viṣaya-saptamī*).

Otherwise, according to the method you have stated, by the principle of "doubling of a single vowel" (*ekāj-dvirvacana*), it would follow that the substitute applies to the aggregate as a whole; in that case, the aforementioned resolution would clearly be inconsistent.
Therefore, it should be understood that the occurrence of various grammatical operations takes place by taking only the subsequent portion (the suffix) as appropriate.

Since the prohibition of *guṇa* obtained from the rule "bhūsuvoḥ" applies to a stem (*aṅga*) ending in those [roots], the form *bobhūtu* is a restrictive rule (*niyama*), and thus there is no contradiction.
Consequently, forms such as *avadhyāt* cited by Mādhava and others for the root *han* with *yaṅ*-elision are indeed questionable; this is explained in detail elsewhere.

Now, one might object: "In the rule *vṛddhir yasyācām ādiḥ*, since the *ik-paribhāṣā* (the maxim regarding the short vowels i, u, ṛ, and ḷ) would apply, forms such as *śālīya* would not be established. To this, he says:
**Paribhāṣā 101:** A *paribhāṣā* applies during the formulation of a rule (*vidhi*), not during its restatement (*anuvāda*).
The meaning of that [saying] is this: the *paribhāṣā* which serves as a regulator does not apply to qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) that are themselves being referred to (*anūdyamāna*).

This is based on reasoning (*tarka*): although it is impossible for *paribhāṣās*, which are auxiliary to an injunction (*vidhi*), to have a connection with the enjoined element (*vidheya*) because the former is not established (*asiddha*) at the time of the latter, they nonetheless fulfill their purpose by regulating its qualifiers; therefore, there is no evidence for them to regulate those very qualifiers.
Furthermore, the inclusion of the word *sthāne* in the sūtra “udīcām ātaḥ sthāne” is the indicator (*liṅga*) for this [paribhāṣā].
Otherwise, since that [meaning] would already be obtained by the paribhāṣā “ṣaṣṭhī sthāne,” its inclusion would clearly be redundant; therefore, [it serves as an indicator].

No; for this [principle] is subject to exceptions in rules such as “*allopo ’naḥ*” according to the method stated in the *Bhāṣya* on the sūtra “*ṣyaṅaḥ saṃprasāraṇam*” under the rule “*udāttasvaritayoryaṇaḥ*,” and because it is not mentioned in the *Bhāṣya*. Furthermore, there is no connection with the [original] place (*sthāna*).

This is because the meaning that a *paribhāṣā* is to be applied [only where its application is] obtainable is clearly stated in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra “ṣaṣṭhī sthāne,” and because the indicator (*jñāpaka*) you have cited is impossible for that reason.

Furthermore, the inclusion of the word "sthāne" (in place of) there is merely for the sake of clarity. Moreover, the maxim “a *paribhāṣā* is [operative] in a rule” is based on the ellipsis of the words “it is prescribed” (*vidhīyate*) in relation to the two rules “ikoguṇavṛddhī” and “acaśca.”
But elsewhere there is no fruit for her; this is explained in detail elsewhere.

Now, an objection may be raised: in cases such as *namaskaroti devān* ("he pays homage to the gods") and *namasyati devān*, the dative case prescribed by the rule *namaḥ-svasti-* would be unavoidable; therefore, he says:
"The case ending denoting a kāraka (participant in an action) is stronger than a case ending based on a governing word (*upapada*). (Paribhāṣā 102).
And the status of being a case ending denoting a *kāraka* (participant in action) consists in being a case ending whose meaning is a generator of action (*kriyājanaka*).
Since this [quality] also belongs to the nominative (*prathamā*), it too is a *kāraka*-case ending; this was indicated in the *Bhāṣya* on rules such as "sahayukte" (Pāṇini 2.3.19).
And this [definition] is indeed based solely on the explicit statement of the grammatical tradition (*vācanikī*).
For this very reason, by this principle, the locative case expressing the substratum (*adhikaraṇa-saptamī*) is stronger than the locative case expressing the condition (*bhāva-saptamī*),
as indicated in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule "tatra ca dīyate" and explicitly stated by Kaiyaṭa.
By this, the view that "the status of being a *kāraka* consists in being connected with an action" is refuted,
because even the locative case in the rule *“yasya ca bhāvena”* is connected with an action.
Furthermore, those who claim that the *kāraka* case-endings possess greater force because they denote a state resulting from a connection with a primary action [are also refuted].
Since both [the *namas* and *varivas*] are caused by their connection with an action (*kriyā*), their [inclusion in the rule] is clearly inappropriate;
furthermore, the mention [of them] in the Bhāṣya under the sūtra "namo-varivaḥ" for the purpose of excluding the fourth case in examples such as "namasyati devān" would otherwise be inconsistent.

By this, the view that "the relation between action and its factors (kāraka) is internal (antaraṅga), and thus the case-ending caused by it is antaraṅga, whereas the relation with the meaning of an upapada is based on some action-factor and is therefore external (bahiraṅga), and thus the case-ending caused by it is bahiraṅga," is refuted; for in the case of *namasyati*, there is no syntactic connection (*anvaya*) at all unless there is an action-factor even in respect to the object denoted by the word *namaḥ*.
And here, even the referent of the word *namas* possesses the nature of an action (*kriyātva*), just as the head does in the case of the verb *muṇḍayati*.

Furthermore, in rules such as *sahayukte*, the nominative case is used for the primary element; this [usage] was introduced in the Bhāṣya for the sake of establishing the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), as explained in detail elsewhere.

But would there not be the undesirable consequence (āpatti) that even the preceding [sound] in forms such as *adamuyaṅ* would undergo elision (*muk*)? To this, he says: "A modification affecting a non-final [sound] applies to that which is in the vicinity of the final. (Paribhāṣā 103)
The meaning is that when both a root-initial [nasal] and a non-root-initial [nasal] are simultaneously applicable in a single application, it is the non-root-initial [nasal] that applies.

Otherwise, if [the rule applied] to the beginning of a verbal root (*dhātu*), then *natva* (the substitution of *n*) and *satva* (the substitution of *s*) would occur only in forms such as *anetā* and *asotā*, but not in forms such as *namati* and *siñcati*.
Furthermore, "the final modification" (*antyavikāra*) is an indicative mark (*liṅga*).
That which has the same position as the final [element] is "co-located with the final" (*antyasa-deśa*).
This status is to be understood as existing between the final phoneme and the phoneme [undergoing the modification] when there is no intervention by any other [phoneme].

For this very reason, the rule "na samprasāraṇe" (P. 6.1.37) is purposefully stated for the sake of forms such as *viddha*. Furthermore, the non-application of rules such as "allopo 'naḥ" (P. 6.4.134) in cases like *anastakṣṇā*—where the initial sound is not the letter *a*—is also a result of this [interpretation]. This is because the meaning "the elision of the vowel *a* belonging to an *aṅga* ending in *an*, when followed by a suffix beginning with *yaj* etc. or *sva* etc. is more appropriate from the perspective of the *aṅga* itself, since the expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) regarding the suffix arises specifically within the domain of the *aṅga*. Thus, it refers to the *aṅga* as a whole.

This [paribhāṣā] is more appropriate than resorting to various cumbersome assumptions in multiple places—such as [the assumption that] the *an* [augment] follows what begins with *yaj* and so on—because this [interpretation] is more fitting.
Nor should one be misled by the thought that this [paribhāṣā] was rejected in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra “*ṣyaṅaḥ saṃprasāraṇam*” (P. 6.1.13);

for even after demonstrating that the results stated in the Vārttika can be established otherwise through various cumbersome assumptions, there remain those specific purposes which this paribhāṣā serves.
For that purpose, this [rite] must be performed; the counteracting of defects is established by the mention of "counter-measures" (pratividhāna) in the concluding statement.
And its purpose is expressed by the word "desiring to cleanse" (mimārjiṣati).

In that case, since reduplication (*dvitva*) is internal (*antaraṅga*) prior to the application of *vṛddhi*, and since the operations concerning the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsakārya*) apply subsequently (*paratva*), it is necessary [to state the prohibition] in order to prevent *vṛddhi* from applying to the vowel *i* of the reduplicated syllable. Nor can the desired result be achieved by the subsequent shortening of the reduplicated syllable after *vṛddhi* has occurred, because of the maxim "that which has already operated upon a particular object does not operate again upon that same object" (*lakṣye lakṣaṇasya*). Thus, the rule is required.
As for what was stated in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra “na samprasāraṇe” — namely, “there are no purposes for this paribhāṣā in this sūtra”—
its meaning is this:
there are no purposes for this paribhāṣā within the scope of this particular sūtra.
"Because in [the derivation of] *vyadha* and so forth, there is an absence of *samāna-ādeśa* and *yaṇ*. The reading "these are not its purposes" is also seen in some places.
This is indeed based on explicit scriptural authority (*vācanikī*).

And this is clear from the Bhāṣya on the sūtra "ṣyaṅaḥ" and on the sūtra "adaso 'seḥ," by means of the statement "some [hold that it applies] to that which is in the vicinity of the final letter"; the details are found elsewhere.

Now, one might object: since the rule "avyaktānukaraṇasyātaḥ" prescribes the substitution of the subsequent form (pararūpa), in cases such as *paṭat* and *paṭiti*, the rule "alontyasya" would instead apply to the final letter; therefore, he says:
When a suffix is devoid of meaning (anarthaka), the rule regarding the final letter does not apply, except in the case of a modification of the reduplicative syllable (anabhyāsavikāra).
When "non-repetition" (anabhyāsa) is stated, as in the case of "avibharti" and so forth, by the rule "bhṛñām it," [the substitution] applies only to the final [consonant].
Repetition is meaningless because there is an absence of meaningful function.
However, it has been established elsewhere that only the subsequent portion (the *uttarakhaṇḍa*) is meaningful;

this is clear from the *Bhāṣya* on the sūtra "al-antyāt" [Pāṇini 1.1.52]. Furthermore, since the [opponent's] arguments regarding the results being otherwise established have been refuted, let this be understood from that very source.

But surely, in cases such as *brāhmaṇavatsā ca brāhmaṇīvatsaśca* ("the daughter of a Brāhmaṇa and the son of a Brāhmaṇa"), the rule *pumān striyā* (Pāṇini 1.2.67) would entail a single-remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) compound, because there is no distinction created by anything other than femininity and masculinity; therefore, he says: "Between the principal and the non-principal, the grammatical operation applies to the principal. (Paribhāṣā 105)
Therefore, there is no fault, because there exists a distinction created by non-primary femininity and masculinity that is distinct from primary femininity and masculinity.
This is clear from the Bhāṣya on the two rules "napuṃsakamanapuṃsakena" [Pāṇini 1.2.69] and "napuṃsakam napuṃsakena... [Pāṇini 1.2.70].

Furthermore, it is stated in the Bhāṣya and Kaiyaṭa’s commentary on the rule "hetumati ca" [Pāṇini 3.1.26]: "The primary factor is more powerful than even that which is internal (antaraṅga) or that upon which one depends."

But would not the prohibition of the suffix *ṅīp* for the word *mātṛ*, which is occasioned by its being listed among [the words] beginning with *svasṛ*, also apply to the word *mātṛ* when it denotes "one who measures"?
To this, he says:
"The conventional meaning of a whole is stronger than the etymological meaning of its parts. (Paribhāṣā 106)

Therefore, only that which denotes the [object] by its pure conventional meaning (*rūḍha*) is to be understood, not that which denotes the cognizer. The principle that "in the cognition born of etymological derivation (*yogaja*), the presentation of that which is denoted by a pure conventional term unaccompanied by such [etymological] connection acts as an obstacle" is itself the seed of this [distinction]. This is established through linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*).
This point is established by the principle of the *rathakāra* section.
However, some maintain that in the rule *dīdhīvevīṭām*, by means of this paribhāṣā, there is the inclusion of only *dīdhī* and *vevīṅ*,
and not *dīṅ*, *dhīṅ*, and *veñ*.
Regarding the word "vīnām," that is not so; for if that were the case, one would simply have said "div-vidhī-vītām," according to others.
Now, since the substitution of *avaṅ* for *go* before *akṣa* is optional, would not forms such as *gokṣaḥ* also occur in the sense of a window (*vātāyana*)? To this, he says:
"Grammatical operations are also carried out by means of a restricted optionality (*vyavasthitavibhāṣā*). (Paribhāṣā 107)
The systematic arrangement [of grammatical rules] should be understood according to the specific instances [they govern].
This is clear in the *Mahābhāṣya* on the sūtra "śācchoḥ" as well as on the sūtras beginning with "laṭaḥ śatṛ".
When both an injunction (vidhi) and a restrictive rule (niyama) are possible, the injunction alone is superior. (Paribhāṣā 108)

For in a restrictive rule (*niyama*), since the exclusion of others is not explicitly stated, its conceptualization would have to be inferred through implication (*sāmarthya*), which incurs the fault of restating what has already been said; therefore, for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*), it should be understood that it is indeed an injunction (*vidhi*).
This is clear in the *Bhāṣya* on the rules "yasya halaḥ" and "ijādeḥ sanumaḥ," etc.
Now, one might object that by the rule “āśaṃsāyāṃ bhūtavacca,” there would be an extension (atideśa) of both the *laṅ* and *liṭ* tenses just as there is for the *luṅ*; therefore, he says:
"When there is an extension of a general category, there is no extension of its specific instances. (Paribhāṣā 109)
The absence of the causal complex that necessarily brings about the presentation of a specific [meaning] at the time of the presentation of the general is the seed of this [rule].
Therefore, there is no extension (*atideśa*) of those two [suffixes] which are prescribed for a specific form of the immediate past (*anadyatana-bhūta*).
This [rule] is non-eternal (*anitya*).
This is because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the rule *na lyapi*;
thus, by that rule *sthānivad ādeśaḥ*, there is also the extension of specific properties.
All of this is clear in the *Bhāṣya* on the *sthānivat* sūtra.
But would not the rule "titsvaritam" (Pāṇini 6.1.185) cause the circumflex accent (*svarita*) to apply in cases such as *cikīrṣati*? To this he says:
"Between a suffix and a non-suffix, the suffix is to be understood. (Paribhāṣā 110).
And this [rule] is cited in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra "aṅgasya"; furthermore,
it is clear from Kaiyaṭa on that very passage that it does not apply when there is the mention of a phoneme (varṇa).
For this very reason, in the rules *sanāśabhikṣa uḥ* and *vale*, there is the inclusion of the suffixes *san* and *val*.
However, Kaiyaṭa has stated that in the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the rule *titsvaritam*, this paribhāṣā is nowhere relied upon for the purpose of refining the linguistic forms (*lakṣyasaṃskārāya*).
Furthermore, in the commentary on the rule *aṅgasya*, this paribhāṣā was stated by a partisan (*ekadeśin*) for the sake of refuting that [interpretation].

For this very reason, the author of the Vārttika stated, "The mention of the term *pratyaya* (suffix) must be made [in the rule]," and based on the explanation of the two aforementioned sūtras, they say that only the two suffixes are to be understood as being included.

Now, one might object: since the rule "viparābhyāṃ jeḥ" prescribes the Ātmanepada [ending], it would undesirably apply to the sentence "parājayati senā" (he causes the army to be defeated), which has the meaning "the army defeats [the enemy]"; therefore, he says:
"Between that which is accompanied by [another word] and that which is not, only that which is accompanied is taken. (Paribhāṣā 111).
In that regard, it is clearly stated in the Bhāṣya itself that, due to the association with the word *vi*, only the preposition *parā* is understood;
for association occurs only between two similar things, and thus by the term "associated" (*sahacarita*), that which possesses similarity is expressed.
Even in cases such as "Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa," similarity alone is the determining factor.
Furthermore, this follows from the general rule that there is a desire to express two things together only when they are similar, and their joint usage occurs only in such cases;
this has been indicated in the *Bhāṣya* on the sūtra “The second case ending is used after a word joined with a *karmapravacanīya*.”

For in that context, having raised the objection regarding the use of the ablative case by the rule *pañcamy apāṅparibhiḥ*—which prescribes the ablative when *pari* is used as an indicator of a limit (*lakṣaṇa*) and so forth—it is stated: "Although this *pari* is observed to have various applications, both in the sense of exclusion (*varjana*) and non-exclusion (*avarjana*), this [specific] *pari* is an incorrect word (*apaśabda*) in that it is a *karmapravacanīya* used solely for the purpose of exclusion; what other [word] could possibly be its companion, since there is no other [term] with the meaning of exclusion?"
It has been said: "Just as when one needs a cow for assistance, only a cow is brought,
and not a horse, nor a donkey."
Therefore, the status of being an auxiliary (*sahāyabhāva*) is precluded when only similar elements are employed.

Since the meaning of "kṛtvas" (times) would already be understood through association (*sāhacarya*) in the rule *dvistriścatur* (Pāṇini 8.3.43), the explicit mention of "the meaning of kṛtvas" indicates that this [association] is not universally obligatory (*anitya*).
Consequently, in the rule *dīdhīvevīṭām* (Pāṇini 1.1.6), the augment *iṭ* is included despite its lack of association with verbal roots (*dhātu*); this is explained in detail elsewhere.

But would this not mean that the *anaṅ* replacement [for the final syllable] in *asthi* would not apply in the case of *priyasakthanā brāhmaṇena*, because the *aṅga* (the nominal stem) lacks neuter gender? To this, he says:
"Between a directly stated [connection] and an inferred one, the directly stated connection is stronger. (Paribhāṣā 112)
The connection is with that which is explicitly stated (śruta), not with that which is inferred or obtained through context (prakaraṇa) and so forth;
the sense is that direct statement is more powerful than context and the like.

And thus, in that context, the gender marker (*liṅga*) is a qualifier of the *asthi* and so forth alone, not of the *aṅga*; however, in the rules for *śi*, *luK*, and *num*, because the [gender marker] is not being directly mentioned, it is a qualifier of the *aṅga* obtained through the governing context (*prakaraṇa*). For this very reason, in the rule “vā napuṃsakasya,” [the author] did not say “vā śau.”

In this context, the mention of the neuter gender is for the purpose that the rule should apply only when the present participle ending in *śatṛ* (*śatṛ-anta*) itself is neuter— so that it does not apply in cases such as "those families in which there are many who give" (*bahavo dadato yeṣu tāni kulāni bahudadati*),
whereas it should apply in cases such as "those [families] in which many give" (*bahūni dadanti yeṣu te bahudadantaḥ*).
This is clear from the Bhāṣya on the rule *svamornapuṃsakāt*.

However, some say that this is an example where the status of being an effect (*kāryitva*), which is inferred because the letter *r* is included among the *yaṇ*s, is sublated by its status as a cause (*nimitta*) as heard in the rule *aco rahābhyaṃ dve*;
but that is not so, for the point is established by the maxim of the curd and Kauṇḍinya. A detailed discussion of this may be found elsewhere.
But would not the accent prescribed by the rule "tatpuruṣe tulyārthaḥ" apply in cases such as *parameṇa*, *kārakeṇa*, and *paramakārakeṇa*?

Likewise, by the rule "gāti-sthā-ghu-pā-bhū-bhyaḥ," there is elision [of the suffix]. Since the root *pā* (in the sense of "remaining") has undergone the change of *o* to *ā*, the elision might apply even to a subsequent [suffix]. Therefore, he says:
"Between that which is taught by a general rule and that which is taught as a specific word, only that which is taught as a specific word is to be understood. (Paribhāṣā 113)

For a compound and so forth, which is prescribed by restating specific case-endings and the like, is called *pratipadokta* (expressed by its own specific form); that alone is to be understood here, because it presents itself most rapidly.
For the second [type of word] has a delayed presentation;
the form *pā* for the word *pai* is one whose presentation is delayed by means of a prior investigation into its grammatical derivation (*lakṣaṇānusandhāna*).
However, for the root *pibati*, that [form] is more rapidly presented;
for this indeed is the seed of this technical rule (*paribhāṣā*). This has been established even in the case of the mention of phonemes, as it was applied in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra "ot".

As for the claim that this [substitution] does not apply when the phoneme (*varṇa*) is being grasped because of the inclusion of the term "upadeśa" in the rule *ādeca upadeśe* (Pāṇini 6.1.45), that has been refuted in the *Śabdenduśekhara* on that very sūtra and should be consulted there.

Furthermore, this [substitution] is non-eternal (*anitya*), as indicated by the inclusion of the term "mahāvyāhṛti" in the rule *bhuvaśca mahāvyāhṛteḥ* (Pāṇini 6.3.98); the details of this are explained elsewhere.
But in that case, the designation *ghu* would not apply to the roots *dāṅ* and *dodhā* when they have undergone *ātvā* (the substitution of *ā*);
likewise, when *meṅ* undergoes *ātvā*, as in *apraṇimātā* and so forth, the substitution of *ṇ* [for *n*] by the rule “*nergadanada*” would not occur;
and similarly, when *gai* undergoes *ātvā*, the substitution of *ī* by the rule “*ghumāsthā*” would not occur. Therefore, he says:
In the rules concerning the taking of *gām-ādi* [words], there is no distinction.
And here, the evidence is the *pit* designation of the root *daip*.
For that is intended for the purpose of including it in the general term *adāp*;

otherwise, since its inclusion in the positive rule would already be established by its being defined by a technical rule (*lākṣaṇika*), what would be the use of the *pit* designation in the negative rule for the sake of including it in the general term?
And by means of this partial approval, the complete *paribhāṣā* is indicated.
This [rule] sublates the *lakṣaṇapratipadokta-paribhāṣā*, the *niranubandhaka-paribhāṣā*, and the *lugvikaraṇa-paribhāṣā*.
It is clearly stated in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule "dādhā ghu."
In the sūtra "gāti-sthā-," only the form *gā*, which is a substitute for the root *iṇ*, is intended; thus there is no fault, as is explained in detail elsewhere.
The completion of the sentence applies to each [word] individually. (Paribhāṣā 115)
It is like the verb "to eat" in the sentence, "Let Devadatta and others be fed."
[Objection: "In that case, would the designations *saṃyoga*, *saṃjñāsamāsa*, and *abhyasta* also apply to each individual [element]? [Response: He says:
"In some cases, they apply even to a collection (*samudāya*). (Paribhāṣā 116)

Just as in such cases as "Let a hundred Gargas be fined" or "Kings are not [merely] seekers of gold," the grammatical rule is established in accordance with the usage of the linguistic examples (*lakṣya*).

Now, an objection: in the rule *yū strīyākhyau*, if the view that words denote individuals (*vyaktipakṣa*) is adopted, then because of the mention of the long vowels (*dīrgha*), they would not be included by the *grāhaka-sūtra* (P. 1.1.69) due to their not being *aṇ*. Consequently, if any one of the accents such as udātta were uttered, a word possessing a different accent would not receive the technical designation (*saṃjñā*).
To this, he says:
"The qualities (*guṇa*) do not differentiate [the phoneme]. (Paribhāṣā 117).
The meaning is that when there is no effort [to distinguish], a quality uttered in its own form is not a differentiator, nor is it intended; however,
it should be understood that this has no utility in the case of the *jāti* (universal) view.
In cases such as "yū" and so forth, there is no deficiency because the reference is to a genus (jāti) residing in long vowels alone; this is explained in detail elsewhere.

[Objection: Even if the absence of *ṇatva* (the substitution of *ṇ* for *n*) is prescribed by the rule "sarvanāmāni," would not the usage with *ṇatva* still be considered correct in common worldly usage? To this, he says:
"Prescriptive exceptions (*nipātana*) are indeed [only] sublatives. (Paribhāṣā 118)
Because the formation of a nipātana (irregular derivation) begins only when a specific grammatical operation has not otherwise been obtained.

Although it might follow that the word *purātana* is barred by the word *purāṇa* as it is specifically prescribed in the rule "purāṇaprokteṣu," it should be understood that this is not the case because *purātana* belongs to the class of words beginning with *pṛṣodara*.
Others hold that both *purāṇa* and *purātana* belong to the *pṛṣodarādi* group.

This is clear from the commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the *sarvādi* sūtra. Nor should it be argued that, since forms such as *asthyā-* would otherwise have an acute accent on the first syllable by the rule “*nabviṣayasya*” (P. 6.1.173), the substitution *anaṅ*—which must be pronounced with an anudātta tone corresponding to its original (*sthānin*)—is instead pronounced with an udātta for the sake of specific intention (*vivakṣā*), and therefore how can this [the udātta pronunciation] serve as an indicator (*jñāpaka*)?

Because there is no evidence for intending [the preservation of] even the quality of being udātta by means of *sthānivadbhāva* in the case of the word *paramāsthi*, which ends in an *ā*-suffix and has an udātta accent;
for it will be stated that "the substitution of *catasṛ* is an enunciation with an initial udātta," and "the substitution of *vadh* is an enunciation with an initial udātta."

The Bhāṣya passage beginning with “*padādayaḥ* are prescribed as having the acute accent on the final syllable, and *sa-* is prescribed as the acute substitute for *saha-*, etc. is intended on the grounds that, although the Aṣṭādhyāyī is recited in monotone (*ekaśruti*), the occasional utterance of accents such as the acute is for the purpose of indicating specific intention (*vivakṣā*).
Regarding the view that "the recitation is in three accents," Kaiyata and others maintain that the Bhāṣya is intended as an indicator (*jñāpaka*).
Others, however, hold that what is called "irregular formation" (*nipātana*) consists in employing a different usage when another usage would have been expected;
through the deliberate effort toward those specific forms, there arises the intention to express the acute accent (*udātta*) and so forth in each respective instance.

In the case of the form *tisṛcatasṛ*, where an antodātta (accent on the final syllable) would have been pronounced due to its being a *dvandva* compound, an ādyudātta (accent on the first syllable) is instead uttered. Elsewhere, when a specific accent belonging to the substitute (*sthānin*) is to be pronounced, that particular pronunciation is intended for the sake of indicating a specific meaning (*vivakṣārtha*).
From the Bhāṣya on the rule *sici vṛddhiḥ*, it is understood that in this instance there is no difference in the observed form (*lakṣyabheda*) caused by such a modification.

And here, in rules such as *asthidadhi*, since the substitution of *anaṅ* and so forth is already established by their being pronounced with an udātta accent, the explicit mention of "udātta" serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*).

By the statement that [a term] is pronounced in its own form (*svarūpeṇa*), when terms such as "udātta-ādi" are uttered, there is an intention (*vivakṣā*) to refer to those [elements] beginning with udātta, such as in the rule *anudāttāder antodāttāt*.

In the rule *uña oṃ*, although the non-nasalized (*ananunāsika*) form should have been pronounced, the fact that the nasalized (*anunāsika*) form is pronounced with extra effort makes it clear that this [nasalized form] is intended.

In examples such as *pathimathyṛbhukṣām*, although a nasalized vowel should have been pronounced in accordance with the substituend, the fact that a non-nasalized vowel is pronounced indicates that this was not intended.
It is for this very reason that it was stated [by Patañjali] that "there is no effort [to prevent it].
However, the claim that "nipātanas (irregular forms) do not constitute exceptions" is contrary to the Bhāṣya.

Now, if the *uk* vowel were double, since it would be short by its very nature, the shortening of the reduplicated syllable (*abhyāsa-hrasva*) would not apply initially; subsequently, after the application of *halādiḥ śeṣaḥ* and the lengthening of homogeneous vowels (*savarṇa-dīrgha*), the occurrence of a short vowel would follow. To this, he says: "The operation of grammatical rules proceeds like a rain-cloud" (Paribhāṣā 119).

And thus, even when a short vowel has already been shortened, no further shortening occurs by virtue of the maxim "once a grammatical operation has been applied to that which is no longer its target, it does not apply again.
This is stated in the Bhāṣya on the rule *iko jhal*: "The science indeed acts upon what has already been done, like a rain-cloud.
The meaning is that the domain of the shortening rule remains established.
Nor should it be argued that there is no authority for the principle that "the application of a grammatical rule to its subject occurs only once";

for the very rule *samaḥ suṭi* serves as such authority, since by means of the elision (*lopa*) prescribed in *samovā lopameke*, one *s* is dropped, the remaining single *s* undergoes doubling, and that resulting double *s* undergoes doubling again to establish the form with three *s*s.
Furthermore, this has been clearly stated in the *Bhāṣya* regarding rules such as *samprasāraṇācca* and *sici vṛddhiḥ*.
There is no evidence that the Teacher recited the entire Aṣṭādhyāyī in a single monotone (ekaśruti).
In some instances, even a word is recited in a single monotone, as for example, "aikṣvāka" in the sūtra beginning with "dāṇḍināyana."
Although students recite the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*) with a single monotone (*ekaśruti*), like the Veda itself,

they nevertheless maintain that knowledge of [phonetic details] such as the occurrence of acute accents (*udātta-nipātana*) is derived from the commentaries (*vyākhyāna*), just as [knowledge of] nasalization (*anunāsikatva*) and so forth is.

However, regarding the elements to be prescribed (*vidheya*), because of the prohibition "not a suffix" (*apratyayaḥ*), there is no inclusion of homogeneous sounds (*savarṇa-grahaṇa*) on the grounds that [the accent] does not differentiate the quality (*guṇābhedakatva*).
For this very reason, in examples such as *ghaṭavat*, the letter *v* in the suffix *mat* does not become nasalized.
For this same reason, there is the formulation of the rule: *tadvān āsām*.
Otherwise, by the rule *pratyaye bhāṣāyām*, the nasalization would be obligatory.
Thus, there is a detailed explanation elsewhere.

Now, an objection may be raised: since the root *syand* (as in *syantsyati*, etc. lacks the conditions for the Ātmanepada, the prohibition [of *iṭ*] by the rule "na vṛdbhyaścaturbhyaḥ" is considered *bahiraṅga*. Consequently, because it is *antaraṅga*, there would result the optional application of *iṭ* conditioned by the marker *ūṭ*. To this, he says: "And prohibitions are more powerful" (Paribhāṣā 120).
The meaning is that [these rules] are stronger than even those that are internal (*antaraṅga*) or dependent (*upajīvya*).
The mention of "from four" (*caturbhyaḥ*), however, is for the sake of clarity alone;
for this very reason, the rejection of that [rule] stated in the *Bhāṣya* is consistent.
For this very reason, there is no optionality regarding the prohibition of the designation *savarṇa* (homogeneous) and so forth.

Otherwise, according to the Mīmāṃsā method, since a positive injunction (*vidhi*) is stronger as it is that upon which a prohibition depends, its total sublation would be untenable; thus, such an optionality would be unavoidable. This is explained in detail in the *Mañjūṣā*. For this same reason, the rules "in a *dvandva* compound" (*dvandve ca*) and "optionally before the suffix *jas*" (*vibhāṣā jasi*) become meaningful.
The application [of this rule] for the purpose of uprooting [the application of] the *vidhi* (prescriptive rule) is its seed.
This is clear from the Bhāṣya on the two rules: *na lumatā* and *kamerṇiṅ*.

But surely, for those suffixes that are purely self-referential (*atyantasvārthika*), it is untenable for them to possess the status of a suffix (*pratyayatva*), which consists in conveying meaning; therefore, he says:
"Suffixes whose meaning is not specifically prescribed [convey] their own referent. (Paribhāṣā 121)
Since it is also accepted that "that whose meaning is conveyed by its own base (prakṛti) is also a suffix (pratyaya)," there is no fault in its being a suffix.
The phrase "its own meaning" means "the meaning of its own base."
The seed of this [concept] is that, due to the power of a great conceptualization (*mahāsaṃjñā*), when there is a desire for an object, nothing else presents itself;
this is clear in the Bhāṣya on the sūtras beginning with *supi sthaḥ*.
The desired result is established through the division of the rule (yogavibhāga). (Paribhāṣā 122)
The meaning is that this results in the very establishment of what is desired, rather than the production of an unintended consequence (aniṣṭāpādana).
The basis for this is the indication of the non-eternality of that which has been divided by its connection with a second [element] under the same rule (*samānavidhi*).
In the case of synonymous terms, consideration for their relative brevity or prolixity is not observed.
This is indicated by the instruction in the Sūtra: "In each such case, optionally [one of the two alternatives applies], or it is a *vibhāṣā*."
That which is established by an indicator (jñāpaka) does not apply everywhere. (Paribhāṣā 124)
The meaning is that although [the rule] should have been stated explicitly, it is taught through inference for the sake of showing that it is not universally applicable (*asārvatrika*).
Therefore, the intended sense is that one should not raise undesirable consequences (*aniṣṭa*) regarding the technical rules (*paribhāṣā*) established by such indicative evidence (*jñāpaka*).
This has also been indicated in the *Bhāṣya* on the sūtra beginning with "ṅy-āp" and others.

The term "jñāpaka" (indicative) is also an elliptical expression for "nyāya" (logical principle). The intention is that the mention of certain [rules] established by both logical principles and indicatives serves to demonstrate that others are non-eternal (*anitya*).

For example, the rule *sthānivat* ("that which takes the place of another is like the original") is established by the logical principle: "That which occupies the position of something acquires its properties."
And in that regard, it is established by an indicator (jñāpaka) in the rule "analvidhau."

But surely, in cases such as *drogdhā*, *drogdhā*, *droḍhā*, and *droḍhā*, since the substitution of *gh* and so forth would be considered *asiddha*, there would arise the undesirable consequence that doubling occurs first, resulting in *gh* in one instance and *ḍh* in the other; therefore, he says:
That which is not established in what precedes [is considered asiddha] except in the case of doubling.

The meaning is that when a preceding operation is to be performed which is distinct from duality, the subsequent [operation] is already established (*paramasiddha*). The indicator (*liṅga*) for this is the rule established by the governing heading (*adhikāra*), namely, "that which is not established in what precedes" (*pūrvatrāsiddham*). And where there is a difference in the result between being established and not being established, [this rule applies].

In that very context, regarding examples such as *kṛṣṇarddhiḥ*, this [rule] does not apply because there is no difference in form whether doubling occurs before or after the substitution of the voiced unaspirated stop (*jaśtva*). This is explained in detail elsewhere; it is made clear in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *sarvasya dve*.

[Objection: But surely, just as one says "the owner of cows and horses" (*goṣvaśveṣu ca svāmī*), one could also say "the owner of cows and of horses" (*goṣvaśvānāṃ ca svāmī*), because the rule *svāmīśvara* prescribes the use of both the genitive and the locative cases; therefore, he says: "When a usage has been established for one form (*ākṛti*), it will not apply to a second or a third. (Paribhāṣā 126)
This maxim applies where there is the possibility of a difference in meaning due to the employment of another verbal root;
this is explained in detail in the *Bhāṣya* on the sūtra "kṛñ cānuprayujyate" (Pāṇini 3.1.40).
But would not, in forms such as *vivyādha*, the substitution of semivowels (*samprasāraṇa*) for *va* occur by virtue of its higher status after the application of *halādiḥ śeṣaḥ*? To this, he says:
"The substitution of semivowels (*samprasāraṇa*) and the operation dependent upon it are stronger. (Paribhāṣā 127)
The *pūrvarūpa* (single-substitute replacement) [of the semivowel] by the rule "and after a *samprasāraṇa*" (*samprasāraṇācca*) is based on that [substitution].

In reality, however, this [mention of the rule] is redundant; for the inclusion of "both" (*ubhayeṣām*) in the sūtra "in the case of the reduplication in the *liṭ*" (*liṭyabhyāsasya*) has the purpose of ensuring that for both [classes of roots], only the *samprasāraṇa* occurs.
This is clear from the *Bhāṣya* on the sūtra "in the case of the reduplication in the *liṭ*."
The alternative proof for a different result (*phalāntarānyathāsiddhi*) is also clearly stated in that very Bhāṣya:
"In rules such as *ṇau ca saṃścaṅoḥ*, the phrase *saṃścaṅoḥ* and so forth is a locative of occasion (*viṣayasaptamī*); thus, there is no fault even in that case," as explained at length elsewhere.
As for the statement:
"In some cases, a modification takes on the properties of its original base" (Paribhāṣā 128).
Therefore, by the inclusion of the term *hva* in the rule “*ni-sam-upa-vibhyaḥ hvaḥ*,” the inclusion of the root *hveñ* is established.
Likewise—of the *aupadeśika* (original) and the *prāyogika* (derived), the *aupadeśika* is to be taken. (Paribhāṣā 129)
Therefore, the claim that in the rule "dāder dhātoḥ" only a root taught in the original instruction (aupadeśika) is understood—
that is not correct; for those two [interpretations] lack a foundation and are not employed in the Bhāṣya.

Furthermore, because the first [view] is rejected by the Bhāṣya on the rule *grahijyā* (Pāṇini 6.1.16), which states: "A modification does not take on the properties of its original form" (*na ca vikṛtiḥ prakṛtiṃ gṛhṇāti*).
In rules such as *ni-sam-upa-vi-bhyaḥ hvaḥ* (Pāṇini 1.3.30), the root used is *hveñ*;
the usage of *hvayati* in the Sūtra is an archaic (sautra) employment for the sake of phonetic imitation (*anukaraṇe*).

Others maintain that the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs only in the domain of *ātv* (the substitution of *ā* for *e*); this is because it is clearly stated in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule concerning the technical designation *ghu* that the grammatical name *ghu* applies only to those forms as they actually occur in usage, and not to their phonetic imitation (*anukaraṇa*).
Furthermore, even this latter view is unacceptable to both the author of the *Sūtras* and the author of the *Vārttikas*, since they employ the term "instruction" (*upadeśa*) in various places.
For in this grammar, in all instances where there is a mention of a form accompanied by an *anubandha*, the actual form itself is relied upon—namely, "wherein this form occurs.

And the apprehension of the form of a word does not occur without worldly usage; and since in that worldly usage there is no employment of forms with *anubandhas*, a second [non-technical] usage is resorted to.

The statement "What is meant by 'instruction' (upadeśa)? found in the Bhāṣya on the rule defining the technical term *ghu* establishes that the term refers to [the form] when it is not possible for it to be used in actual linguistic practice (*prāyogika*). Furthermore, this view is not supported by the Bhāṣya;
rather, in the Bhāṣya, the phrase "that which possesses an indicatory letter" (*sānubandhaka*) and so forth is intended with reference to the specific subject matter at hand.

In the rule *dāder dhātoḥ*, there is no fault because the word *dādi-* is understood through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) to mean "that which possesses the status of beginning with *da* as taught in the instruction. This is explained in detail elsewhere.
Now, one might object: "In forms such as *ajarghā* and *bebhidīti*, the verbal suffixes (*vikaraṇas*) would apply even when there is *yaṅ*-elision due to the respective qualities [of the roots];
likewise, in *yaṅ*-elided forms such as *bebhiditā*, the prohibition of *iṭ* by the rule *ekāca upadeśe'nudāttāt* would apply. To this, he says:
"That which is indicated by *śtip*, by *śap*, by an indicatory letter (*anubandha*), or by a class-name (*gaṇa*),"...
And where there is the mention of "ekāc" (monosyllabic), these five [rules] do not apply when the suffix yaṅluk is present.
The specification of the suffixal augment (anubandha) is twofold: by its own form and by means of a word such as "having an indicatory *ṅ*" (*aṅitaḥ*). [Examples are: *hanti*, *yāti*, *vāti*.
In the sūtra *sanīvanta*... [the form] *bhareti* is an example; likewise, *dīṅo yuḍ aci*, *anudātta ṅitaḥ*, *divādibhyaḥ śyan*, and *ekāca upadeśe* are examples.
Furthermore, by the rule *sanādyantāḥ*, there is reduplication, and by *bhūvādayaḥ*, it indeed possesses the status of a verbal root (*dhātutva*).
This is because, by means of rules such as *guṇo yaṅ-lukoḥ*, one assumes the non-universality (*anityatva*) of the prohibition;
consequently, the substitution of *bhaṣ* also occurs in forms such as *ajarghāḥ*.
For this very reason, in the commentary of Kaiyaṭa on the sūtra *śvoditaḥ*, the reading is: "In some cases, there is the mention of a single vowel (*ekāj-grahaṇam*)."

By the inclusion of the term *ekāj* (a single-vowel root) in the rule *ekāca upadeśe ’nudāttāt*, this [fact] is indicated through the principle of partial acceptance (*ekadeśānumati*). Otherwise, since a root consisting of more than one vowel (*anekāj*) would necessarily be unaccented (*anudātta*) in its original enunciation (*upadeśa*), the inclusion of that term would clearly be redundant.
That too is not correct, because it is not stated in the Bhāṣya;
and furthermore, because the mention of "ekāj" (a single vowel) is necessary for the purpose of excluding the root *vadh*.
Nor can it be argued that the original form (*sthānin*) of *vadh* is taught as having only a single vowel.

Because it is possible for there to be a direct instruction (upadeśa) regarding this subject, the original form (*sthānin*) is not understood as being "taught" (*upadeśa*); furthermore, the meaning is that the term *ekāj* applies to whatever is delimited by the quality of being taught (*upadeśatva*).
Moreover, the mention of *ekāj* is for the sake of what follows.

For this very reason, in examples such as *jāgaritavān*, the prohibition of *iṭ* by the rule "śryukaḥ kiti" does not apply, because [the condition] of being taught with a final *u* (*ugantatvam*) is taken into account.
It is clear in the *Akara* (the *Mahābhāṣya*) that the term "in the upadeśa" (*upadeśe*) is understood there for the purpose of prohibiting *iṭ* in cases such as *stīrṇam*.

Nor can it be argued that, according to the *Bhāṣya*, in order to allow the application of *iṭ* in forms like *bebiditā*—where the *yaṅ* suffix is elided—the meaning of the rule must be restricted to "from a monosyllabic root that is unaccented and actually heard in the *upadeśa*," and that consequently, a prohibition of *iṭ* in the *san* suffix must be stated.
The statement "he wishes to break" (*bibhitsati*) is intended as an illustration of the faults [in the rule], just like the presentation of faults regarding the *yaṅ*-lopa;
however, the Bhāṣya passage beginning with "in the case of *yaṅ*-lopa," etc., does not concern the *yaṅ*-lopa specifically, due to the force of its opening and concluding remarks.

Furthermore, if that [Bhāṣya] were indeed concerned with that [subject], it would have to be said that there is an omission, because while the status of being a *sthānivadbhāva* is shown for *yaṅ*-lopa, no means [to achieve it] is demonstrated for *yaṅ*-lopa.

In the case of *iḍ* in the context of the *yaṅluk* formation, there is no fault because such forms are not expressed in common usage (*anabhidhāna*), and because all rules are optional in the Vedic language (*chandasi*), whereby no objection can be raised against them.

Otherwise, the question in the Bhāṣya—"What is the purpose of the mention of *ekāj*?"—and its answer—"It is for the sake of *jāgarti* later on, and for the sake of *vadhi* here"—would be rendered groundless. Furthermore, the term *ekāj* cannot be a qualifier of the verbal root (*dhātu*) implied by the term *ārdhadhātuka*.

And thus, in forms such as *bibhitsati*, the subsequent portion— the verbal root (*dhātu*)— indeed possesses the property of being monosyllabic (*ekāctva*), just as it possesses existence (*astitva*);
and this is clear from the Bhāṣya on the rule *dayateḥ*.
And it should not be said that there is thus a lack of connection with the present Bhāṣya; for there is no evidence for an objection being raised or for the connection of what has been objected to.
Furthermore, that [the doubling] is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) only when qualified [by the condition of having a single vowel] is clear from the Bhāṣya on the sūtra "ekāco dve" (Pāṇini 6.1.1).
This has been explained in detail in the *Śabdenduśekhara* following the *Nirūpaṇa*.
However, the status of being a verbal root (*dhātutva*) resides only in the latter portion [of the compound].

For this very reason, in the rule *ekāco baśo bhaṣ*, the Bhāṣya states that the purpose of interpreting the term "ekāca" as being in a non-co-referential relationship with "dhātoḥ"—meaning "of a one-vowel [stem] which is a part of a verbal root"—is the derivation of the form *gardabha*.
However, the form *ajarghāḥ* is not established [as such].

In forms such as *ajarghāḥ* and *bebhidīti*, the suffixes *śnam*, *śyan*, and so forth do not occur because, by the inclusion of the term "and the *carkarīta*" in the list of roots beginning with *ad*, the vikaraṇa suffixes prescribed for other classes do not apply to the *yaṅ*-luṅ (reduplicated without *yaṅ*) formation.

Precisely because of its Vedic character (*chāndasatva*), one should understand that even for other grammatical operations, there is an absence of those forms whose usage is not observed in the Veda, despite being seen there.
In the common language (*bhāṣā*), however, such forms simply do not exist at all.

Furthermore, the mention of [suffixes] such as *śtip* and *śnā*—like the mention of them in rules such as "the root *bhū* becomes *a*" (*bhavateraḥ*)—does not establish their actual meaning; this has been explained in detail elsewhere.

Surely, one might object that the rule should simply be formulated as: "The substitution of *ja* for *ha* occurs before a vowel, and also for *radh*, except when followed by *iṭ* in the non-perfect (*aliṭ*)."
To the question, "What is the purpose of including the term *dviradhi*?", he says: "Because of the weight of the word, the division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) is more significant. (Paribhāṣā 131)
The assumption that each individual word conveys a distinct sentence-meaning clearly entails unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*).
However, this view is not accepted by the Bhāṣya;
it is, moreover, contrary to the Bhāṣya on the rule *ṭāṅasi* (Pāṇini 7.1.12).
And regarding that, many hold that the rejection of the vowel *i* in the substitution of *in* was accomplished precisely by means of a split in the rule (*yogavibhāga*).
Grammarians indeed consider the acquisition of even half a mātrā [of linguistic knowledge] to be like a festival celebrating the birth of a son.
This has been indicated by the sound [of the word] in the *bhāṣya* on the two sūtras "eoṅ" and "aiauc.

In that context, regarding a sūtra composed of multiple words, there is generally consideration for the brevity of the words (*padalāghava*) alone, and not consideration for the brevity of the morae (*mātrālāghava*). Thus [says] the *ūkālo*.
This was hinted at in the *Bhāṣya* on the sūtras beginning with *apṛkta ekāl*.

For in that context, during the discussion regarding the distinction between the mention of *al* and the mention of *hal* in those sūtras, it was stated that if the technical term (*saṃjñā*) were used, the mention of *hal* would be required in the sūtra *ṇyakṣatriya* (Pāṇini 2.4.58) as "aṇiñoḥ" [instead of "ataḥ"], resulting in three words in the case of the mention of *al*;
whereas in the case of the mention of *hal*, there is only one word, as in the sūtra *svādilope ṇya* (Pāṇini 6.4.137), where it need not be stated as "aṇiñoḥ."

It has been stated that there is no difference in terms of brevity [between the two formulations], since one must state "of the uncombined" (*apṛktasya*) and thus there are exactly three words [in the rule]. In the sūtra *aci śnu*, although it would have been established by simply saying *iṇaḥ*, the fact that *yv-oh* is used as a condensed (saṃmṛdya) reference shows that the *iṇ* here does not refer to the previous [term *iṇ*]. This is because it is stated in the Bhāṣya on the *laṇ* sūtra that when there is a case-ending indication or a condensed reference, there are three and a half morae (*mātrā*), whereas in the case of the *iṇ* reference, there are three morae.
Likewise, in the rule *otaḥ śyani*, it need not be stated that [the suffix] is *śit*.

Regarding this, Kaiyaṭa states in his commentary on the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *ṣṭhivuklamu*: "In that [context], it need not be said that [the suffix] is *aśit*; thus, there is not only brevity of syllables (*mātrālāghava*), but also this further purpose."
"Generally speaking"—may there be auspiciousness.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Remainder of the Treatise."
Thus ends the Paribhāṣenduśekhara, composed by Nāgojībhaṭṭa, born from the womb of Satī and son of the venerable Mahopādhyāya Śivabhaṭṭa.
